Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:32:53 GMT

Andy Burnham has promised to end decades of government inaction by fixing adult social care in England - and did not rule out tax rises to help pay for it.

The prime minister said it was a "major dereliction of public duty" that successive governments had failed to address the crisis, adding there would be "difficult decisions" on funding but he was determined to "get it right."

His plans include a new national care service, with more pay and better training for care workers, and closer integration with the NHS.

He announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer instead of 2028.

In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms.

"I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"

For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".

But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.

The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.

Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.

He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.

The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".

Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.

The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

On the cross-party talks, Burnham said there has been 22 failed attempts to make progress in almost 30 years.

The PM said: "We're going to have to find common ground here if this is to be a lasting solution."

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed said the first "constructive" discussion had left him feeling "hopeful" and more meetings will be required to find consensus.

He said: "Everyone will have to accept things we might not like in order to work together - but I think that's what the public want and expect us to do."

Sir Ed, who has a disabled son who needs round-the-clock care, said the system "just isn't working" and any solution must have family carers "at its heart".

Reform UK leader -and the party's health spokesman - Nigel Farage said Reform had not been invited to the talks because the government "don't want to hear a fresh, reforming voice".

Asked how a new plan should be funded, Farage said his party would oppose a "death tax" and argued that "efficiencies" could be found that would make social care cheaper.

He also argued that adult social care should be delivered by local councils not "centralised in Whitehall".

Green Party social care spokesperson Ellie Chowns said: "If Andy Burnham is serious about doing things differently and tackling the crisis in care, he must work collaboratively with the Greens and other parties to do so."

Two firefighters die in Crete as wildfires threaten parts of southern Europe

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:23:41 GMT

Two Greek firefighters have died after they became trapped tackling a wildfire that swept through the Rethymno area of Crete.

Gale-force winds whipped up the flames prompting the evacuation of several villages, in the latest summer wildfire to break out in southern Europe.

In southern Turkey, the main Fethiye to Antalya highway had to be closed and part of a hospital evacuated because of a fire in Muğla province.

Meanwhile, a fourth heatwave of the summer has begun in Spain and France, and firefighters are trying to prevent a flare-up from major wildfires that have just been brought under control.

Witnesses said several fires broke out on Crete and spread fast, with the worst fire front extending as far as 15km (9.3 miles). The fire department said the two men who died were working near the western city of Rethymno.

Wildfires have also broken out elsewhere in Greece, on the islands of Paros and Lesbos in the Aegean Sea, and the southern town of Trifylia on the Greek mainland.

In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned the next 12 hours will be "decisive" in putting out a wildfire near the capital Madrid. "Things are progressing favourably, with maximum caution," he told reporters, because of higher temperatures, lower humidity and the risk of gusts of wind.

More than 43,000 hectares (108,000 acres) has already burned at Burgohondo in Ávila province, 150km (93 miles) west of Madrid. It is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history. In total this year more than 207,000 hectares of land have been burned by wildfires in Spain.

One of the team directing firefighting operations, Francisco Bolaños, said that while the fire had not "moved a centimetre during the night", there were concerns it could re-ignite because of the higher temperatures, and the focus was on stabilising a perimeter of 180km (112 miles).

Authorities have allowed thousands of people to return to their homes after restrictions were lifted in the areas of Toledo, Madrid, Ávila, and Castellón.

In the Madrid region alone, 24,000 people have been told they can return and lockdowns on another 20,000 have been lifted.

Among those returning to their homes were about 1,000 residents of the towns of Navas del Rey and Chapinería to the west of Madrid who had been staying in Leganés, a town on the south-west fringe of the capital.

The mayor of Chapinería, Lucía Moya, told Telemadrid that the consequences for the town were very severe and that "many residents have lost their homes and jobs. Getting back on track is going to be an arduous task".

Many of the 2,000 people forced to flee the fires in the nearby Tiétar Valley were looked after by volunteers in the town of Talavera de la Reina, some distance south of the fire.

However, some 300 of the evacuees remained on Wednesday morning and Mayor José Julián Gregorio told Europa Press that they would receive "the same level of care as on the first day".

One fire remains out of control, at Vall d'Uixó north-west of Valencia.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.

In south-west France, the largest fires in the Gironde region are described as "still stabilised" despite several flare-ups, however officials warn of dry winds and temperatures of up to 41C (106F).

The mayor of Le Barp, south-west of Bordeaux, Blandine Sarrazin, warned that the situation was "getting harder", after two fires had broken out the day before, and said everyone had to be "hyper-vigilant".

Flare-ups were also reported not far from Lanton on the eastern shore of the Bay of Arcachon.

Gironde and the Landes are among 16 departments or districts are under orange heatwave alert.

The fire service has had to deploy special measures in Gironde to protect a number of sites linked to France's defence and aerospace industries. The so-called "Seveso" sites include plants that manufacture hazardous materials for missiles and rockets.

Although no fatalities have been reported in the fires surrounding Madrid and in Castellón on the east coast, authorities in the southern city of Seville say a woman, who was badly burned in the Los Gallardos fire in Almería earlier this month, has died of her injuries in hospital.

Fourteen people died in the Almería fires, including UK and Belgian nationals as well as US, French and Spanish citizens.

Fires are also burning in neighbouring Portugal, in the north-eastern district of Vila Real.

Civil protection officials have told public broadcaster RTP there is an active front of a kilometre and they are keeping a close watch on a local water treatment plant and a gas depot near the town of Valpaços.

Serial killer given whole life orders for murdering two men

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:10:40 GMT

Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said.

He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.

Their remains were discovered close to Desborough's woodland cabin near Sticker in Cornwall.

It was while he was on remand charged with their murders that he strangled his cellmate, Steven Kempster, at HMP Exeter.

The judge at Winchester Crown Court said the offences had an exceptionally high level of seriousness and it was rare to impose such a sentence with no chance of parole.

Desborough was also sentenced to five years on each count of preventing the lawful burial of Aquilino and Coleman, who were last seen alive on 18 April 2025 and on 3 June 2025 respectively.

In victim impact statements read out in court, Coleman and Aquilino's families spoke of their anguish imagining the pain and fear the men suffered.

Coleman's brother, Tony Nye, said there "weren't enough words in the English language" to describe the suffering Desborough had caused his family.

"You have taken from this world my big brother in the most disgusting and horrific way," he said.

"The world will see you for the vile degenerate coward you are. There will be no forgiveness for you in this world or the next."

His mother, Sandra Coleman, said: "You took my firstborn son. You destroyed any hope of us coming together as a family.

"You have given me a life sentence of pain, despair, anxiety and hopelessness."

Aquilino's uncle David Bonomi said his nephew was a "friendly, talented artist" who had been killed in a "brutal, cruel and evil manner".

He said the family had reported him missing as it was "very unusual for him not to have been in contact" as he called his mother every day.

Speaking earlier about the review of the four unexplained deaths, Det Supt Rachael Bentley, from Devon and Cornwall Police, said: "As a major crime investigation team we were informed by the coroner's officer for His Majesty's Coroner that there were four deaths at Sandy Lodge.

"As part of the investigation, a detective inspector, separate to the investigation but within major crime, did a review of those deaths, and that included commissioning some more forensic work, some CCTV, and statements."

Inquiries were ongoing and Desborough was "not a suspect at this time", Bentley said.

"We don't believe there is a link at this time, but I said it's an ongoing investigation," she added.

Bentley said police attended each of the deaths at Sandy Lodge and inquiries suggested natural causes but coronial investigations were paused when Desborough was arrested for murder.

Desborough dismembered Coleman and Aquilino's bodies, tried to burn their remains and hid them in woodland in Sticker.

As part of a lengthy search of dense laurel and bogland involving about 100 officers, police found thousands of bone fragments in a stream and body parts in a shallow grave.

Several handwritten notes were also found inside the cabin, including one headed "Bug out list", another "Hostiles" and a diagram labelled "Kill Zone".

Closing the case to the jury, Ahmed Hossain KC, said Desborough was capable of switching to "very serious violence".

Bentley described the killings as "callous and cold-blooded", as "both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend" before he brutally murdered them and "savagely desecrated their bodies".

Desborough killed Kempster in Exeter Prison on 15 September 2025, just three days after they started sharing a cell.

The court heard Desborough was irritated by his cellmate's snoring and returning of unwashed cutlery.

The night before the murder he warned he would kill him if he continued to snore.

Some tech shares are plunging - what does that mean for the AI revolution?

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 15:32:28 GMT

Sharp falls in the value of chip makers have stoked investor concerns that the euphoria around artificial intelligence (AI) related companies is fading.

The AI revolution has promised to reshape the way we work and live and has created vast wealth for investors in a handful of companies predominantly in the US and Asia.

Companies are desperate to be the winners of a transformative technology that many have compared to the advent of the internet, the telephone, even electricity itself.

As Sir Demis Hassabis, founder of UK company Deepmind, which was eventually bought a decade ago by US giant Google, has commented that Artificial Intelligence "cannot be compared to standard technological breakthroughs, not even ones as consequential as the internet or mobile. It is much more akin to the discovery of electricity or fire."

Referring to the fact that many chips are made of silicon, which is essentially sand, he added "we've essentially found a way to make sand think. It's miraculous."

The euphoria for this technology has boosted the value of some world's biggest companies even as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on the building blocks of the technology.

But over the last few weeks, the value of some of the companies that make those building blocks has plummeted - prompting some to question whether what some have dubbed "the AI bubble" is about to burst.

Some of the sharpest falls have been in Asia, with shares in Korean chip makers such as SK Hynix and Samsung down 46% and 35% respectively over the last month as investors worry the recent boom in demand for the chips that power AI is unsustainable.

Yet these shares still are up threefold and fivefold respectively over the last year, leading many to conclude that some caution and profit taking after such massive gains was inevitable – and indeed healthy.

The South Korean stock market is notoriously volatile, but concerns have spilled over into the big US companies.

Shares in Google and Tesla plunged briefly before recovering last week after both firms pledged to spend billions more on AI in the months and years to come despite so far it losing them money.

And with other big names such as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon reporting their latest financial results this week, investors have the opportunity to scrutinise just how much these companies are now betting on AI.

On Wednesday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq ended the trading day about 9% below its June record high, driven down in part by worries over heavy AI spending.

"There is still a healthy degree of scepticism about the ability of these investments to generate a commensurate level of return," Russ Mould, an investment director at AJ Bell, said.

But according to leading tech investor Eileen Burbidge despite the concerns there's not yet a serious reckoning.

"The AI bubble hasn't burst but it's letting out air," she told the BBC.

One of the other triggers for the concerns has been a reported breakthrough in the manufacturing process by a Chinese company, potentially making China more self-sufficient in chip design and production.

That has added to lingering concerns that the big AI companies – Meta, Alphabet, Open AI, Anthropic – will find it hard to charge end users enough to justify the hundreds of billions being spent on buying the chips and building the data centres that power the technology.

As a result, firms that have announced big increases in spending on AI have not always been welcomed with the same enthusiasm by investors.

For example, SpaceX – which is predominantly an AI company - has seen its shares fall 14% from its much-hyped debut on the stock market and nearly 50% from its peak in June.

Apple – which has largely sat out the AI arms race – has seen its shares rise 21% over the last month to reclaim its title as the world's most valuable company from chip maker Nvidia.

Meanwhile London's benchmark FTSE 100 index which have some have dubbed the "anti-tech index", briefly touched a record high - one of the few periods in recent years where it has benefited from not being tech-heavy.

Historically it is possible for investors to lose money even if the technology they are backing succeeds.

For example, while railways transformed economies – particularly in the US – plenty of people lost money along the way. Unlike rail tracks – which once built are good for decades – data centres are likely to need upgrading frequently to include the latest and fastest processors.

Add to that lot, concerns that some of the big AI companies have taken big stakes or lent money to each other leading to circular funding that means that any potential failures could have a damaging impact on the fortunes of others.

There is also increasing cultural opposition to the build out and adoption of AI.

A growing number of national, state or local governments are pausing, banning or restricting new data centre construction on environmental grounds thanks to their vast water and energy needs.

Meanwhile, high profile AI advocates have found themselves booed by students who fear that AI will replace many graduate level jobs.

Despite all of that, Eileen Burbidge is still positive. "I see the glass half full - if you bought shares in chip makers a year ago you are feeling pretty good right now."

But there is no doubt that investors are watching companies plans for spending and their projections for when they get paid back with post euphoric scrutiny.

Prince Harry media battle legal bill expected to cost millions

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 15:04:34 GMT

The Duke of Sussex and other high-profile claimants who lost their High Court privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail face a potential legal bill of millions of pounds.

The group - which includes Sir Elton John, Baroness Doreen Lawrence and Elizabeth Hurley - sued Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL) over claims of unlawful information gathering.

But earlier this month, all their claims were dismissed by Judge Mr Justice Nicklin following an 11-week trial.

At the High Court on Wednesday, the parties in the case began a two-day hearing to decide who will pay what legal costs for the mammoth trial.

In written submissions, lawyers for the Duke of Sussex and the other claimants described the costs incurred by the Daily Mail's publisher - almost £34.5m as of 9 July - as "eye watering".

They claimed that ANL had exceeded its approved costs by over £18.6m, and added the group was insured to cover some of the publisher's costs.

Nicholas Bacon KC for the claimants told the court the group took out insurance cover in the sum of £16.2m, and that ANL had "overspent what they'd told us they'd actually spent".

The total bill the claimants could face has not been decided.

But the "current level of cover would be insufficient to meet their total costs exposure, possibly to the tune of many millions of pounds.", the court was told.

ANL has argued the claimants should pay back full costs incurred by the publisher and has applied for the costs to be paid on an indemnity basis - a more favourable financial payout.

The publisher has argued the claimant's side acted unreasonably during the case - a conduct clause which could trigger indemnity cover.

In written submissions, lawyers for ANL said: "Where claims involve wide-ranging allegations of dishonesty and serious criminal conduct against named individuals, a focused, responsible and proper approach is required as the norm.

"The Claimants' conduct of this litigation wholly disregarded these key disciplines. In many cases this was in the face of repeated warnings by the court as to the proper approach to be taken."

Lawyers for the claimants said they conducted themselves "honestly and in good faith" and argued that an outcome where the claimant's had to pay full costs would be "unjustified", and added that it would have a "particularly harsh impact on the claimants who will bear personal liability" for cover in excess of their insurance.

"They have approached this litigation in good faith, under the burden of decades of intense, intrusive media scrutiny into their private lives."

The hearing continues.

More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 14:37:30 GMT

Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covers much of central, eastern and southern England, and is a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.

It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.

North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.

Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.

The full list of English regions in drought conditions are:

There is no single definition of drought, but it usually refers to a period of prolonged unusually dry weather that can have impacts on people, nature and the environment.

The EA considers all of these factors before deciding whether to declare a drought in England.

The declaration is a public sign that the EA is stepping up its response to the dry conditions, including increased monitoring and controls on how much water can be taken from rivers and groundwater.

It can mean hosepipe bans being introduced if they are not already in place.

"The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it," said Helen Wakeham, director of water at the Environment Agency and chair of the National Drought Group.

This year's drought is somewhat unusual because January and February were very wet for much of the UK, helping to replenish reservoirs and groundwater.

But late spring and summer have been exceptionally hot and dry. The quick switch between wet and dry conditions is sometimes called "climate whiplash".

In particular, July has seen 7% of the average levels of rainfall in England so far, with just 1% across southern England. Some parts of Devon and Hampshire have gone more than a month without rain.

"The warm and exceptionally dry conditions experienced across much of England over recent months are continuing to have a significant impact," said Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office.

Early August could bring some rain to parts of the country, but the Met Office has said there is no sign of sustained rainfall that would make a significant difference to the dry conditions.

The combination of low rainfall and prolonged high temperatures - meaning greater evaporation of moisture - has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

These conditions have led to a "flash drought", the EA has said. This is where drought begins suddenly rather than over many months or years.

Today's announcement means there have been three droughts in the past five years – 2022, 2025 and now 2026.

While droughts happen naturally, scientists say that climate change is raising the risks, with higher summer temperatures drying out soils more quickly. This can lead to more severe and longer-lasting droughts.

Some researchers have also highlighted underinvestment in water infrastructure as an issue.

The EA has previously warned that England's public water supplies could face a shortfall of 5 billion litres per day by the middle of the century without urgent action.

"This drought isn't just about a lack of rain," said Prof Hayley Fowler of Newcastle University. "It's the result of hotter temperatures from a warming climate, rising water demand, ageing infrastructure and too much water being lost through leaks."

The government has committed to improving the water industry and water companies have announced plans for investment, but bills are rising as a result.

The dry conditions have consequences for nature, with Atlantic salmon unable to move upstream where river flows are low. Agriculture has also taken a hit.

Paul Tompkins, deputy president of the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales (NFU), said: "Farmers and growers have always had to contend with the weather, but what they are experiencing now is climate change in action. More extreme conditions [are] making it harder, riskier and more costly to produce the nation's food."

He added the issue of drought is something that "should matter to everyone" as it affects the country's food security.

Some areas of the country have now entered their fourth heatwave of the year.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts have come into force for parts of the UK, with temperatures potentially peaking at 35C in parts of south-east England on Wednesday.

The hot, dry weather has created ideal conditions for wildfires to spread. The National Fire Chiefs Council has warned that wildfire risk "remains elevated across the UK".

More than 200 wildfire incidents have been reported in England and Wales over the past two weeks, it said.

The Met Office has separately announced that the new June temperature record set last month was even higher than previously thought, following verification processes.

The previously-reported figure of 37.7C in Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June 2026 has been updated to 38.0C – smashing the UK's previous June high of 35.6C.

Additional reporting by Jess Carr

Saltburn suspend Devine after 'finger-clicking' claim

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 13:36:52 GMT

Devine had previously played for Pudsey St Lawrence in the Bradford Cricket League

The Saltburn player at the centre of an alleged cheating scandal has been suspended by the club for the "foreseeable future".

The club were placed under investigation on Monday by the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League following a complaint made in the aftermath of their 159-run win over Norton in a second XI Division 2 match.

Brian Devine, the Saltburn player at the centre of the allegations, is alleged to have clicked his fingers as the ball passed the bat of Norton's Noman Shabir during the match and was taken by wicketkeeper Josh Bowes. Following an appeal, the wicket was given.

Video footage of the incident went viral online and has been reported on around the world.

A club statement read: "This is issued in response to the widely publicised complaint made against a Saltburn Cricket Club member and, as a consequence, against the club more generally.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully investigating with the NYSD's [North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League] investigation.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us. The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the forseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation.

"Initial discussions have already taken place between club officials and the league.

"This has been a very distressing and stressful experience for all those concerned, and we would ask that this reality is borne in mind and that personal boundaries are respected, as we are an amateur club entirely run by volunteers."

Saltburn's second team had been due to play on Wednesday night in a cup game against Marton's second team.

However, Saltburn conceded the match at around lunchtime. BBC Sport were told that Saltburn were unable to get a team together because of the "holiday season".

Since the original video was posted on Monday evening, other videos involving Saltburn and Devine from previous matches have also been posted alleging similar incidents.

The original video has received over seven and a half million views on X and Devine has been dubbed as 'Clicky Ponting' on social media. The BBC has approached Devine for comment.

A meeting on Tuesday night was held between Saltburn, the league and legal representatives though any outcomes from that meeting are yet to be made public.

The league, Norton and the England and Wales Cricket Board have all declined to comment on the incident.

Saltburn's second team were due to play against Marton in a first-round match in the Division Two Hundred competition, a 100-ball-per-side format akin to The Hundred.

Reports from elsewhere earlier this week claimed that Spices, a local Indian restaurant to Saltburn, was to drop its sponsorship of Devine.

Spices owner Akmol Hussain has told BBC Sport that the restaurant has only ever sponsored the club rather than any individual players and is happy to continue doing so, pending the investigation.

"We'd like to continue sponsoring the club, but we want the issue to be dealt with," said Hussain.

"We see [Brian] as a representative of the club, not the owner of the club. Cricket is a gentleman's game.

"We want to continue supporting the club. It should be truly investigated and dealt with by the league."

BBC cancels Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 13:02:12 GMT

Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo have been cancelled by the BBC, as the corporation makes further financial savings.

The main Mastermind series will continue, with Clive Myrie remaining as host, but the celebrity spin-off will end after the next series, which has already been filmed.

In a statement, the BBC said it was "incredibly proud of all three of these much-loved shows" and thanked the programmes' production teams.

"Unfortunately," it continued, "we have to make some really tough choices in light of our funding challenges, and these savings have been identified from the Entertainment genre."

Viewing figures for all three shows have fallen over recent years. Celebrity Mastermind has dropped from an average of 4m viewers in 2017, to 1.7m for its most recent series.

Blankety Blank, meanwhile, has gone down from 5.5m viewers in 2021 to 2.3m for the most recent series.

And Live at the Apollo has dropped from around 1.3m viewers in 2018 to around 660,000 on its most recent series. These figures include catch-up platforms such as iPlayer.

The BBC said: "These difficult decisions form part of the BBC's previously announced first phase of its proposals to make £500m of savings over the next three years.

"BBC Content has a target of delivering a minimum of £100m of recurring annual savings which will result in a reduction of around 100-150 hours of originated TV programmes across genres by the end of 2027/28."

The corporation added that further savings across its content division will be announced in the coming months.

Live at the Apollo, which has been running since 2004, also has one further series already filmed, but will not continue after that has been broadcast.

The show is normally anchored by a well-known comedian, who introduces two other comics to present their own stand-up routines at London's Hammersmith Apollo.

The programme has acted as a springboard for emerging comedy talent, and helped boost the early careers of Michael McIntyre, Kevin Bridges, Micky Flanagan and Sarah Millican.

Although Live at the Apollo will end, the BBC said it would "shortly be announcing digital plans focused on stand-up and emerging comedy talent".

They said the ongoing pivot to digital would "ensure we continue to support the stand-up community in a rapidly changing and increasingly competitive media landscape".

Bradley Walsh, who presents Blankety Blank, said earlier this week that the show was currently on ice because he was too busy to film another series.

The presenter told the Radio Times it was "one of my favourite shows" but that he "physically does not have the time" to film another series at the moment because of other commitments.

Blankety Blank launched in 1979 and initially ran for 11 years, presented by Terry Wogan and Les Dawson.

It has since been revived several times, including a popular 1990s run hosted by Paul O'Grady's alter-ego Lily Savage.

The current incarnation, presented by Walsh, has been on air since 2020, when the success of a one-off Christmas special prompted the BBC to commission several more series.

Celebrity Mastermind, which is filmed in Belfast, launched in 2002 and has also been presented by Magnus Magnusson and John Humphrys.

It was a spin-off from the main Mastermind series that launched three decades earlier and saw members of the public answer questions on general knowledge as well as a specialist subject.

The BBC said: "We will still continue to commission ambitious Entertainment shows and invest in distinctive UK content from a wide range of independent production companies of all sizes."

The corporation also said it would "prioritise digital innovation that can serve fans of these shows and beyond".

Amelia Dimoldenberg: I wouldn't invite Andy Burnham on Chicken Shop Date - but I'd love a chat

BBC News Wed, 29 Jul 2026 05:02:05 GMT

Amelia Dimoldenberg is the queen of the deadpan silence.

But when I ask her if she would ever invite the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, on to her wildly popular YouTube series, she doesn't skip a beat.

"I don't think that maybe he's my type for Chicken Shop Date," she declares.

That might disappoint "social first" Burnham, who's made it clear he plans to court content creators to help get his message out.

Still, Dimoldenberg - who has become one of the UK's best-known content creators with millions of followers - says she's not against the idea of the prime minister collaborating with people like her, and in fact would "love" a chat with him.

While some warn it's a way of dodging serious scrutiny of policies, she views it as "a positive thing" to be working with social media influencers, "because that is now where so many people get their news".

"I don't think it means he's only going to be speaking to vloggers forever, really," she adds.

I meet Dimoldenberg not in a chicken shop, but in a studio in BBC Broadcasting House in central London. She's OK with that though ("I love the pot plants," she says. "It's fantastic. I'm very happy to be here.")

It's been more than a decade since she set up Chicken Shop Date. Since then, she's interviewed everyone from Cher to Ed Sheeran, and has become a celebrity in her own right.

The show is based around her trademark dry, awkward flirting style. In person, I find her inscrutable. You get the sense she's judging your questions (I was secretly relieved when she told me later they were great).

But she visibly lights up when talking about her free summer course, the Dimz Inc. Academy, which she launched to train up people aged 18-24 and help them get into the creative industries.

The course offers guaranteed paid work placements, mentoring and an opportunity to gain experience across digital media. She is now bringing it back for a second year, and has extended it from one week to four.

"I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she explains.

"So it was always such a big ambition of mine to be able to give that back to young people when I was able to."

Behind it is a serious issue. Dimoldenberg points to the high number of young people not in employment, education or training - a group known as Neets.

"That's really a big crisis. So there is no better time to be trying to do what I can to support the next generation of young people," she says.

She added that while Burnham may not be welcome on her YouTube series, she would "100% love to have a conversation with him" about what he's doing to tackle youth unemployment.

"I think having more training schemes, apprenticeships is really, really vital in helping young people," she says.

Away from her Academy, Dimoldenberg is hugely busy building her media empire.

The second series of Passenger Princess, her comedy series which sees her interview some of Formula 1's biggest names while learning how to drive, has just dropped on YouTube.

She also hosts red carpet interviews at the Oscars - following a tried-and-tested formula of comedic flirting and uncomfortable silences - and runs her own production company.

But she doesn't take any of it for granted. Before going on a red carpet, she does copious amounts of research. "[It's] like you're really studying for your A-levels again," she said. "I make sure that I have specific questions for every single person that I might meet."

Next up, she's starring in a rom-com - "playing myself", she says, angelically - and says she wants to do more directing, having recently got behind the camera for Maisie Peters' music video for single My Regards.

Meanwhile, Chicken Shop Date continues to go from strength to strength.

The show is billed around interviewing musicians, actors and comedians over a plate of nuggets. Politicians don't really make the cut (it's not just Burnham), and neither does royalty ("the Royals are just not really my type either".)

Her chemistry with the Spider-Man actor Andrew Garfield sent the internet into meltdown, and led to speculation that they were romantically linked in real life.

When asked why that didn't work out, Dimoldenberg says she was too busy and "just couldn't make the time," but she is sanguine about it. "You know, these things happen," she muses.

So what's next for Dimoldenberg? I wonder whether she has her eyes on a pivot to a traditional TV couch format - perhaps picking up from Claudia Winkleman, whose show ended after one series - but she doesn't seem interested.

"I feel like what I have with Chicken Shop Date is essentially a late night talk show," she says.

"And I think that there wouldn't really be a need for me to do something other than that right now while I have Chicken Shop Date, because to me it serves the purpose of what a chat show is."

Dimoldenberg has previously indicated that she will close the shop when she gets the Canadian rapper Drake on her show.

"Well, the stars haven't aligned yet, but you never know what might happen in the future," she says of her Drake bid. "Maybe I have to go to Toronto, but no, I'd much rather he come to me."

For now though, she bats away any suggestion that she's ready to end her series, even though she's arguably now more famous than some of the people she interviews.

"I still feel like there are dates that I really want to do," she says.

"I need fall in love, you know? I need to meet my one true love. So I have to carry on until that happens."

The evidence that shows today's 20-somethings really do have it worse

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 23:52:23 GMT

Young people in their 20s are facing a tougher start to adulthood than any generation in almost half a century, according to analysis of UK data on housing, employment and wealth, carried out for the BBC.

More than 40% of 25-year-olds are now living with their parents, their wages have stagnated and employment has fallen, show the figures which compare key metrics for different generations at age 25 stretching back to the early 1980s.

The findings are underscored by the experiences of young people themselves who, along with parents, have contacted BBC Your Voice about their circumstances, with many saying they were frustrated about being accused by older generations of not trying hard enough.

We asked the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) to gather and analyse government data, for the first time, to see if this generation really does have it worse.

The biggest change it found was where those in their 20s are living.

The number of 25-year-olds owning their own home has plummeted from 43% in the mid 1980s to just 15%. There is a simple reason for that: it is too expensive.

The data shows that housing costs for renters or people with a mortgage in their 20s are the highest they have ever been for them at this age, and they now take up a higher share of income than for their parents or grandparents.

And that's not even factoring in the rising cost of affording to run a home, where bills have spiralled rapidly, hitting Gen Z hardest as its wages are lower on average than other age groups facing the same rising prices. The result is the number of 25-year-olds living with their parents has risen from 25% in the 1990s to 42% today.

It is a hurdle that Gen Z is experiencing on a unique scale, but the impact is being felt by their parents too as their lifestyles and futures are being clipped by having young adults still living at home.

Adam Daytona, 26, moved back home this year to live with his parents. He says: "I think there's no world where it's normal to be 26 years old still living at home. It's unfair on me, it's unfair on my parents.

"To state the obvious, I'm not going to bring a girl back to my parents' house. So it would have 100% affected that part of my life, which does get me low, obviously.

"People say your 20s are the best years of your life and these are the worst years of my life, by far."

Adam's parents Jane, 57, and Neville, 64, say: "I think it's very difficult for them. They're not able to buy houses like we were able to.

"We were more than happy for him to come home but obviously, you know, we're getting older and it would be nice to have a place to ourselves."

There's been a dip in employment rates for Gen Z compared with the generations that came before.

The jobs squeeze has been felt especially among young women who had seen decades of growing opportunity as more entered the workplace.

But this current generation of 25-year-olds is the first to see a drop in employment rates, down from 77% 10 years ago to 71%.

For men, the fall is almost as stark. Men aged 25 are seeing a lower rate of employment than their age-equivalents in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, with employment rates dropping from 84% to 76%.

The number of applications before a success, the frequency of job losses, and the unknown challenge of AI in the workplace mean that the entry into working life is getting off to a much rockier start for this generation.

Daisy Edwards, 25, is back home with her parents in Guildford after losing her job in London. She says: "When I lost that job, I immediately started job searching and that was when it became clear quite how fleeting that London lifestyle was. I think it was pretty instant that I ran out of money.

"I'd had a few job interviews but I really committed to job searching. I was applying for maybe five or six jobs a day sometimes.

"I think it can really get you down and the longer you are unemployed the more you worry about things, like you don't want to pay to go out."

Dave, Daisy's dad, says: "That's a big difference to me having worked in the same company for 32 years. I've only ever had one job interview and I'm still there.

"The amount of job applications [Daisy] did was crazy. You had that spreadsheet. And often people don't get back to you. I would not like that."

Daisy has since found a full-time job.

It's clear from the data that 25-year-olds who are in work are likely to be earning more than their parents were at that age, and a lot more than their grandparents received. But after big wage growth for 25-year-olds from the 1980s through to the early 2000s, hitting an average of £28,526, all of that stopped.

"The big picture is stagnation," says Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the IFS. "It's not that these people are worse off than those that came before them, but it's that they're no better off and that progress has stalled."

Those born between 1987 and 1991 were entering the workforce just after the financial crash and saw a big fall in earnings. They are, in fact, the group who received the lowest average wages of any 25-year-olds over the last three decades. Since then, wages for 25-year-olds have crawled back up, almost to the point they were 20 years ago. Those waves of economic shocks, the pandemic and cost of living crisis mean that wages for 25-year-olds are only just above £28,000 now, after adjusting for inflation - and that stagnation hits people at the start of their careers hardest.

Society also has an expectation in that each generation will do better than the next, and when reality and expectations don't match there's inevitable disappointment.

Rachel Diamond, 23, moved from her family home in Oldham to Portsmouth to follow her dream job as a graduate engineer. She earns in the early £30,000s and says: "I was quite lucky when I got my job straight after uni. So I've kind of done everything right, but still I'm not saving any money from my paycheck, like months and months, just because it's so expensive with renting and bills. I don't think people realise how expensive it is to rent.

"That's the thing, like council tax, you only get 25% discount, so that's expensive on my own. Again, that's a choice, living on my own, but still."

Rachel's dad Paddy says: "When I started out in work I was in a similar situation to Rachel. I moved away from home and I lived on my own because I didn't know anybody where I was moving to, and certainly it was hard for me, and it seems to be, equally as hard, if not, well, probably harder for Rachel.

"I bought my first flat when I was in my early 20s. I was earning £20,000 a year and my first flat was £36,000."

The hope is that Gen Z will still achieve these milestones, potentially just a little later on, and that salaries and employment rates will recover as this group progress into their 30s.

For this generation, recognising the new terrain they are facing means comparison is impossible. Plenty have adopted a new mind-set, holding society's goals more loosely, and learning to thrive on shifting sands.

That's something Shahida, 22, has adopted through her job hunt process. Before landing her dream gig in the Ministry of Justice, she says the search to find work "took a lot of resilience".

"It did result in a lot of tears and a lot of self-doubt at the beginning and I think that's completely normal and it's part of the process."

While Shahida says she hopes she doesn't take her job for granted, she says she's "happy to say that I work in a place that I really enjoy".

Spectacular fossil preserves internal organs of ancient marine reptile

New Scientist July 29, 2026

A tiny, long-necked marine predator that lived 245 million years ago is the oldest reptile ever found with an intact digestive system.

The exquisitely preserved fossil, including almost the entire skeleton as well as the stomach, liver and intestines, was found in Yunnan province in China in 2023 and is named Austronaga minuta.

The shocking fossils that show T. rex wasn’t the king of the dinosaurs

Even blood vessels and the scales of a partially digested fish meal are visible in the remains.

Advertisement

“A fossil this age with such clear preservation of its organs is really a world treasure,” says John Long at Flinders University in Adelaide, Australia, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Austronaga dates back to the Triassic Period, when dinosaurs first evolved, but it isn’t a dinosaur. It belongs to a broader group called archosaurs, which includes dinosaurs, birds and crocodiles, but not other famous marine reptiles like mosasaurs or ichthyosaurs.

Free newsletter

The archosaurs were incredibly diverse in the Triassic and included “all kinds of interesting and strange-looking reptiles”, says Stephan Spiekman at the Natural History Museum Stuttgart, Germany, a member of the team that analysed the fossil. Only later, during the Jurassic and beyond, did they become more restricted, mostly being limited to dinosaurs, including birds, and crocodiles.

This specimen is a mere 60 centimetres in length, but as it is the only known example and the reptile’s age at death is unknown, it is impossible to say whether the species grew larger, says Spiekman.

However, he is confident that it was unlikely to have reached the size of its very long relative Dinocephalosaurus, the “Chinese sea dragon”, which could easily grow to over 4 metres.

“This was certainly a good and agile swimmer, mainly using its tail for swimming, its long front flippers for steering and its long neck to catch fish,” says Spiekman. “Austronaga probably would have looked a little like a lizard or a croc trying to be a seal or an otter and likely would have had scaly skin, for example.”

The fossil shows that the basic plan of the reptilian digestive tract has changed little in 245 million years, he says, and the “straight and simple intestines is what we see in most modern predatory reptiles, including those eating fish”.

Although the fossil is of high quality, the internal organs of Austronaga are only preserved in two dimensions. This is unlike those of a 380-million-year-old fossil of an armoured fish that Long and his colleagues described in 2022, which is regarded as having the oldest known organs of any vertebrate.

“But this is still an incredibly well-preserved fossil,” he says.

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeb7528

A handy guide to the science of super-long fingernails

New Scientist July 29, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

When news editor Alexandra Thompson sent Feedback some research about the social science of long fingernails, a paper that runs to 20 pages, we knew we had to read it. Never mind Alex’s remark – “I don’t think long fingernails is that deep” – Feedback was delving in.

The work has the delightfully verbose title “From status symbol to polysemous sign: Interpreting the meaning of artificially extended fingernails”. Wondering why people sometimes wear “artificially elongated fingernails” and how this behaviour is interpreted by the rest of society, the authors examined 45 newspaper articles and identified “eight interpretive frames” through which we can understand the trend for super-long nails.

Advertisement

Some of what is happening can be traced back to Thorstein Veblen’s classic analysis The theory of the leisure class: An economic study of institutions (1899). Veblen posited that the ruling class are engaged in “conspicuous leisure” in order to differentiate themselves from those doing actual work. One way to do that is to grow your nails really long, or wear nail extensions, to signal that you don’t have to work with your hands. However, the authors of the study don’t think that is what’s going on today.

They say that “the clear legibility of long nails as a symbol of leisure has been lost in contemporary societies”, since nail extensions are now found “on the hands of service workers as well as managers”. Instead, what is happening is frantic innovation in the beauty industry, driven by “capitalist market mechanisms”. This is accelerated by social media, where nail artists show off their most extravagant creations, with the result that “the status of nail work shifts from a routinised service to an autonomous art form whose value lies in complexity, originality and photogenic quality”. And that barely scratches the surface (see what we did there?). Never mind seeing a world in a grain of sand, you can see all of human society in a fingernail.

If we hadn’t enjoyed this paper enough, the citations are a gold mine. We had no idea there was a book called The Finger: A handbook, but we want to hand out some sort of prize to the person who came up with that subtitle.

We also want to point out that the authors of the nails paper missed a trick. The proper use of super-long fingernails is to make really good tapping sounds in ASMR videos. We had to rewrite part of this column at the last minute, so we put on one such video to ease the resulting stress, only to wind up blissing out for half an hour and then writing the remainder in a panic.

Feedback is pleased that our readers continue to bring us unhelpful units of measurement. Thanks go to Tony Levitt, who was at the Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences in Cambridge, UK, when he found a display explaining what goes into making a wind turbine. Apparently, it “can require over 1000kg of rare earth elements to build (the same weight as 2500 tins of baked beans!)”.

As Tony realised, this will look very different depending on whether the cans contain baked beans or not, and the display doesn’t specify. Tony decided to investigate. “Looking in our kitchen cupboard I found a solitary can, labelled as ‘400g net’, ” he writes. “According to my kitchen scales the combined can and contents actually weighs 468g.” If Feedback’s maths is right (and it frequently isn’t), a full can is about seven times heavier than an empty one. We therefore find ourselves knowing the amount of rare earth elements needed to build a wind turbine, but only to within a factor of seven.

“To be fair to the Sedgwick, it is a great little museum,” adds Tony.

Meanwhile, Elizabeth Osbos pointed us to a marine forecast warning of a “rapidly rising swell”, posted on X on 6 June by New Zealand’s MetService – Te Ratonga Tirorangi. Specifically, “Combined wave heights in eastern offshore waters could reach or exceed the height of the Ohakune Carrot”.

Feedback wasn’t previously aware of the Ohakune Carrot, but we have familiarised ourselves. The small town of Ohakune lies at the heart of a major carrot- and parsnip-growing region, and to commemorate this industry, it has a giant fibreglass carrot standing by the road. The carrot is 7.5 metres tall and may be the largest model carrot in the world.

New Zealand readers: is the height of the Ohakune Carrot so generally and universally understood that it can be safely used to convey the heights of dangerous ocean waves?

In our ongoing quest for the science-themed tourist attraction with the most limited possible audience, we mentioned Denmark’s Gas Museum as a place that not many people would want to go to (30 May). This included John Blakey, who alerted us to its existence, but hasn’t actually attended.

But it has competition. Rebecca Ferguson (the professor of learning futures at the Open University, not the actor) and Bill Dickinson both wrote in to tell us about another museum of gas: the Fakenham Gasworks Museum in Norfolk, UK.

“I wouldn’t want to gaslight John, but he may have forgotten [it],” writes Rebecca. She adds that “TripAdvisor ranks it fourth of the top attractions of Fakenham – beating both the Chocolate Factory Shop and the ruined abbey”.

Bill says the staff are very friendly, cheerfully turning a blind eye when he inadvertently stayed half an hour after closing time.

Are flies following a strategy when they keep hitting windows? Part 3

New Scientist July 29, 2026

When wasps, bees and flies continually clatter against the glass of my conservatory attempting a means of escape, are they following a strategy? (continued)

Wai WongMelbourne, Australia

Advertisement

Australia, particularly Melbourne, is renowned for its abundance of flies, so I have quite a bit of experience with them. Their behaviour is rather different from what your previous correspondent describes.

In the absence of any scent of food, a fly in an open space usually flies randomly in search of food. So, even when there is no wind, a fly can enter a house via an open door or window by chance. Inside the house, it usually spends some time exploring and then tries to leave. To find an exit, it will fly towards a light source and that is why it often keeps flapping around or banging on a closed window. If the window is open, it seems to be able to sense the incoming fresh air and finds the way out against the air current.

To let out an annoying fly that keeps roaming around your house, the best strategy is to turn off all the lights and close all curtains, bar those in one small room. Within an hour, it will settle around the windows of that room. Close the door and open the window, and it can’t wait to escape.

Our verdict on Claire North’s space opera Slow Gods: a big thumbs-up

New Scientist July 29, 2026

The New Scientist Book Club has spent July reading Claire North’s space opera Slow Gods. Set in the far future, it follows the fortunes of a civilisation that has just learned that their planet will be destroyed by a supernova – in 100 years’ time.

“What does it mean to look into the heavens and know the exact date when a star will die and with it, your world?” North wrote in a fascinating essay for book club members on why they started the book with this conceit. “What choices do you make, and what price would you pay to save yourself – or your civilisation?”

Alongside this end-of-the-world tale, Slow Gods is also a love story between North’s protagonist Maw, a pilot who can navigate the dangers of faster-than-light travel but who is a little prone to murdering people, and Gebre, a citizen of that planet on the brink of annihilation, Adjumir.

Advertisement

Read an extract from Slow Gods by Claire North

Our science-fiction columnist Emily H. Wilson had heartily recommended this one: “It has been a while since I have read a piece of science fiction so purely delightful.” I was also enraptured. North’s writing was elegant, insightful and effortlessly funny (I hate try-hard humour in my fiction). And the concept at the heart of the story, the idea of how a civilisation might deal with imminent, but not all that imminent, destruction? It was fascinating and terrifying; as North told me in our interview for book club members, this is a deliberate parallel with climate change. “Subtle metaphor it is not,” they said.

Slow Gods wasn’t only a hit with me and Emily – I think it’s one of our most popular books so far with members. “The writing is gorgeous, and it has the big concept space opera feel that I really like,” wrote adidubey on our Discord channel. “One of the more satisfying reads we have had,” added Matthew. “This book club usually picks things I wouldn’t and some are good and some less so (none that I have not finished) but there is a lot of variety and it gets me out of my rut of only reading the familiar.”

I did find the opening a little stodgy and slow to get going, which is often a problem for space operas, as the writer looks to set their galactic scene. Butterfly368 was with me on this: “The beginning was a bit slow and confusing, but the deeper I got, the more invested I became. It’s one of those books that gradually pulls you in rather than grabbing you from page one,” they wrote. “I’m also enjoying its commentary on the meaning we create in our lives and on society and culture more broadly. It’s given me quite a bit to think about.” Melissa, however, loved it from the first. “50 pages in and totally engrossed. I’ve felt gut punched with recognition at some of the terrible treatment of people but also laughed into an empty room a couple of times. Whyyyyyy do I have to go to work?” she wrote.

Why I started my sci-fi novel with a world-ending supernova

Barbara Howe had some interesting comparisons to make with some of her favourite reads. “Reminded me a bit at the start of [Ann Leckie’s] Ancillary Justice, mainly in how much I was struggling to understand what was going on, and how many questions were raised early on that didn’t get answered until much later – if at all,” she wrote. “Also, whenever [Maw] talked about having trouble with social situations and understanding his feelings, I was reminded of Murderbot ‘having an emotion’.”

North, incidentally, had some interesting things to say in our chat about Maw’s struggle to fit in; he “is the protagonist you write when you are an adult diagnosed with autism late in your life”, they told me. North and I also dug into the multiple pronouns used in this story – something Carrie noted on Discord, writing that “I’m really enjoying the world building and while they can take a little getting used to, feel that the introduction of new pronouns really add to the story and provide insight into the cultures we’re being introduced to”. “People exist on a spectrum,” said North in our chat. “In the English language, we may still only really have ‘he’ and ‘she’ as the commonly accepted expression of gender, but that spectrum is enormous. It ranges from Arnold Schwarzenegger through to Harry Kane through to Alan Carr, then straight on keeps on going. The enormity of that spectrum feels too big for ‘he’ and ‘she’ to actually cover.”

Alan_P was another big fan. “I absolutely loved it. I’m looking up other books by the same author in my library which is something I rarely do,” he wrote. “I also (unexpectedly for me – I’m not a fan of romance in general) found myself really enjoying the love story at the centre of the book. For me it’s the very clever way that the author has woven these different themes of not quite requited love, galaxy spanning science fiction, commentary of contemporary events and a really good story that makes it one of my favourites in a good while.” A bit of a success, then!

What changes will occur on Earth as the moon moves further away?

New Scientist July 29, 2026

What changes will occur on Earth as the moon moves further away from us?

Ron DippoldSan Diego, California, US

Usually, my answers are: “Oh, this is so much worse than you even imagined!” But in this case, the answer is “not much”.

Advertisement

The moon is about 384,400 kilometres from Earth right now and our days are about 24 hours long. The moon pulls on Earth’s oceans as the planet rotates below it, causing tidal bulges at the points closest to and furthest away from the moon. Those bulges drag on Earth through the seafloor, slowing down its rotation and causing its days to be about 1.8 milliseconds longer per century. That energy is transferred to the moon, which is kicked into a slightly higher orbit, and is thus retreating from Earth at about 3.78 centimetres per year. We have fossil proof from corals that roughly 1.8 billion years ago, our year was about 485 days long because Earth was rotating much faster – leading to approximately 18-hour days. In a billion years or so, at current rates, an Earth day will be around 27 hours long and the moon will be some 10 per cent further from Earth, about 400,000 km away.

Usually my answers are: ‘This is so much worse than you imagined!’ But in this case, the answer is ‘not much’

This is the time in the future when everything changes, because the sun will be about 10 per cent brighter. This will trigger a runaway greenhouse effect on Earth, if we haven’t already done that to ourselves, and the oceans will completely boil away. The moon will still have Earth’s rocks to drag on, but those aren’t nearly as flexible as water, and without the massive friction of tides on Earth’s seafloor, the moon will almost stop moving further away and the length of Earth’s day will almost be fixed. And then, about 4 billion years after that, the growing sun may or may not envelop Earth and the moon, but will at least turn their surfaces to magma. At that point, the moon may start moving further away again, but we won’t care.

Practically, the moon continuing to move further away in the next billion years only causes two minor effects. First, because tidal effects fall off by the cube of the distance between the moon and Earth, if the moon moves 10 per cent further away, this would reduce tides by about 25 per cent. Four-metre tides become 3-metre ones. Second, it is entirely a coincidence that the moon is just the right size to cover the sun as seen from Earth and cause a total solar eclipse. In about half a billion years, as the moon continues to move away, its apparent size will shrink and it will no longer cover the sun. There will only be annular eclipses – a dark moon surrounded by the ring of fire of the sun peeking around it. But for the sentient rodent people of Earth in 600 million years, the moon moving further away will be the least of their concerns.

Mike FollowsSutton Coldfield, West Midlands, UK

Tidal interactions cause the moon to move away from Earth, currently at about 3.8 cm per year. This process also lengthens both the moon’s orbital period and Earth’s spin period. Assuming these processes continue for tens of billions more years, Earth’s spin period will eventually equal the moon’s orbital period, and the two bodies will both become tidally locked.

The same face of the moon is always turned towards Earth. Eventually, Earth will reciprocate: anyone on the moon’s near side would always see the same face of Earth fixed at the same point in the sky. Earth and the moon will each then permanently show the same face to the other.

Lunar tides will become weaker because the moon’s tide-raising effect decreases roughly with the inverse cube of its distance from Earth. Over millions of years, this would alter coastal environments and ocean mixing, with ecosystems evolving in response.

The moon will also appear smaller in the sky. In about 600 million years, it will no longer be able to cover the sun completely, so total solar eclipses will cease.

The moon helps to stabilise Earth’s axial tilt, which is presently about 23.4 degrees and naturally varies only between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees. As the moon moves further away, this stabilising influence will weaken, allowing larger variations in Earth’s tilt and potentially more extreme long-term changes in climate and the seasons.

The moon may have influenced Earth’s history. Some researchers have suggested that the repeated wetting and drying of intertidal environments, driven by the moon’s tides, may have favoured the chemistry leading to life, echoing Charles Darwin’s famous speculation about “some warm little pond”. Together with its stabilising influence on axial tilt, the moon may therefore have played a significant role in making Earth habitable. If so, were it not for the moon, there might have been nobody to observe its slow recession.

Worry about what your children eat, but don’t forget your own diet

New Scientist July 29, 2026

Chidren are an impressionable lot. In our youth, we are like sponges, picking up habits and neural pathways that will resonate for the rest of our lives. It is no wonder, then, that countries including the UK, Portugal and Mexico have enacted policies to restrict the advertising of unhealthy food to children, in a bid to tackle soaring childhood obesity levels. But if this makes you think that adults are off the hook, then think again.

As we explore, eating appropriately for your age matters no matter how old you are. If you are middle-aged, you may have noticed the warning signs: a horrible hangover after drinking an amount of alcohol that would have left you unaffected decades earlier, or getting increasingly jittery after drinking coffee. These are indicators of more global changes occurring in the body, making us less and less able to tolerate a subpar diet. Breaking bad diet habits – a glass of wine after the kids have gone to bed, or a sneaky croissant from a coffee shop because you skipped breakfast – as we age is just as important as instilling healthy eating in children.

Breaking bad diet habits as we age is as important as instilling healthy eating in children

What’s more, once we reach the age of 60, it becomes ever easier to fall into a “nutrient gap” – when a slowdown in our metabolic rate means that we eat less, but age-related physiological changes mean that we actually need more vitamins and minerals from every bite of food.

Advertisement

That’s the bad news. Recognising these changes in our metabolism and responding accordingly – you know the drill: eating more vegetables, legumes, whole grains and fish, and less ultra-processed food high in sugar, salt and saturated fat – can help set you up for a healthy old age.

But don’t wait until you are already in your latter decades to take action. A number of studies show that, if we tune up our diet in middle age, this can have a big impact on our health and wellbeing years down the line, while a younger biological age also helps you reap the benefits of a good diet. Ditch the junk and your older self will thank you.

Patient beds angled in ED corridors, hospital makes plans to pitch tents in winter surge

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026

Christchurch Hospital's emergency room is struggling with not enough beds for patients. Photo / RNZ

By RNZ

Christchurch Hospital has emergency plans to pitch a tent outside as corridors fill up with patients in beds, according to one doctor.

And in some cases, beds are already being angled in corridors in order to fit more in.

Hospitals around the country are also feeling the pressure of winter sickness, and, while the Government put $25 million into extra staffing and beds to get ready, Christchurch Hospital emergency specialist Dr Dominic Fleischer says there still isn’t enough.

Speaking to Morning Report, Fleischer said it was busy – but not unexpected.

While an increase in patients is a “normal” winter occurrence, the number needing to be seen seemed to get worse each year – and this year is “certainly worse” than last.

Patients being seen in hallways and waiting rooms was not new, Fleischer said. But where beds used to be parallel parked in the corridors, they were now having to angle them to fit in more.

This essentially blocked off the space and he wasn’t sure what the next option was.

“This is sort of innovation in a dangerous manner,” he said.

“Either we have to go up and bunk some patients or we have to go out, go out into the car park or the ambulance bay, and put patients in tents.”

Fleischer said plans were drawn up for using tents outside but officials would hold off on that as long as possible as the “look will be atrocious”.

But “corridor medicine” was bad and patients couldn’t be looked after properly, he said.

“Our corridors are full and getting worse. Worse than last year and I’m sure next year will be worse than this year.”

There were not enough monitors for patients in corridors, no call buttons or meal service, he said. Patients felt vulnerable and it was not a dignified way to treat them.

“In every way it’s substandard.”

“I’ve accepted it for a few minutes while patients are waiting to go to a bed in the ward, but there are patients there for hours or overnight.

“You come in the next morning and the patient’s spent the entire night in a corridor with no sleep. It’s distressing and upsetting to them and to the staff, of course, because it’s just a horrible way to treat someone, and it’s getting worse.”

Fleischer said there was no easy solution, but easier access to GPs after hours would help.

Corridors start filling up from around 5pm with patients who could not get care elsewhere and Fleischer said it was common for patients to call their GP and be told to go to emergency because no appointments were available.

It was also common for the one 24-hour emergency clinic to turn people away because it, too, was overwhelmed.

Those people then went to ED at the hospital, Fleischer said.

Sickness was increasing and some staff were exhausted but “it’s what we do”.

Earlier this month, Health NZ announced that it was adding 30 more temporary beds than initially expected to hospitals around the country to meet winter demand.

The $25 million funding boost in March added 71 beds to hospitals before the colder months.

The number of extra beds was expected to be 103 by mid-July.

Thirty-five beds were added to hospitals in the midland region; 12 at Waikato, 18 at Rotorua and five at Thames, with 12 at Wellington Hospital.

In the South Island, 12 were added at Burwood, eight at Christchurch, and 14 across the Southern region.

“In addition, we are expecting 14 in Middlemore to open on July 8 and a further eight in Christchurch to open on July 17, totalling 103 nationwide,” Health NZ said earlier this month.

“The slight variation from the original plan’s bed alignment is due to hospitals reviewing demand and mak[ing] changes accordingly.”

Show me the money: Why the next pandemic response might not be much improved

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026
