There’s an oft-repeated phrase in the fine print of the Government’s report responding to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Covid pandemic.

It essentially says that, yes, implementing this recommendation would be fantastic in an ideal world, but that world presupposes infinite resources the Government doesn’t have.

When Covid hit in early 2020, as bodies filled streets in parts of the world where the morgues were too full, the shortcomings of our health resources and decades of underinvestment were laid bare.

We scrambled to get PPE (personal protective equipment).

We didn’t have enough ventilators. Contact tracing teams were hobbled together, sharing information between regions by phone because the country’s health data system wasn’t linked.

The health system survived mainly because New Zealand was mostly Covid-free from May 2020, through the first and most of the second winters, to August 2021.

Nor did it crumble in early 2022, because Omicron was much less deadly or severe than the Delta variant it displaced.

It’s not hard to see how the system might have collapsed had elimination been unattainable, or had Omicron caused much more severe health issues.

These were the worst-case scenarios where an abundantly resourced health system would have offered an effective line of defence.

The commission has, understandably, told the Government that such abundance would improve our preparedness for the next one.

The Government has, also understandably, accepted these recommendations in principle, adding in the fine print of its report that their implementation depends on finances.

A health system that can rapidly scale up key public health functions?

“Accepted in principle as the intent is supported, but full implementation is contingent on funding beyond current baselines,” the fine print in the Government report, released yesterday, said.

A health system with information and data capability to deliver a pandemic response?

“Accepted in principle ... but full delivery is contingent on sustained investment in line with the Health Digital Investment Plan.”

Ensuring health and disability service continuity and resilience during a pandemic?

“Accepted in principle ... but full implementation is contingent on reprioritisation within current programmes and targeted investment, which will require further scoping.”

Determining the costs and benefits of improving ventilation in hospitals and healthcare facilities?

“Accepted in principle ... but several factors limit the ability to determine a detailed cost-benefit analysis without additional estate baseline information, precursor investment, resourcing and prioritisation.”

You get the idea.

A Government with cash overflowing from its pockets would gladly do all of these things and do them yesterday.

But those pockets today are far from overflowing, as the Government balances its financial credentials on lowering debt and spending responsibly, while also keeping what it can for the next storm or oil price shock.

Throw in an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and an election in November and you can see why, politically, it’s a hard sell.

Imagine the sales pitch: “Vote for us. We’ll commit massive amounts of funding to preparing for a future crisis that may or may not hit any time soon, and which may or may not threaten people’s lives or livelihoods in the same all-encompassing ways the last one did”.

Even if the Crown account was healthier, wouldn’t that money be better spent on key infrastructure that is definitely needed (even in health, where patients in Christchurch Hospital are being treated in corridors), rather than funding a generous buffer in the health system that would help on an everyday basis, but only really be needed in an extreme scenario?

There are plenty of recommendations, though, for the Government to commit to without emptying what’s left of the contents of its wallet.

Better transparency, stronger safeguards for people’s rights, analysis of the state of trust and social cohesion, more fulsome planning, cleaner lines of accountability, improved co-ordination between monetary and fiscal policy.

These low-hanging fruits have all been happily plucked, and may well mean an improved response in the next pandemic than what otherwise might have happened.

But they are all relatively minor compared to the state of the health system, which will inevitably be the foundation of whether the next pandemic response will succeed.

The likelihood of abundant resourcing can be assessed with a quick glance at the state of the books:

Not very likely, in other words.

That may leave us in much the same position, when the next pandemic inevitably arrives.

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Waikato father films himself sexually abusing 5-year-old daughter, sends images to US paedophile

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026

The girl's father told a pre-sentence report writer that the “deviant” streak in him went too far down a rabbit hole and it was all “a terrible misunderstanding”. Photo /123RF

This article describes sexual offending against a young child and may be upsetting for readers.

A man who made videos of himself sexually abusing his 5-year-old daughter – before sending screenshots to a co-offender overseas – was busted by a United States sheriff who was monitoring his associate’s behaviour.

After making two long films of himself sexually assaulting his daughter, the man used them to create six shorter videos and 182 images, while telling his American off-sider that he would take more requests: “no matter how weird”.

He’s since told a pre-sentence report writer that the “deviant” streak in him went too far down a rabbit hole and it was all “a terrible misunderstanding”.

The man appeared for sentence in the Hamilton District Court on Wednesday, when he was granted permanent name suppression, purely to protect his child, and sent to jail.

He had earlier admitted 12 charges, including two of doing an indecent act on a child, knowingly making an objectionable publication, distributing that publication, and three representative charges of possessing objectionable publications.

“You were supposed to care and protect her,” Judge Kim Saunders told him as she sent him to prison.

“Instead, you abused her.”

The victim’s grandmother, aged in her 70s, has now become the girl’s fulltime caregiver.

In her victim impact statement, she said the victim was a “bright and bubbly girl who has had to experience something no child should have to endure”.

The victim had days where she displayed “concerning” behaviour and she now worried about the long-term impact the abuse would have on her.

“I sincerely hope she can recover without carrying the burden of what has been done to her.

“It’s devastating to know, that someone who should have protected [victim] has instead caused her such harm.”

The abuse began in August last year when the man set up a recording device in his bedroom.

He took off his daughter’s pants and underwear and posed her on his bed.

He then filmed himself offending against her as the victim protested.

Despite her protestations, he videoed himself abusing her again a week later.

He then took eight screen shots, which revealed the victim’s genitalia and bottom.

The man then used his Gmail account to email the eight screen shots to a person in the United States in which he offered to take requests “no matter how weird”.

From one video, he made three separate, shorter videos; two that were 11 seconds long, and another, 23 seconds.

The next day, the New Zealand Online Child Exploitation Team received information from a sheriff’s office in Colorado about the man’s imagery being sent to a suspect there.

A forensic examination of his cellphone found 282 images, and 47 objectionable videos.

Six of the videos and 182 images involved his daughter, the rest were downloaded or sent directly to him from others.

Thirty-three images and 31 videos were put into the most serious category, 1A, and included the sexual violation of a baby that was still in hospital with its name tag on its wrist.

There were 12 videos and 250 images in the second most serious category, where his daughter’s imagery sat.

There were also two images and five bestiality-related videos, involving a woman and animals.

Crown prosecutor James Lewis said the offending involved a high degree of premeditation and breach of trust on a vulnerable victim, in circumstances where he was her sole caregiver.

While the defendant should get a full guilty plea discount, he lacked insight into what he’d done.

When asked what drove his offending, he told a report writer; “I am not sure”.

“That deviant streak in me that went too far down the rabbit hole and it was a terrible misunderstanding,” the man said.

“I have done wrong and I want to make it right, and will do anything I can to help.”

The man also “politely declined” to comment on the driver of his offending, refusing to confirm whether it was sexually motivated or by monetary gain, Lewis said.

The man’s counsel, Tom Sutcliffe, said there wasn’t much difference between the submissions of the Crown and his own. However, he disputed that his client had a lack of insight into what he’d done.

“I can’t imagine there’s anybody who does not commit offending of this nature that doesn’t have some degree of insight, otherwise they wouldn’t be committing the offending.

“But that shouldn’t be taken as a broad-brush approach to then decline what would otherwise be an appropriate discount.”

He said his client was co-operative with police and pleaded guilty almost immediately.

“As he put it, he has gone down a rabbit hole and there was a deviant streak that took him there, he can’t explain why he did what he did.

“He’s a man who is wanting to put things right, and he’s clearly open to rehabilitation.”

Judge Saunders said it surely went without saying that children were “the most innocent vulnerable among us”.

“And I cannot think of any more vulnerable victim than your 5-year-old daughter.

Contact the Open Justice team

“The harm to her as she matures cannot be calculated and one can only hope that she gets the support that she needs so that your offending against does not define her life.

“And of course society abhors the exploitation of children in that way.”

What she also found “troubling” was the fact the man was willing to make more material involving his child.

She took an overall starting point of five-and-a-half years before allowing a 25% discount for his guilty pleas, and a further 5% for his prospects of rehabilitation.

Judge Saunders jailed him for three years and 10 months and granted him permanent name suppression.

Belinda Feek is an Open Justice reporter based in Waikato. She has worked at NZME for 11 years and has been a journalist for 22.

‘Same temperature as outside’: Dunedin students still living in frigid flats

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026

Students in some Dunedin flats are living in unsafe, unsatisfactory housing, say student leaders. Photo / RNZ, Bella Craig

By Tess Brunton of RNZ

Dunedin university students continue to live in flats that are colder inside than out, despite meeting Healthy Home Standards.

Advocates are calling for action over the frigid flats.

Second-year student Rosie moved into a Leith St flat after a year in a student hall, where her room was warm and insulated.

The low standard of living came as a shock and she did not know any flats that could be considered warm.

Her flatmates wear jackets inside and she was sick for most of the first semester.

“We’re all pretty restricted on our power use. We don’t use our communal heat pump.

“We probably each individually have an oil heater in our rooms and we use that a couple of hours a day because rent is so expensive and power is so expensive in general, we’re pretty reluctant to do that.”

Her flat is about 100 years old.

“They couldn’t access the walls to put insulation in and so there’s only double glazing in one room, no insulation in the walls or underfloor because they, you know, quote marks, couldn’t access it, but we don’t know how true that is,” she said.

“It’s honestly the same temperature as outside.”

She did not think it was fair that students paid so much to live in these conditions.

On Castle St, The Feisty Goat is up to healthy homes standards, kitted out with insulation, heating and ventilation.

But resident Dylan said the 145-year-old house was freezing despite the landlord’s efforts.

“We love the house, like it’s real, real cool. Like we have a lot of fun, but it does get like freezing cold, especially at night.

“We’ve all got like girlfriends and we spend a lot of time spending the nights at their houses because it’s actually too cold to sleep here, especially in the winter.”

The heat pump did little to heat the home and remained turned off most of the time, he said.

Instead, most of the flat used dehumidifiers.

“I got this big jacket from my mum that she got given that she didn’t need up in Auckland. So I took it down here, and it’s been probably the most worn item of clothing between the whole flat.”

He was hopeful the flat would be much warmer after draughty gaps were filled this week, using air-sealing technology.

Otago University Students’ Association president Daniel Leamy said it was almost impossible to find a decent-quality flat.

“Perhaps in the 21st century, we maybe shouldn’t be subjecting our young people to a, quote, rite of passage that essentially just means you live in unsafe, unsatisfactory housing.”

The Healthy Homes Standards were good, but they were the bare minimum, and were not enforced, he said.

Students often knew their homes were not up to scratch, but many would not risk taking their landlords to the Tenancy Tribunal.

“The problem is the power dynamic between landlords and tenants is so, so unfair on young people who want to get a good reference so they can actually get more housing and another place to live, say next year if they move on.”

He is calling for more efforts to improve the housing stock, and said students could access help from the association’s support centre.

Green Building Council residential impact manager Matthew Cutler said the old, cold student flats of Dunedin were well known.

“Some of the conditions here are just so bad for students, and we’ve become, as a culture, kind of accepting of that, and I don’t think that should be acceptable.”

Draughty homes were a common problem as there was no requirement to measure the air-tightness of homes in New Zealand, unlike in many other countries, he said.

It should be easy to heat a home to a healthy standard, but it was often not the case.

“The Healthy Homes Standard is a really good start, but without a true warrant of fitness or an energy performance certificate, which is something that’s very common in the residential sector across the world and certainly in the OECD, then it is really just the first step, and there’s a lot of room to improve that.”

Those improvements could include monitoring indoor air quality and enforcing the Healthy Homes Standards, as they relied on self-reporting.

Cannabis bust: 16 arrested as $6.5m haul seized in Rotorua, Auckland raids

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Up to $6.5 million worth of cannabis has been seized in Rotorua after police swooped on what they say is a large-scale organised crime ring.

Police say they have dealt a major blow to the drug market, busting an alleged commercial-scale growing operation and making 16 arrests after finding houses “packed to the brim” with cannabis plants.

Bay of Plenty Police field crime manager Detective Inspector Lindsay Pilbrow said in a media release the operation shut down 14 grow houses in Rotorua and removed the cannabis from the black market.

Five residential properties, 21 bank accounts and two vehicles were restrained under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act.

Of the 16 Vietnamese nationals arrested, 14 were facing charges relating to cannabis growing and associated offences. Two were arrested in relation to alleged Immigration Act Offences.

Twelve of those arrested appeared in the Rotorua District Court yesterday, with the remaining set to appear today.

This week’s arrests follow a similar operation in Auckland last year, where more than 10 tonnes of cannabis was destroyed by police following raids on clandestine grow houses believed to be run by Vietnamese organised crime groups.

Over four weeks ending in August, Operation Beryl busted 120 properties converted into weed nurseries.

Police estimated last year’s haul was worth more than $50m on the black market.

This week’s raids, codenamed Operation Harvey, followed a six-month joint investigation between police and Immigration New Zealand officers from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.

The operation targeted residential rental properties allegedly being used to house large-scale commercial cannabis-growing operations involving Vietnamese organised crime groups.

On Tuesday, 25 warrants were executed across Rotorua and Auckland.

It involved more than 220 staff from across Bay of Plenty, Waikato and Auckland districts, as well as support from Genesis Energy to make the properties safe and assist with the investigation phase, police said.

Of the 21 residential properties searched in Rotorua, 14 had active and significant cannabis grow houses operating in them and 10 were rental properties located in residential areas.

Police allege all the houses had been using stolen power illegally diverted from nearby power boxes – with conservative estimates noting they had been illegally diverting about $30,000 worth of power a week to run the grow houses.

“This was a well-organised, significant and well-resourced grow operation with all the properties linked to the same criminal network,” Pilbrow alleged.

Police believed the drugs were destined for sale to other organised criminal groups to on-sell.

“Over 3500 high-value plants were seized along with 97 pounds of dried cannabis head packaged and ready for the wholesale market,” Pilbrow said.

He said the cannabis seized had a bulk sale value of $1.8m, but has a potential street market value “well in excess of $6.5m depending on how it is sold”.

Alongside cannabis, tens of thousands of dollars of cash were seized, along with cannabis-growing equipment.

“The scale of this operation is one I’ve not seen before. It is a multimillion-dollar business used to fund other organised criminal activities. We believe the equipment located and seized at the grow houses is worth more than $1m alone,” Pilbrow said.

“Many of these houses were packed to the brim with cannabis plants at various stages of growth. Houses had been altered to allow maximum use of space, with specialised timing and ventilation systems fitted to assist in the growing and to also avoid detection.

“This will deal a significant blow to those involved. These organised criminal groups have embedded themselves within communities simply to cause harm. Not only does the drug use put people at harm, but the associated offending such as the theft of electricity is a significant risk to households and members of the public,” he said.

The operation remains ongoing, with further search activity planned in Auckland and the Bay of Plenty. Further arrests and charges have not been ruled out.

Pilbrow said illegal drugs harmed people and communities, and tackling the issue required a collective effort.

Police encouraged people with information about drug-related offending to come forward.

“Unfortunately, Police continue to see an increase in rental properties in suburban areas being converted into large-scale cannabis growing operations funded and controlled by organised criminal groups.”

A property on Hamon Place in Rotorua was among those raided this week. A team of police spent most of Tuesday afternoon at the property.

Police staff carried large lamps and steel grates on to the front lawn of the property.

A neighbour, who did not want to be identified, said there was a strong smell of cannabis as soon as police arrived and opened the doors and windows.

Twelve people arrested as part of the raids appeared one-by-one before Judge Joanne Wickliffe at the Rotorua District Court yesterday.

They were represented by Auckland barrister Callum Fredric and assisted by an interpreter. Crown Solicitor Amanda Gordon appeared for the prosecution.

Most of the accused indicated they wanted to be deported. Judge Wickliffe said they would need to leave the country by August 31 or enter pleas in court via a video link from prison.

The charges the accused faced included cultivating cannabis, possession of cannabis for supply and possession of equipment used to cultivate cannabis. Cultivating cannabis carries a maximum prison sentence of seven years.

Eight Vietnamese people, who said they were friends of those appearing, sat in the public gallery during the appearances.

Some of the women among them cried when one of the accused appeared in the dock.

Judge Wickliffe acknowledged the public gallery, saying it was a difficult day for them.

Police encourage landlords and property managers to look out for signs that a property may be being used for illegal drug cultivation.

This activity can cause significant damage, pose a fire risk and may jeopardise insurance payouts.

Landlords had obligations to carry out due diligence on prospective tenants. Police recommended reference checks, meeting tenants face-to-face and checking IDs and income verifications.

“If tenants have a preference to pay rent in cash or offer to pay more to avoid inspections, that should be a red flag.”

Other warning signs could include blacked-out or permanently covered windows, extractor fans, ventilation systems or unauthorised structural changes to the exterior of the property or signs that an electricity meter has been tampered with or bypassed.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 27 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Jamie Lockett: Ninja, rebel and accused terrorist dies aged 64

New Zealand Herald July 29, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Rebel and rogue, Jamie Lockett was a persistent thorn in the sides of many. He died last week. “Good,” said one person. Daughter Victoria Carter reveals the dad she suspects others did not know. David Fisher - who knew Lockett for 25 years - reports.

Jamie Lockett has died, ending a decades-long battle with authority and, above all, the police.

Best known as one of those arrested during Operation Eight in Te Urewera in 2007, Lockett, 64, was a rebel looking for a rebellion: a repo man, an investigator, a prosecutor, a litigant, a protester, a bodyguard, a mechanic, and a ninja.

He was also a father. His unexpected death last week from a stomach aneurysm has left his daughter, Victoria Carter, bereft.

Lockett died on July 22, five days before what would have been his 65th birthday.

The man she knew was generous, loving and warm although, yes, Lockett could be menacing. And, yes, Lockett hated the police.

Carter: “I said to dad recently, ‘Dad, I really love peace, calm and harmony’. He said, ‘I didn’t come to this planet to promote that. I promote nothing but chaos, mayhem and madness’.”

Many who knew Lockett will recognise that. Carter – talking to the Herald on what would have been her dad’s birthday – though, says there was more.

“At the same time, he was very gentle, loving and soft. Underneath it all, he had a very gentle soul. I saw another side to dad not everyone got to know.”

When the Herald began calling people after his death, some declined to speak. Told Lockett had died, one said: “Good.” Another said: “I don’t want to speak ill of the dead”.

I first met Lockett more than two decades ago. “He loved the media,” Carter told me. Mostly he did, but over the years he alternately threatened me, tipped me off, and invited me for a cuppa.

Lockett brought chaos into the lives of many, especially those who believed they held power over him. He frightened some badly, and sometimes deliberately, while those closest experienced him as a funny, generous and gentle giant.

At an easy 1.9m in socks, Lockett at his peak seemed almost as broad.

Thick arms ended with a couple of ham-hock hands that were capable of surprisingly subtle work – Lockett spent hours hunched over a laptop, thin glasses perched on the end of his nose, tapping out a fresh legal summons or a letter intended to expose what he believed was corruption in the state.

As physically menacing as he could be, his real satisfaction came from the imagined damage caused by a court summons or private prosecution.

Lockett was an Auckland Grammar boy who grew up on the more comfortable side of Auckland, son of the managing director of the successful Morgan Furniture.

At Grammar he met property developer Mark Lyon. By the early 2000s Lyon’s life had descended into methamphetamine use and scandal.

Lockett was Lyon’s bodyguard and minder at the millionaire’s Remuera mansion, regularly clearing it of party-goers and sex workers when all threatened to spin out of control.

In the end, there was too much to control. It was Lockett guarding the remnants of Lyon’s Remuera mansion after it caught fire in 2002 when journalist Donna Chisholm arrived at the gates.

An angry and seething Lockett was at the front gates holding a samurai sword. “I’m going to kill a man,” he said.

A week or so later, I met Lockett inside the mansion. We met in a long hallway – Lockett creeping toward me in a ninja stance, sword raised above his head. “I thought I was going to have to kill you,” he said after we had introduced ourselves.

When school finished, Lockett trained then worked as a mechanic. He travelled and lived overseas before returning to work at the furniture business his father ran, then later as a bouncer on nightclub doors. Budokan karate was a significant influence, leading to a lifelong passion for martial arts.

Lockett would tell people he was a ninja. When he played rugby, that was his name on the field.

His great pride was NZ Tracers and Investigations, the repossession and people-finding business he built in the late 1990s.

Carter, 34, remembers adventures. “I remember when I was little going out spying. Then his repo days got a little bit scary.”

Lockett took on jobs others would avoid. He would take back cars from the loosest and roughest places in Auckland.

And he was good at the work. He knew systems and how the courts and government worked. He knew those pathways you could follow to find home addresses, phone numbers, family members – all critical for repossession work and debt recovery.

Car dealer John Murphy recalls hiring Lockett. Finance payments weren’t being made on a vehicle; others had tried and failed to recover it.

“I’d heard of Jamie. I rang him up. All of a sudden the car comes back on a transporter.” Somewhat disbelieving at his rapid success, Murphy took possession of the car and paid Lockett his fee.

“I thought, ‘We’ll use you again’. Then the finance company rang and said not to. They said, ‘We don’t tolerate people who pull out spearguns’.”

Murphy recalls Lockett as the life of the party, at the time, and always with “girls on his arms”.

“People grew up and moved on. Jamie was still very much a teenager at heart.” In Murphy’s eyes, that never really changed.

By the early 2000s, Lockett was fully beyond the rigid rails his Grammar classmates rode to corporate leadership and riches. The turmoil of the fire at Lyon’s mansion and the drama that followed ramped up his frustrations with the world.

Lockett looked at that inflexible pathway his classmates had taken and just wanted to smash it. To Lockett, such a route created a power structure. When some take power, others lose it. He railed against the exercise of power by those who had it, especially the police.

As he would tell it, that began when - allegedly - a police officer spat in one of his shoes. His relationships with gang members also likely brought him increasingly close to people under police scrutiny.

Lockett did not see himself as a criminal, despite convictions and a willingness to cross legal lines. He saw himself as siding with people he believed had been abused by a system he had set himself against.

Lockett formed friendships with gang members, including men whose lives had been shaped by state care and abuse. He tended to deal with individuals rather than patches and had little affection for those who attached themselves to organised crime groups during the early methamphetamine boom-times of the late 1990s and 2000s. To hear Lockett tell of it, that was just another power structure.

This, and his own particular way of engaging with authority, meant his name and face became well-known to those charged with enforcing the law.

Documents show Lockett was first convicted of a crime in 2004, picking up convictions for assault, trespass and threatening behaviour in the years that followed.

He was arrested on dozens of occasions. Aside from those convictions, Lockett asserted in an interview in 2008 that he had faced 100 charges in the district court and had beaten every single one.

Examination of those cases at the time revealed no fancy lawyer’s work. Rather, Lockett was so aggressively irritating to the police officers he encountered that critical errors (and sometimes elbows) occurred during the arrest process and poisoned the case against him.

A staple in Lockett’s life was Murphy. For a period, Murphy provided a home for Lockett and Carter at his comfortable, multimillion-dollar Remuera mansion.

It was there in 2005 that the Grammar boy and the Irishman became campaigners for Māori sovereignty. I watched Lockett and Murphy attach and fly a tino rangatiratanga flag on the front lawn.

They hooted with laughter at the idea of upset Victoria Ave neighbours, but both Lockett and Murphy had adopted a different lens to view New Zealand’s history. For Lockett, what began partly as provocation developed into a serious engagement with Māori sovereignty and New Zealand’s colonial history.

Carter remembers her dad’s enthusiasm for New Zealand’s story, including the days before Europeans turned up. “It was in his soul.”

For Lockett, his embrace of Māori sovereignty led to his connection with others of similar views and then his arrest in the Operation Eight raids.

Carter’s memory of that time is of constant police surveillance, oppressive to the teenager she was becoming. Lockett would be on the television news and in newspapers.

Carter: “He was fighting for freedom. He always said ‘I’m fighting for New Zealand’”.

He also said at the time: “I’m going to war on this country.”

Lockett was never convicted over Operation Eight. In September 2011, the Supreme Court ruled on the legality and admissibility of covert surveillance evidence gathered during the investigation. Charges were dropped against Lockett and 12 others.

For Lockett, it was just another Monday. He had plenty of other battles he was fighting, mischief to cause and laughs to have.

One episode from around that time captured Lockett in miniature: menace, mischief and work most people would not touch.

Lockett had been hired by a landowner whose debts cost him a piece of land he did not want to relinquish. His task was to scare off anyone turning up to the remote property in the northwest of Auckland.

When the new owner turned up with a Herald journalist and photographer in tow, Lockett growled and stomped, then charged towards the car. The terrified visitors bolted and left.

An hour later, as the journalist and photographer regaled the newsroom with their “brush with death” story, Lockett was sitting in a cafe across from the newsroom showing another journalist - me - the video he had captured of the encounter.

He howled with laughter over a flat white and a cheese scone. It was all pantomime to Lockett. For those on the receiving end, it was awful.

Lockett embraced and rejected the label of anti-establishment. Rather, he hated what he saw as injustice. He saw the establishment – and particularly the police – as perpetrating that.

For decades he delighted in calling officers “poo-lice”, drawing out and separating the syllables as offensively as possible. When he saw a police constable, he was delighted because he knew how careful and deliberate mispronunciation of that rank would cause fury.

Lockett never stopped. Just weeks before he died, he fired off an email to Police Commissioner Richard Chambers loaded with legal language, facts and claims. “He was still very much fighting them until the day he died,” Carter said.

By then, Lockett was long gone from Auckland. There was a period in Tauranga when he pinned his hopes on a boat called Green Pastures that he had dreamed of sailing out of the harbour and into a life of freedom.

“Then the boat got seized,” Carter recalls.

She said her dad had also been “trespassed from Tauranga, from the whole city”.

From there, Lockett went to Northland, living in Paihia and then Haruru. He found new causes, new friends, new police officers to irritate.

I last spoke to Lockett at the NZ First election party in Russell, in the Bay of Islands. He was in fine fettle, told me my job was to hold people to account and that I hadn’t done enough. I last heard from him a few months ago when he told me he wanted to kill me. The message before that was an enthusiastic offer to drop by for a chat.

Carter, always close to her dad, moved to the North for a while and spent time. She was there the night of the election party, and for other memorable moments that are now a cherished and finite pool of memories. They sailed together, won a regatta, shared a home, and recorded content for a podcast she intended to create with her dad.

It started with Operation Eight.

“I wanted to dive into dad’s brain and find out how that happened.

But there were so many places it could have gone. For a long time, Carter was a part of Lockett’s unpredictable ride.

“I wouldn’t change a thing in my life. It shaped me,” she said.

Last week, Carter had not heard from her dad for a few days and was worried. “He always answered my calls.” A welfare check on Wednesday morning found Lockett dead.

So now Carter grieves. A celebration is planned for August or September. It will be well-attended. It’s likely, given some of those who will want to come, that police will also attend.

They won’t be welcome, which is just how Lockett would want it.

David Fisher is based in Northland and has worked as a journalist for more than 30 years, winning multiple journalism awards including being twice named Reporter of the Year and being selected as one of a small number of Wolfson Press Fellows to Wolfson College, Cambridge. He joined the Herald in 2004.

Family of a man and woman killed on Auckland’s North Shore say they are “shattered” as they come to grips with the tragedy.

Two people described by neighbours as “nice, quiet people” were found dead and a third person was injured at two homes in neighbouring suburbs on Tuesday night.

A 41-year-old man has been charged with two counts of murder and one of attempted murder.

A nephew of the slain couple who lives overseas, told the Herald the family is “shattered” by the tragedy.

He said his father had now lost his only surviving brother and is asking for privacy as he comes to term with his loss.

Police were called to a home on Seon Pl, Birkdale at 8.21pm after reports a person had been stabbed.

Acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie said a man at the home received moderate injuries and was taken to hospital.

The accused man was arrested at the scene.

After a conversation, a welfare check was done at a property on Lingfield St in Glenfield, 5km away, where a man and woman were found dead.

Goldie said there was no ongoing threat to the wider community.

“This is an awful set of events. I know this will leave many in our community unsettled, but what I can say at this early stage of the investigation is that the offender and victims are all known to each other,” she said.

No one else was being sought in relation to the incident.

A Lingfield St neighbour said about six police cars lined the street when he got home from work about 11pm.

He said he would occasionally stop and talk to the people living in the house, and that they were “nice, quiet people”.

“It’s very sad.”

A neighbour of the Seon Pl address told the Herald his mother ran into his room and told him to look outside.

“It was pretty scary. The street was lined with cops and there were about 10 of them with flashlights surrounding the property.

“Meanwhile, a guy was getting arrested out on the street.”

The accused man appeared in the North Shore District Court yesterday and entered no plea.

He is due to appear in the High Court at Auckland next month.

New Zealand’s skies have lit up for a second night in a row as skygazers report more suspected meteor sightings.

Experts confirmed on Tuesday night a fireball meteor had raced across the North Island sky, with reports of a very bright flash followed by thunderous booms.

Then last night from 8.30pm meteor sightings were again reported from across the North Island, including by skygazers in Auckland, Taranaki, Central Plateau, Bay of Plenty and Manawatū.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

One South Aucklander posted to a local community Facebook page they had seen a flash of light while walking up their driveway.

“It looked like a shooting star but after the flash it was still visible for about five seconds,” the person wrote - begging others to confirm the sighting as the rest of their household was questioning their sanity.

Another person was out fishing when they saw an apparent meteor, saying they were “mesmerised” by its glowing trail. it left behind.

Others reported a “flash in the sky then a trail towards Karioitahi Beach”, on Auckland’s southwest coast, a “bright green” light in the sky, and a “beautiful” shooting star darting low in the sky before burning out.

Reports came from Taupō, Wellington and Feilding, while one Masterton resident reported “huge loud booming and then a crackling like firecrackers”, saying they had been “a [teensy] bit scared” by the end.

Newstalk ZB’s Marcus Lush Nights also received a flurry of reports, with one person spotting the meteor while bringing in the cows. Another said they had seen a meteor north of Stratford, saying it “exploded very quickly - all over in about three seconds”.

Commenters on Weatherwatch’s website reported seeing one or more meteorite flashes from 8.30pm to 9.30pm, including one travelling east to west over Auckland and another reporting a “fireball in Waiwera”.

“Saw a large meteorite high in the sky looking west down Khyber Pass in Auckland city,” another wrote. “Amazing to see such a bright shooting star with all the city lights!”

After Tuesday’s meteor sightings, Te Whatu Stardome head of education Kaitlyn Martin told the Herald a fireball is larger than a typical meteor, causing bright flashes where a typical meteor would just streak across the sky.

“What you’re actually seeing is that rock breaking into small pieces.

“It’s a little bit like the difference between burning a log or burning little chips of kindling or wood shavings.”

The rock breaking means more surface area, causing it to burn faster, she said.

“That’s why it very quickly goes from just looking like a normal meteor to having that bright bang, that bright light in the sky that you see in the video.”

The Prime Minister has defended taking two trips in Defence Force helicopters between Auckland and Hamilton, costing more than $20,000.

One of the choppers was used to pick up Christopher Luxon from Auckland to take him to a farmer’s rally at Mystery Creek in 2024, and another flew him from Tāmaki Makaurau to Hamilton for a visit to the Kmart distribution hub in April last year, Stuff reports.

The Prime Minister travelled to the Mystery Creek function, a Federated Farmers public meeting, in a helicopter from the Royal New Zealand Navy.

The crew flew from Auckland’s Whenuapai Airbase to the Mechanics Bay helipad in the central city before going to Hamilton, at a cost of $7650.

When travelling to the Kmart distribution centre, a chopper flew to Auckland from Ohakea Air Base near Palmerston North and then to Hamilton.

The chopper went back to Auckland before returning to the Manawatū Defence Force base, according to the publication.

The 5.9 hours of flying cost $12,691.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister told Stuff that using Defence Force flights may cost the taxpayer less than using commercial flights.

“The New Zealand Defence Force is required to fly their aircraft regularly to maintain operational readiness and aircrew must complete a set number of flying hours each year. Therefore, taking the Prime Minister, accompanying staff and security personnel on these flights does not impose additional cost to the taxpayer.

“Given that, we’d note the cost to the taxpayer may, in fact, be less than it would have been if commercial flights had been used,” the spokesperson said.

Google Maps shows travelling from Mechanics Bay to Mystery Creek is around a one hour and 30 minute drive.

Driving from Mechanics Bay to the Ruakura Superhub, where the Kmart distribution centre is, would take around one hour and 26 minutes.

Labour’s Kieran McAnulty told Stuff there were other viable options for the Prime Minister to get to Hamilton, such as driving.

He said using the Defence Force when there are emergencies, severe weather or tragedies was legitimate, but Luxon’s use in this case “doesn’t quite sit right”.

Documents obtained by Stuff showed Luxon has taken 41 domestic flights with the Defence Force, which did not appear to be related to a disaster or emergency response, it reported.

In 2008, the Brumby Labor government declared the EastLink tollway open. It was delivered on budget and five months ahead of schedule.

Between 2014 and 2018, Daniel Andrews’ government removed 29 level rail crossings, also on time and budget – a feat that helped him convincingly win a second term as premier. As Liberal scion Michael Kroger remarked after the 2018 landslide, new infrastructure was “a very visual sign of a government doing something”.

To Labor, this seemed like both good policy and good politics – and under Andrews and his transport minister, Jacinta Allan, the government’s ambitions grew exponentially.

1:03

New Victorian premier to call Royal Commission

Ben Carroll has said he will call for a Royal Commission into the construction industry in his first act as premier of Victoria.

Eight years later, Labor faces an uphill battle for a fourth term, and Allan is the nation’s least popular politician by far. On Tuesday, she was humiliatingly blasted out of her job.

The story of what happened in Victoria has emerged, piece by piece, in hundreds of investigative news stories in The Age, The Sydney Morning Herald, the Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes over more than two years. A commission of inquiry holding public hearings in Queensland has brought out more, as has a scathing report by anti-corruption investigator Geoffrey Watson.

Until now, though, Labor in Victoria has shown little interest in peering under the rock. Allan’s successor, Ben Carroll, promised to change this and announced a royal commission. It will run in parallel to Labor’s campaign for re-election in November.

This scandal has its roots in 2014, the year of Andrews’ first victory. That year, a small group of men started moving to Melbourne from Queensland, where they represented a union, the Builders’ Labourers’ Federation, the subject of a much earlier industrial scandal.

When these men arrived, they were welcomed with open arms into the Victorian CFMEU. Ushering them through the door was long-time chief John Setka.

What they then set about doing has likely cost the state billions. It’s wrecked the reputation of a once-proud union, cost the premier her job, brought a 12-year-old government to its knees and scandalised a state.

By the time he quit Brisbane for Melbourne in 2014, construction union organiser Joe Myles already had a long rap sheet. In 2010, he delayed a $350 million building project in Brisbane and called a supervisor a “f---ing little grub”. He was fined $5000. It was the first of more than 20 times Myles was to be hauled through the courts for coercion, obstruction, breaching safety laws and causing illegal stoppages.

The broader union movement, believing the industrial laws to be bad, and therefore worthy of being broken, made no apologies. So when a factional dispute in Queensland saw Myles and a number of other BLF officials kicked out in 2014, nobody questioned Setka’s willingness to take them in.

The Victorian strongman put Myles in charge of an outpost of his operation – civil construction.

Until then, the CFMEU almost exclusively represented workers on big-city construction sites. It was lucrative and centralised work. Another union, the Australian Workers’ Union, had a near monopoly over civil work – roads, bridges and other infrastructure.

Long disparaged in labour movement circles as “the boss’s union”, the AWU struck reasonable agreements and stuck to them. It was under these deals that EastLink was built and the level crossings removed.

“Most of the work is in local government, and there’s not much money in it,” Watson told this masthead.

But as Victorian Labor’s infrastructure ambitions grew, the equation changed. Apart from the expanding level crossing removal program, Andrews and his transport minister, Allan, backed the West Gate Tunnel road project, announced in 2015 with a price tag of $5.5 billion, the Metro train tunnel in 2016 at $10.9 billion, the North East Link road promised in 2019 at $15.8 billion, and the big one, the Suburban Rail Loop, promised in 2018 for $50 billion.

“All of a sudden, the money is huge,” Watson said, “and it becomes very attractive [for the CFMEU] to move in on it.”

Myles was just the man to do it. He moved against the AWU, and hard.

On a Regional Rail Link site in 2013, Myles insisted that a large builder appoint a CFMEU delegate. When the builder argued that the AWU was already on site, Myles blockaded it and stopped a concrete pour. Fifty-nine tonnes of concrete was wasted. A Federal Court judge fined Myles and the union, saying the official had “a deplorable history of offending”.

To rid a site of the AWU, Watson wrote in a report tabled at the Queensland inquiry, Myles and the CFMEU used bogus safety claims, illegal industrial action, threats, violence and verbal abuse. Behind him as he issued these threats was a group of frightening men – many of them bikies or former bikies.

“Several had convictions for violent crimes – one had killed a man,” Watson wrote.

One was Joel Leavitt – a CFMEU health and safety representative and alleged “full-time bikie” with the Rebels. Watson described him as “an allegedly brutal criminal” well known to police. One night in 2023, Leavitt was shot at the Rebels clubhouse in Melbourne and dropped at hospital in his government-funded, Big Build-provided car.

Other CFMEU officials at the time had drug-trafficking convictions. One was a professional boxer with close personal ties to underworld figure Mick Gatto.

These men were making industrial demands on behalf of the CFMEU underpinned by a “pervasive” threat of violence, Watson wrote. As the AWU melted away, big building firms capitulated to the CFMEU’s demands to buy temporary industrial peace.

On one site, sources claimed to The Age investigative reporter Nick McKenzie, they were helped to make their decision by pressure from then-minister Jacinta Allan’s office.

Until June 2022, a level crossing removal site in Sunbury called Gap Road was covered by an AWU enterprise agreement and an associated labour hire company supplying the workers. Myles insisted the CFMEU control the site, and a labour hire firm close to him, BK Labour, take over the contract.

The builders, CPB and John Holland, resisted, knowing how much CFMEU involvement would increase both the cost and the difficulty of the project. They reported their concerns to the government that, according to McKenzie’s reporting, the CFMEU’s presence would add an extra $2 million labour hire cost for taxpayers.

The government officials overseeing the project then passed onto CPB and Holland a reply from the office of the minister, Allan. They felt they were asked: “Could they just cut a deal with the CFMEU?” To fail to do so, project sources told McKenzie, might risk their chances of winning another lucrative contract on the forthcoming airport rail project. The builders cut the deal. Allan, this month, denied the claims her office had intervened.

Over six or eight years, the CFMEU takeover of Victoria’s Big Build was virtually complete.

Once in control, the union and its hangers-on extracted the spoils. Ultimately, wrote Watson in his investigative report, “the Setka-led Victorian branch of the CFMEU was no longer a trade union, it was a crime syndicate”.

The CFMEU had the power to say who worked on a site and who did not. Among those whom their delegates approved were members of outlaw motorcycle gangs. Eventually, all the gangs were represented, Watson says: the Rebels, Hells Angels, Finks, Bandidos, Comanchero and Mongols. In some places, they wielded huge influence.

One project, the Hurstbridge rail upgrade, became the site of a turf war between Comanchero and Rebels gang members – all union members and delegates – in which patched Comancheros spent hours circling the site on their motorcycles after the Rebels ousted them.

“According to intelligence sources, this stare-down was actually a fight over which bikie gang would be permitted to control drug distribution,” Watson wrote in his report. “Picture 200 or more men aged between 18 and 30, each earning well over $100,000, confined within the area of a single building site – that is a drug dealer’s dream.”

CFMEU officials installed friends and family to lucrative positions. Many “worked” ghost shifts – being paid big money by labour hire firms associated with the CFMEU and not turning up. On some projects, McKenzie reported this was suspected to have cost millions of dollars.

Leavitt, the Rebels member and CFMEU delegate, ran a pay-to-work operation, Watson reported, demanding potential employees pay him cash in return for getting a job – then occasional further payments to keep it.

On particularly lucrative shifts on the Hurstbridge rail upgrade, CFMEU gatekeepers had charged workers outright cash fees of $500 to $1000 just to be placed on the roster, McKenzie reported.

This was nothing compared with the CFMEU’s own extortion – for a builder to get a contract on a Big Build site required an enterprise bargaining agreement (EBA) with the union. The CFMEU, not the government, controlled which companies could work on the site. No actual bargaining was entered into – companies were forced to buy the union’s template – and depending on the contract, Watson wrote, the going rate ranged between $250,000 and $1 million.

“Under Setka’s leadership, CFMEU EBAs were bought and sold as commodities on a kind of black market,” he wrote.

2:09

First day of hearings in CFMEU inquiry

Geoffrey Watson SC was called as a witness in the first day of hearings in the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU in Queensland.

The union also bestowed lucrative EBAs on companies run by friends. “John Setka is one who confers these favours,” Watson said. “Gatto and his friends … beneficiaries.”

Among those who won a sought-after EBA was a company called Women in Construction. As McKenzie reported in May, the company won Big Build contracts encouraged by Labor’s gender equity policy, but the company was actually owned by a male serial domestic violence abuser and managed by a male convicted drug trafficker also accused of family violence.

The atmosphere for women on some sites was appalling, Watson reported. Women workers were recruited from strip clubs then paid cash to perform in the shed during work hours.

1:51

CFMEU officials in abusive confrontation on major project

Two officials threatening a labour hire operator at a construction site

One shocking outcome came early in the reporting. He revealed allegations of threats made by CFMEU senior organiser Joel Shackleton to the Aboriginal owner of a company working with an AWU enterprise agreement.

Shackleton was caught on video telling the owner he would “f---ing end you, c--- … I’ll f---ing take your soul and I’ll rip your f---ing head off”. Shackleton was later charged over these comments and is fighting the case in the courts.

One of the company’s former employees, Ben Nash, working his very first shift for a new firm, was told he would never be welcome on the site because the CFMEU didn’t like his old employer. He was told to “f--- off”, then, according to his mother, was “locked in a shed for three or four hours – just a young boy with mental health issues”.

After this shift, Nash returned home. He died that night after taking too much prescription medication. His mother blames the CFMEU.

Emails revealed last year show Victorian government ministers, MPs and a senior staffer in Allan’s office were told about the CFMEU’s campaign against the Indigenous firm. In the lead-up to the 2022 state election, they promised to do something. After they won the election, those commitments disappeared. The Indigenous-owned company eventually collapsed because of a lack of work.

Then there was Gatto. When disputes arose between the CFMEU and anyone else, the underworld figure – a mate of Setka – swooped in, for a fee. Up to 15 building companies, according to McKenzie, were making regular “retainer” payments to the infamous standover man, and other underworld figures, to prevent their site being shut down and costing them a fortune.

In his report, Watson called this the “Gatto extortion model”. It had all the hallmarks of an old-fashioned protection racket.

Site closures could cost contractors anywhere between $50,000 and $500,000 a day. Watson wrote that by “protecting” them from industrial issues, Gatto was earning well over $5 million a year.

Gatto has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Some of that money, of course, was ultimately paid by taxpayers – mostly in Victoria but also nationally due to federal government contributions – as part of the escalating costs of the Big Build.

How much did it cost? Some projects, such as the North East Link, more than doubled their original multibillion-dollar budget. Every other Big Build project has undergone multimillion-dollar hikes, though the full accounting is difficult to discern from available information.

It’s clear, though, that unlike EastLink and the early level crossing removals, these projects will not be delivered on time and on budget. A current estimate is that the full suite of projects will cost taxpayers $109 billion – enough to drive Victoria into multi-generational debt.

Watson made a guess – which he says is conservative and based on interviews with an experienced industry insider and other witnesses – of about how much was wasted via union corruption alone. The figure was $15 billion.

McKenzie’s reporting shows Jacinta Allan was involved, as the minister responsible for the Big Build, or premier, a number of times.

The Gap Road allegation suggests that in 2022, Allan’s ministerial office pressured the builder to agree to replace the AWU with the CFMEU. The demand was made, according to the allegation reported, under an implied threat that the builder might miss out on future work if they did not. Allan has denied this was the case.

The following year, 2023, Allan was briefed on corruption in the Big Build by public servants warning her of malfeasance, McKenzie reported. She did not sign their briefing note and said this week she had never seen it. In the same year, she attended the funeral of John Setka’s father.

In May 2024, Allan was given a “Consolidated Issues Document” by a senior figure inside the Metro Tunnel project. The document showed labour costs had blown out from $299 million to $901 million, with $200 million attributed to “industrial action … which is a direct result of an act or omission of the state”. The builder threatened to sue the government and Allan ultimately approved an $837 million no-admission payout in response.

In July that year, McKenzie began his reporting, along with a team of journalists from this masthead, the Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes. After they sent questions to Setka, the union chief resigned immediately.

4:12

Victorian premier quizzed after CFMEU allegations

Nick McKenzie has quizzed Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan after an investigation by this masthead, AFR and 60 Minutes sparked a construction industry crisis.

When the first report appeared in this masthead and on 60 Minutes, the Albanese government appointed an administrator to the union, who set about the task of trying to clean it out. Mark Irving took on the role and was quickly receiving death threats, along with ACTU secretary Sally McManus, then-workplace relations minister Murray Watt, and McKenzie. Irving hired security. McManus has revealed she left Melbourne for a time. McKenzie moved house.

Allan responded by suspending the CFMEU’s Labor Party affiliation, stopping its political donations and referring the matters to Victoria Police and the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission.

She also commissioned a report – with a tight time frame – by former Department of Justice secretary Greg Wilson, and insisted she had “zero tolerance” for intimidating behaviour.

The Wilson report came back just before Christmas in 2024. It failed to identify any specific instances of corruption or criminal infiltration and did not hold any official or politician to account. IBAC, Victoria’s under-equipped anti-corruption agency, said it could not accept Allan’s referral because it did not have sufficient powers.

After that, Allan’s response was a combination of tough talk and weak action.

The Wilson report, which recommended a few administrative changes, was intended to “help us tear a rotten culture out by its roots”, she insisted.

But Watson – who was working for Irving’s administration – dismissed the Victorian report as akin to a cover-up. This was not any fault of Wilson, he stressed. It was because the scope of his investigation had been so limited.

Repeatedly, Allan urged people to refer matters to police, and expressed puzzlement that they would not take that route. Police told McKenzie people were too terrified to speak, and that Victoria Police was not the right agency to unpack the allegations – some of them criminal, some not.

This month, Allan apologised in an opinion piece published in this newspaper.

“Like every state and every major economy, Victoria experienced inflation over the past decade,” she wrote, insisting none of the many warnings about criminal infiltration and intimidation unearthed in McKenzie’s reporting had made it to her at the time.

“We now know that criminals operated on some of Victoria’s construction sites. There was violence, intimidation and organised criminal behaviour. That is shocking and unacceptable. It should never have happened … I’m deeply sorry that it happened on projects funded by the Victorian people. Now the question is how we stop it happening again.”

If that was the question, she was adamant the answer was not a royal commission. She told her colleagues it would be costly and time-consuming and would fail to change the culture in the state. They would just have to “grind it out”, she said.

But as the election approached and her approval rating plummeted, this refusal began to look like evasion. Her detractors in the party room circled, and as the ongoing revelations drowned out almost all other political conversation in Victoria, Allan made one last attempt. On Monday, to a group of ministers who had already turned against her, she put a proposal to beef up police powers.

It was too little too late.

“I saw nothing to suggest that she was personally corrupt,” Watson told this masthead after her resignation on Tuesday. “I just believe she was an inept politician in the way she managed these affairs with the CFMEU.”

Allan cannot avoid this legacy. She was there from the start. But, says Watson: “Politicians don’t like royal commissions because you don’t know what they’ll find. They can go anywhere. I feel as though she thought there was going to be some embarrassment.”

The original investigation: Explore the multipart investigation that plunged the construction industry into crisis.

Damning probe: Corruption buster Geoffrey Watson’s full report of his investigation into the CFMEU contained an extraordinarily damning exposé of corrupt and criminal behaviour.

The cost: ‘Extraordinary, unforeseeable’ and extremely costly: CFMEU price tag of each Metro station revealed.

Biggest projects affected: Eleven of the biggest infrastructure projects in Victoria – including the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop and North East Link – are the subject of 56 separate allegations of fraud, corruption, theft and criminal behaviour.

Administrator fights back: CFMEU’s new administrator has declared the culture in the union’s Victorian arm remains broken.

‘Grind it out’: Allan defends her royal commission refusal to cabinet. Should have called Saul: Economist’s verdict on inflation versus corruption.

Treatment of women: A company that secured huge contracts as the leading women-led supplier of female workers on Labor’s Big Build is owned by a male serial domestic violence abuser, was managed by a male drug trafficker also accused of family violence and has deep links to bikies and violent criminals.

Turmoil within the administration: The senior barrister appointed to clean up the corruption and crime-tainted CFMEU, Mark Irving, quit in a major challenge to the Albanese government’s attempts to reform the sector.

Warning to state: The Allan government’s infrastructure tsar privately warned the premier of serious wrongdoing on Labor’s $100 billion Big Build.

Hollywood producer charged with seven counts of wire fraud in $100m scheme

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 21:38:29 GMT

Jason Cloth of Joker and The Green Knight diverted funds from entertainment investors toward his personal life

A federal grand jury in Chicago has charged the Hollywood producer Jason Cloth with seven counts of wire fraud for allegedly defrauding investors of $100m, according to federal authorities.

Cloth, who has credits on the blockbuster 2019 film Joker and critically acclaimed hits like The Green Knight, told investors their funds would go toward a motion picture and a gaming entertainment investment platform, among other media-related projects, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in the US district court for the northern district of Illinois.

Instead, the grand jury found, Cloth diverted the money toward his personal life, including the development of a real estate project in Canada.

Cloth told some investors their funds were inaccessible due to the bankruptcy of a production company, which according to the indictment was a false claim. He also allegedly ran a Ponzi scheme, using funds from investors to pay back his previous investors.

Cloth’s alleged scheme lasted from 2019 to 2026.

If Cloth is convicted of the charges, he will have to forfeit at least $12.25m and could face a hefty prison sentence. Each count of wire fraud carries a maximum of 20 years behind bars.

Cloth has also been embroiled in civil litigation over allegations of fraud. A Florida jury ordered him to pay $19.6m to an investor on The Pathway, a TNT docuseries about the NBA draft, Variety reported in 2024.

“He’s made a career of telling people whatever they want to hear in order to get what he wants,” said David Jonelis, the attorney who represented the investor at the time, according to Variety.

Man who stabbed Salman Rushdie in 2022 convicted of federal terrorism charges

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 21:38:10 GMT

Jury found Hadi Matar, who is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence, guilty of all charges against him

A man was convicted on Wednesday of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing of Salman Rushdie, the author who has faced a decades-old death threat over his novel The Satanic Verses.

A jury found Hadi Matar guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.

Matar declined to take the stand, with his attorney Nathaniel Barone saying earlier this week: “At this time, the defense rests.”

Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction in the August 2022 attack on an amphitheater stage. The federal conviction carries a potential life sentence.

Prosecutors allege Matar shared propaganda videos before the attack and communicated with an Iran-based contact who claimed to know “where to find Rushdie”. They also say Matar asked whether the fatwa against Rushdie was still active.

Rushdie, who was about to speak on writers’ safety, was slashed 15 times in front of a stunned audience. He was gravely wounded and lost the sight in his right eye.

Speaking from the stand last February, Rushdie said: “I became aware of a great quantity of blood I was lying in. My sense of time was quite cloudy, I was in pain from my eye and hand, and it occurred to me quite clearly I was dying.”

Following the attack which also wounded Ralph Henry Reese, the moderator at Rushdie’s lecture which he was set to deliver, Rushdie was left permanently damaged in his right eye.

According to a federal indictment, Matar’s motivation for trying to kill Rushdie stemmed from a 2006 speech delivered by Hezbollah’s chief at the time, Hassan Nasrallah. In the speech, Nasrallah had endorsed a decades-old fatwa, or death warrant, placed on Rushdie by Iranian religious leaders more than 35 years ago as a result of his novel, The Satanic Verses, which won Rushdie the Booker prize in 1981.

In 2022, following Rushdie’s stabbing, Matar admitted to having read only “a couple pages” of the book which Iranian religious leaders denounced as blasphemous.

In April 2024, Rushdie, who was born in India and moved to Britain as a teenager, wrote a memoir on his attempted assassination, which he titled Knife.

“After I finished writing the memoir, almost immediately, it’s like a door in my head opened and the stories came back,” Rushdie said at Tulane University’s New Orleans book festival in March.

“I’d been really worried that I wouldn’t be able to write fiction any more … because of trauma and the shocking impact of what happened,” he added.

Rushdie also said he was tired of being everyone’s “free speech Barbie”, adding: “It’s a subject I’m anxious to change.”

“I don’t feel symbolic … I feel actual. I feel like I’m a working writer trying to make his work,” he said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

Trident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy Burnham

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 21:30:43 GMT

Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement

Andy Burnham will place the renewal of Trident at the heart of his vision of a reindustrialised Britain on Thursday when he travels to Barrow-in-Furness to launch the next phase of the nuclear submarine replacement programme.

The new prime minister intends to emphasise that defence spending on projects such as the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats built in the Cumbrian town is a case study of taxpayer investment revitalising communities around the UK.

“Keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government – but security is not only about what we build; it is about who builds it, and who benefits from it,” Burnham said ahead of his visit to England’s north-west.

A new phase of contracts worth £8.4bn, part of the already agreed Dreadnought programme, will help support 18,000 extra jobs in nuclear defence by 2030 and 22,000 additional apprentices by 2035, Downing Street said.

“To every young person across the country, I want you to know that there is a path for you into a reindustrialised Britain, and it starts with the apprenticeships we are funding through this investment today,” the prime minister added.

The visit also presents an opportunity to reinforce Burnham’s pro-Trident credentials. The prime minister voted to build the new submarines in 2016, when the Labour party split over the issue and its then leader, Jeremy Corbyn, voted against.

Wes Streeting, the new defence secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, were also among the MPs who voted in favour, though other another key figure in Burnham’s team, Louise Haigh, who runs the new office of the prime minister, voted no.

The UK’s military nuclear activities currently support 47,000 jobs, including 13,500 in the Barrow shipyard. Its surrounding constituency historically switched from Labour to Conservative, and was retaken by Labour at the last election in 2024.

Burnham, who has had limited previous engagement with foreign and defence policy, entered office just over a week ago and immediately lent into a Nato commitment to increase defence spending by over £25bn a year to reach 3.5% of GDP by 2035.

A row over whether his predecessor, Keir Starmer, was serious about the pledge led to the shock resignation of Healey as defence secretary last month. Starmer was so seriously undermined it precipitated his own departure.

When Healey quit, he also called for military budgets to hit 3% of GDP by 2030 as an interim target to show the UK was committed to the Nato goal. Starmer had only been willing to offer an increase to 2.68% of GDP.

But on Wednesday, at a press conference, Burnham declined to commit to hitting 3% by 2030. Instead he referred to the UK pledge to meet the Nato target to increase it to 3.5% of GDP by 2035, reiterating comments already made by Streeting and Healey.

“When it comes to defence, obviously those commitments … relate to the parliament after this one,” Burnham said. “In terms of our Nato commitments, I have been very clear that we will honour those commitments. It does mean being prepared to look at challenging issues,” he added.

The new Dreadnought submarines are intended to replace the ageing Vanguard-class submarines, one of which is always at sea carrying Britain’s nuclear deterrent. Each of the existing submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities.

The largest share of the latest phase of work in the Dreadnought programme is being awarded to BAE Systems, the owner of the Barrow shipyard. The British defence giant has been awarded a new £5.9bn contract to complete the build of the first four new boats, HMS Dreadnought, so it can be ready for service in early 2030s.

The work is part of the overall £31bn Dreadnought programme, which is so complex it includes a £10bn contingency to cover overspends. Concern about the scale of the programme has meant it has already been placed on amber alert by government procurement monitors.

Trident warheads are designed and built at AWE in Aldermaston and Burghfield in Berkshire, which employ 9,000, while a further 4,000 at Rolls-Royce in Derby help build the nuclear reactors that power the Dreadnought and other submarines used by the Royal Navy.

Fed holds interest rates steady despite Trump’s renewed calls to lower them

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 21:06:08 GMT

Rates remain unchanged for fifth time since December as tenuous Iran peace deal pushes energy prices up again

The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in a divided vote, indicating growing pressure on the central bank to address heightened inflation.

The Fed’s federal open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, with three dissenting members indicating a preference to raise the rate by a quarter-percentage point. It was the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision.

Cooler inflation data published earlier this month may have eased expectations for an imminent rate hike, but Kevin Warsh, the new Fed chair, said in a news conference that the committee was less interested in “any one piece of data” and was more focused on overall trends. The tenuous peace deal between the US and Iran has also sent energy prices creeping up again.

Warsh has repeated that he wants policy decisions to emerge from a “good family fight” and said on Wednesday he “got one” during his second Fed meeting as chair.

“Most of our discussion was on the big questions that matter to the conduct of monetary policy,” Warsh said. “We didn’t hide from them. We weren’t scared of them. There was a lot more interaction between my colleagues, it was a real family fight. My view, which you’ve long heard, is that’s the better way to get policy right.”

Just two weeks ago, one of the dissenting bank presidents, Lorie Logan of Dallas, made the case for “modestly higher interest rates”, arguing in public remarks that they would better balance the “outlook and risks” for the Fed’s dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.

“Inflation has been too high, for too long, and does not appear to be on track all the way back to 2%,” she said. “And the inflation risks are to the upside. The labor market, meanwhile, is solid. Without any policy restraint, these conditions are likely to continue until there’s an unanticipated shock.”

Logan joined Beth Hammack in Cleveland and Neel Kashkari in Minneapolis in the dissenting minority. The three bank presidents have formed a bloc before, most recently in April when they all disagreed with the committee’s decision to include a forward looking statement, or “easing bias”, in the Fed’s news release.

Though Warsh was adamant about delivering price stability in Wednesday’s news conference, it was unclear exactly what tools he planned to use to achieve that goal. While he said that interest rates could be used as “part of that solution”, he added: “I wouldn’t say it’s in isolation.”

Warsh has signaled he is ushering in a new era at the central bank, one that emphasizes a reservedness toward forward guidance. At his first meeting in June, he announced five new taskforces – comprising economics professors, business leaders and former central bank governors – that are meant to rethink how the Fed approaches its communications, data, balance sheet policy, inflation framework and the impact of artificial intelligence on its policy judgments.

The US-Israel war with Iran, which has endured since the end of February, has pushed energy prices higher for American households and businesses.

The Fed’s main tool to combat higher prices has traditionally been to hike interest rates, which raises borrowing costs and, in effect, cools the economy. But Trump has persistently and aggressively called for rate cuts since the start of his presidency, going so far as to attack the previous Fed chair, Jerome Powell – who is still on the Fed’s board – with verbal insults and target him with a Department of Justice investigation for failing to deliver.

Fed governors periodically release forward-looking projections illustrating when they think further rate changes will occur. Last month, half of all Fed members projected at least one rate increase this year, in a U-turn in outlook from just months earlier, when a majority of Fed members called for at least one rate cut over the same time period.

Wednesday’s decision is the fifth time rates have been left unchanged since December, despite Donald Trump’s renewed calls to lower rates.

Trump on Monday repeated his push for lower interest rates, adding that the US “should have the lowest rates in the world”.

Trump spared Warsh from any blame, calling him “fantastic” and implying Warsh would want to cut rates despite the opinions of his fellow board members, who Trump called “very political”.
