Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver for England

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 21:05:10 GMT

Ngake left Cameroon due to homosexuality laws

She fled from London 2012 village and slept rough

First Madias Ngake lifted the weight of an upright piano to her shoulders. Then, with another staggering act of power and defiance, she sent a 128kg barbell high above her head.

And, just like that, the 34-year-old Team England weightlifter had won a silver medal and written one of the most remarkable stories of these Games.

Fourteen years ago, Ngake fled the London 2012 Olympic village after finishing sixth in her competition and ended up sleeping rough for a month.

The reason? She was competing for Cameroon, where homosexuality is illegal, and someone in the team had found out that she was a lesbian. And so began a journey that led to Ngake giving up elite sport for more than a decade, deciding to come back in 2023, and then transferring allegiances to Britain a year later.

“When I left the Olympics in 2012 I got on a bus,” she explained. “After the last stop, they told me this is closed, so I can’t go anywhere. So I decided I will sleep outside at the bus stop. I slept rough for about a month. Nobody looked after me.

“I had to leave because someone on the team knew about my situation, that I am a lesbian.”

But having won a European medal earlier this year, Ngake showed her strength as she led the women’s 87kg competition after the first event, the snatch, with a powerful lift of 108kg.

That put her 3kg clear of Australia’s Eileen Cikamatana. However in the clean and jerk, Cikamatana was able to thrust a barbell 140kg over her head like it was a rag doll to score a combined lift of 245kg – a new Games record – to take gold by 6kg.

But Ngake was not too disappointed afterwards. Asked if her life was like a movie, she replied: “Yes. And I never believed I would ever be here.”

Ngake’s hair was dyed red, the colour of her home country. Afterwards she said that it had been the idea of Emily Campbell, Team GB’s double Olympic medallist, who competes on Thursday.

Ngake also explained it was only after 2017 that she was legally able to work. She was an office cleaner in Leeds for nine years, earning about £2,000 a year. However she has recently moved to Nottingham to train as a full-time athlete and hopes to make the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Amazingly, if she was to win an Olympic medal, it would be her second one. That’s because in 2019, she was awarded a bronze medal from London 2012 after three weightlifters who finished above her at the Games were disqualified for doping offences.

However, as the medal was sent to Cameroon, Ngake has never seen it as she has not been back to her home country.

“I would like to have it, yes,” she explained. “But I don’t think it’s going to be possible because the medal is in Cameroon and there is a situation and I don’t want to do politics.”

But Ngake knows how to do medals. And her adopted country were certainly delighted on Wednesday night.

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 19:56:46 GMT

Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival

No further action will be taken by police after Zack Polanski shared a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.

The Metropolitan police’s decision comes after the Green party leader for England and Wales said he had made an “inadvertent mistake” and would not apologise to Nigel Farage.

Polanski told the BBC’s Newsnight programme he had accepted a request to collaborate with a photographer on Instagram, with the first photo in a set of 20 showing himself, and the fifth showing the T-shirt.

The image was later removed from Polanski’s feed, with the Greens saying the T-shirt was “clearly in poor taste”. Polanski told Newsnight: “As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down.”

A Met spokesperson said: “We absolutely understand the reaction to this image being shared online, particularly in the context of increasing threats toward politicians.

“While there will be people who will argue that those who shared the image in this Instagram post should be subject to criminal action, our review has concluded that on this occasion, the threshold is not met.”

Polanski repeatedly ruled out apologising to Farage. “If I’d done it deliberately, I’d be apologising,” he said. “But because this was a mistake, I think the important thing is that I point out it’s a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence and also crucially make a commitment to be better on my social media.”

Reform UK had reported Polanski to the Metropolitan police. Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, accused him of “inciting murder”. Farage called for Polanski to be arrested.

But the Met said that after “conducting inquiries” it had concluded that it was unlikely that the sharing of the image online would constitute a criminal offence.

However, it added that the wearing of the T-shirt should be recorded as a crime and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset police, which covers Bristol, where the photo was taken.

Writing in the Daily Mail, Farage said Polanski must “face the consequences of his appalling decisions”, adding: “Political violence is real, it is serious, it needs dealing with.”

Polanski stressed on Newsnight: “This was not my post, it was a collaboration from a photographer. It had 20 images and I just didn’t look carefully enough and I accepted it.

“As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down. I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it’s quite obvious that I’ve not done anything wrong other than making an inadvertent mistake. That being said, if the police do want to talk to me, of course I’m very happy to cooperate.”

A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: “It’s truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won’t apologise for inciting murder. He admits it was wrong. He admits it’s dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party.”

Stephen Fleming to be appointed England Test coach after impressing ECB

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 19:30:36 GMT

New Zealander will succeed Brendon McCullum

Likely to start on South Africa tour in December

Stephen Fleming is expected to be named as England’s Test coach, after impressing the England and Wales Cricket Board in a series of interviews over the past two weeks. The 53-year-old would work alongside his predecessor, compatriot, former teammate and friend Brendon McCullum, who remains in charge of the white-ball teams.

Fleming stood down as head coach of the Indian Premier League franchise Chennai Super Kings – as well as their subsidiaries Joburg Super Kings in South Africa’s SA20 and Texas Super Kings in America’s Major League Cricket – this month. That announcement was made after CSK finished eighth out of 10 teams in this year’s IPL, following on from a last-place finish in 2025, but also less than 24 hours after McCullum was sacked by the ECB as Test coach.

It is expected Fleming will be in place for the tour of South Africa starting in December, but the three-Test series against Pakistan that begins at Headingley on 19 August may still be overseen by an interim, probably Marcus Trescothick.

Fleming has extensive experience of English cricket, not just from playing 10 Tests and 17 ODIs in this country between 1994 and 2004, but also from spells at Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire. He also coached Southern Brave in the Hundred for two years, leaving in 2024.

He was approached by England in 2009, shortly after he retired as a player, only to turn them down. “I was flattered to be offered,” he said. “It came down to the fact it wasn’t my time. If I get another couple of years [as a coach] I can see if it is what I want to do and if I would be any good at it.”

England ended up turning to Andy Flower, who, having been the early frontrunner to replace McCullum, has now returned the favour by rejecting the job and opening the door for Fleming’s appointment.

Fleming’s relationship with McCullum gave him an advantage over his rivals for the England job, the Australian Tom Moody, the former England batter and Afghanistan coach Jonathan Trott and Richard Dawson, the head coach at Glamorgan.

Beyond their friendship, the pair have been business associates at two companies, the software company CricHQ and the export business Quality New Zealand. Daniel Vettori, another former New Zealand captain coaching in England, at Sunrisers Leeds, described the pair as “very good friends” with “a lot of similar traits”.

Two people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct of a sexual nature by Jeffrey Epstein, a major donor, according to an investigation that also uncovered dozens of allegations spanning decades against nearly 50 other people.

Interlochen Center for the Arts operates a summer camp and performing arts school that draws students from around the world. It hired a law firm in 2024 to investigate reports of sexual abuse by faculty and staff. Subsequently, it expanded the work to include information about Epstein, the 66-year-old financier who killed himself in jail in 2019.

Interlochen removed Epstein’s name from a lodge after he was convicted of sex offenses in Florida in 2008. The building, renamed the Green Lake Lodge, was recently demolished after the US justice department released millions of pages about him that had been compiled over the years.

Sanghavi law office says it collected 70 accounts from alumni alleging “physical conduct of a sexual nature” by 47 faculty and staff members affiliated with Interlochen from the 1950s through the 2010s, most before 2000.

“The information gathered during this investigation is, simply, devastating,” the 97-page report says, noting that alumni reported grooming, flirting, sexual touching and sex.

Interlochen said it has provided names of people accused of misconduct to Grand Traverse county authorities in northern Michigan to determine what steps, if any, might be taken. None are currently employed there and more than a third are dead.

“We are deeply sorry for the harm experienced by members of our community and extend our apologies to those impacted by abuse at Interlochen,” president Trey Davey and board chair Barrett Rollins said in a letter to the community posted online.

“While the vast majority of the incidents described in the investigation took place many decades ago, and reports of abuse at Interlochen have significantly decreased over the past 25 years, the passage of time does not diminish the experiences of our alumni,” they said. “Sexual abuse committed by an adult in a position of power or trust against a student is wrong, then and now.”

Interlochen today “is fundamentally different from the institution described in this report”, Davey and Rollins wrote, with comprehensive safety policies and a changed culture.

Epstein, who played the bassoon, was an Interlochen camper in 1967. He donated more than $400,000 to the school between 1990 and 2003.

Two women told investigators that Epstein engaged in conduct of a sexual nature with them, one of them at the Interlochen lodge that bore his name.

He brushed against her body “over her clothes, in a manner in which he indicated was accidental”, according to the report.

Epstein also paid for her to visit him in New York while she was a student. She said “every time he was ‘handsy’ with her, she would freeze until he would stop”, the report states.

The other woman said she gave Epstein a massage at his home, according to the report, and he may have asked her to remove her top. She never had any further contact with Epstein or his girlfriend, Ghislaine Maxwell.

Outside of the school investigation, at least two Interlochen alumnae made allegations of grooming and abuse against Epstein and Maxwell, according to federal records and media reports. Their identities were not made public.

One testified against Maxwell in 2021 when she was convicted of sex trafficking. It is unclear whether those women spoke to the law firm hired for the Interlochen investigation.

Hackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and police

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 19:10:32 GMT

Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals

The Department for Education and a police database have been targeted by a cyber-attack, exposing more than 740,000 pieces of data.

Details of government officials, senior school leaders, university staff, police officers and members of the public have been taken by hackers.

Just over 600,000 lines of data have been stolen from the DfE’s help-desk portal. They show parent and staff contacts including full names, email addresses, phone numbers and job titles, according to a “leak” website set up by the hackers.

A smaller package of similar data has been taken from the department’s Turing portal, which manages a scheme for students studying abroad.

The hackers have also breached the police national legal database (PNLD), which provides legal assistance to UK police forces. The cybercriminals claimed to have taken 135,000 pieces of data.

The PNLD said the details taken related to “police officers and those working in criminal justice including their name, the force or organisation they work for and their work email address”.

Some names and addresses of members of the public who had previously submitted a question to the Ask the Police service had also been taken. It said the database did not hold confidential victim, witness or offender information.

While embarrassing, the breach of the police legal database is not thought to be serious.

A previously unknown hacking gang calling itself ExfilSquad claimed it had carried out the attack and posted samples of the data on its leak site, a typical gambit for cybercriminals seeking money for the information they have stolen.

The hackers are demanding a payment from the DfE and PNLD in exchange for not posting all the data, according to screen grabs seen by the Guardian.

The message states that only a small sample of data has been posted for now but indicates that all of it will be uploaded if the DfE, PNLD and other hacking victims do not make an unspecified payment.

“The payment we request of you is simply a rounding error compared to the litigation costs of your data leaking. Be smart and just pay,” said the gang.

The message is apparently directed at 14 hacking victims including the DfE. The list of alleged victims includes a UK university that has been contacted by the Guardian.

Sophos, a cybersecurity company that provided the screenshots, said the data samples appeared to be legitimate. It added that an account on the social media platform X apparently belonging to the group had been suspended but had been illustrated by a picture of a cybersecurity researcher who had been targeted before by members of the Com, a sprawling ecosystem of native English-speaking hackers.

However, it is understood that the DfE has not seen evidence that ransomware – a type of malicious software that locks up a victim’s IT systems – had been deployed in the hack.

The Times, which first reported the DfE hack, said the data included details of government officials, senior school leaders and university staff. The DfE is responsible for early years, schools, higher and further education in England.

The PNLD hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.

One senior source briefed on the PNLD leak said: “The risk is low. The question is, if you use your password for the PNLD, do you use it for more sensitive systems?”

The database is hosted by West Yorkshire police and is open for forces across England and Wales to view.

The source added that it was “early days in our understanding of what has happened.”

Any hack of two other police databases – the police national database and the police national computer – would have been deemed far more serious. It is not believed that any direct information about officers in sensitive postings could be gleaned from the data leaked.

The government said it was working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and the National Crime Agency on the DfE hack. The DfE and PNLD have also reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office, the data watchdog.

The DfE said “swift action” had been taken to contain the incident.

“The information involved is limited to customer service contact details relating to individuals and organisations,” it said. “No other data has been accessed.”

It is understood the help-desk data includes different sets of data that cannot be connected to each other easily.

Uefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardens

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 19:07:37 GMT

‘Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition’

Uefa has called an emergency ­meeting of its 55 members for Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. A European boycott of Fifa tournaments is among the options under consideration.

As the next major event in the Fifa calendar, a boycott of next year’s Women’s World Cup has been ­mentioned in preliminary ­discussions, although there would be a reluctance in some quarters to make the women’s game suffer as a consequence of a protest against Fifa proposals that primarily revolve around ­monetising the men’s World Cup and Club World Cup.

Uefa’s initial condemnation of Fifa’s plan to “sell the soul” of ­football has received strong backing from Concacaf – the North, Central ­American and Caribbean ­confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). If their members follow their leads there should be sufficient votes to block the proposal.

Those three confederations make up 143 of the 211 Fifa members, but unanimity is not guaranteed, as was made clear when Czechia’s ­football association became the first in Europe to back the plan.

Having received more than 200 ­letters of endorsement backing his re-election next year, Infantino is confident he has enough votes – although it is unclear whether the proposal requires a simple ­majority to be passed. Several sources have said that creating a new commercial entity – Fifa Forward Enterprise [FFE] – and selling a 20% stake to investors would necessitate a change of Fifa statutes, which requires a 75% majority that would be much harder to obtain.

On Wednesday evening, Infantino released a video to address the ­backlash. “FFE is actually a ­proposal, an offer,” he said. “It’s part of a democratic process – a ­consultation process – and, above all, it is an opportunity but not an ­obligation. It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally.”

Earlier, Uefa redoubled its attack on Fifa by accusing the world ­governing body of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends” after it emerged that ­Infantino had ­presented members with a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an ­initial payment of $20m (£15m) from the proposed sell-off.

A further $20m for each ­association would also be made available at a later date, although it is unclear whether accepting the money would equate to a formal ­endorsement and therefore remove the need for a vote.

“Today we have learned of Fifa’s deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn,” Uefa said. “This says everything you need to know about this plan. But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition to Fifa’s scheme. Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It’s time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans.”

Uefa’s second statement of condemnation followed a similarly strong intervention from ­Concacaf, which is particularly ­significant given the confederation has just hosted the most ­lucrative World Cup and covers the region that has brought the proposed new investment from the New York-based Thrive Eternal.

The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, was instrumental in the success of the US, Mexican and Canadian bid for the tournament, but along with the seven other Fifa vice‑presidents and Fifa council members he was kept in the dark over the plans.

“Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,” Concacaf said. “We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

“We share the ­disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the ­relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

“As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the confederations and every member association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.

“This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the Fifa family will act in the same manner.”

The AFC issued a similar statement of disapproval, which significantly is understood to have the backing of the Saudi Arabian football federation, a close ally of Infantino and the host of the 2034 World Cup.

“The AFC was not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels,” it said.

“While the AFC recognises the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation.

“Decisions that may reshape the commercial and financial future of the game require comprehensive prior engagement with confederations, member associations and other relevant stakeholders before any proposal is made to the appropriate decision-making bodies.”

Elite clubs also expressed their unhappiness, with the European Football Clubs organisation pointing out that Fifa had not consulted it despite the two bodies having signed a memorandum of understanding.

“As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in Fifa’s competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude,” it said.

“EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.”

Three firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfires

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 18:30:27 GMT

Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell

Three Greek firefighters have died while tackling wildfires on the island of Crete and in the south of the mainland, the Greek fire department has said, as extreme heat hinders efforts to control blazes ravaging southern Europe.

The arc of brutal fires, which runs from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean, and from the Scottish Highlands to the south of Spain, has alarmed experts because many of the fires have been out of control and burning close to towns and cities.

Temperatures exacerbated by the climate crisis reached 38C on Wednesday in Bordeaux in France, where firefighters kept a huge blaze in nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on record had been “technically stabilised”, according to the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Dozens of ground crews had managed to contain the Madrid fire overnight, emergency services for the region said on Wednesday morning, but a separate fire near València, where temperatures will peak at a cooler 32C, is still out of control.

In televised comments from the Navalcarnero command centre on Wednesday morning, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the situation near the capital was improving but stressed it was the first time in Spanish history that a wildfire had been raised to “operational level 3”, with the national government taking over the disaster response.

“I believe the next 12 hours will be very important,” he said. “They are going to be decisive in consolidating the work done by the national civil protection system.”

Accompanied by strong winds, the fourth heatwave of western Europe’s scorching summer has alarmed firefighters, who warn it makes blazes harder to quell and raises the risk of fires restarting in areas that have been stabilised. New fires also prompted evacuations in Greece and Turkey.

French authorities benefited from a calm night on Tuesday that allowed flare-ups to be swiftly extinguished but warned of “unfavourable” developing weather conditions that could hamper progress. The prefecture of Gironde said 126 firefighters had been injured since the start of the fire but the total burned area remained stable at 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) on Wednesday morning.

Wildfires have burned a record-breaking area of France, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows, while France and Spain have experienced record-breaking numbers of fires for this time of year. More than 330,000 people in southern Europe have been forced to flee their homes and hotels.

Officials began to lift evacuation orders on Tuesday as fires were brought under control, allowing tens of thousands of people living in towns near Bordeaux, Madrid and València to go back to their homes. Some of them returned to find burnt-out buildings and charred belongings.

José Fernández, a 74-year-old pensioner, told AFP he had “no money, no documents, no home” after he came back to the remains of what used to be his house in Pelayos de la Presa, in the Community of Madrid. “This place has been reduced to a total ruin.”

Europe’s wildfire season is growing hotter and longer as carbon pollution heats the continent twice as fast as the global average. Repeated heatwaves this year have dried vegetation and turned forests and shrubland into tinderboxes, alarming EU officials, who have said wildfires could still be burning in November.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, thanked firefighters for their “courage and commitment” on Wednesday.

“As the fires in France and Spain continue to ravage, European solidarity knows no limit,” she said in a social media post. “Romania and Greece have decided to extend their missions, continuing their support to the affected regions. And from Saturday, Poland will join the fray.”

Earlier this week, the European Commission said it had sent France seven planes and four helicopters from countries as far away as Sweden and Turkey, while in Spain, it said it had mobilised six planes from Greece, Italy and Turkey, along with 134 personnel and 41 vehicles from Portugal. A Super Puma helicopter from Serbia was expected to arrive in Madrid on Wednesday, according to Spain’s interior ministry, with 40 personnel and 18 vehicles to shortly follow.

The European Union’s crisis management team said on Wednesday it expected difficult weeks ahead, fearing a further outbreak of wildfires in Italy and Greece later in the summer.

Maria Zuber, a senior official at the EU’s emergency response coordination centre (ERCC) in Brussels, which coordinates the dispatch of firefighting planes, equipment and teams to countries that have asked for help, said the next few days would be “very difficult” for France and that “now we see it will go to Greece”.

Moisés Galán Santano, a wildfire expert at the ERCC, said more needed to be done to prevent wildfires and that it would be a task for many years. “The [emergency] response is not only the answer. It’s the last answer. But it’s not all the answer. We need to focus on prevention.”

Earlier this year, a policy paper from the European Commission set out how countries could better prevent and recover from wildfires that are expected to become bigger and more damaging across the continent. It promoted measures such as more extensive grazing, the restoration of wetlands, rivers and floodplains, better data on forest fires and raising public awareness of risky behaviour and safe evacuation.

Scientists say western Europe’s scorching summer has been deadly, costly and exacerbated by fossil fuel pollution. Rapid analyses have found June’s heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” in a world without climate breakdown, while the recent level of soil dryness in western Europe – a driver of bigger blazes – was made five times more likely. The heatwaves are estimated to have claimed at least 10,000 lives and cost grain farmers €2bn in lost crops.

Vula Tsetsi, a co-chair of the European Green party, called on European institutions to take action on Wednesday and noted the European Commission had not yet published its heating and cooling plan, which was expected in April.

“Climate-driven heatwaves and wildfires are already claiming lives, destroying homes and ravaging forests at a record pace,” she said. “There is a widening gap between the scale of Europe’s heatwaves – literally hitting every EU country – and the absence of decisive European action.”

Brave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social care

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 18:15:54 GMT

Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change

For campaigners perpetually disappointed by the failure of England’s political classes to fix England’s creaking adult social care system, the fear was that Andy Burnham’s long-trailed speech on Wednesday would be less Brave New World, more Groundhog Day.

Burnham acknowledged he had been here before. Back in 2010, as health and social care secretary, he unveiled extensive proposals to overhaul social care, only for them to collapse amid rightwing media hostility and furious political rows about “death taxes”.

The new PM might talk a good game about expending political capital on an issue close to his heart, but recent history suggests that social care reform invariably ends up in what the King’s Fund thinktank calls the “Westminster graveyard of good intentions” – 22 official reviews in the past 30 years, all which have come to nothing

Burnham sketched out his broad ambitions for social care reform in a brisk, partly off-the-cuff speech at a Jewish care home in north London on Wednesday. There was, as expected, little policy detail, but enough to show a clear direction of travel.

He would be accelerating Louise Casey’s review of social care, which under Keir Starmer had been slated for 2028, effectively pushing it back into a putative Labour second term. Lady Casey’s recommendations for a National Care Service would be published within 12 months. He would back Casey “100%”, he promised.

He was dropping no clues as to what it might look like. It could be “fully fledged or lesser options or something in between”, he said vaguely. Casey would come up with funding options. But it wasn’t just about money: the quality of social care had to improve, work more closely with the NHS, be built around the needs of care users.

There would be investment and focus on the social care workforce, boosting pay and training. He wasn’t opposed to private providers (which currently provide most care in England) but he wouldn’t put up with “profiteering” by care firms. There needed to be more support for unpaid carers, too often broken by their sacrifices.

The key message, however, was about politics. Blame for the dire state of English social care lay with his generation of politicians, he said. They had serially ducked the challenge of reform, put point-scoring before fixing injustices, fomented a political culture of risk aversion and inertia.

“How have we got to a position where it’s too difficult to fix the basic care that we give to each other, that fellow human beings receive?” he asked.

He arrived at No 10 promising he would do politics differently, but this was a challenge to the other main political parties to do the same. He wouldn’t be drawn on whether he’d raise tax to reform social care, but it felt like he was prepared to test the very idea that a government might raise taxes to fix a glaring social injustice.

“If everybody, on the NHS principle, contributed a little, it would mean everyone could protect the majority of what they’d worked for,” he said at one point. “Now I know the Mail and probably the Telegraph doesn’t support that. But I don’t know – do people support that?”

The consensus in the social care world was that this was an impressive start. “There was a sense of excitement in the room,” one veteran campaigner said. “He had every opportunity to downplay expectations but he didn’t.”

Burnham showed passion, humanity, and a grasp of detail. He framed the injustices simply. He strikingly compared the inequity of social care in England with the privatised US healthcare system: “The vulnerable pay with everything and it can completely leave them with nothing.”

For once, some observers said, with a flicker of amazement, there was clear political will, from the very top, to break the entrenched consensus that fixing social care is impossible. It’s early days, but for now there is the rare whiff of hope and optimism.

Battles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes that

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:48:10 GMT

Burnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denial

“People pleaser!” That’s the insult Andy Burnham’s enemies sneer at him. And yes, he will need all his mightiest people-pleasing talents to win over voters to contribute to a new national care service. Choosing this forever failed policy (22 major reviews over three decades) as his first great challenge is a remarkable act of bravery. No mere people pleaser would dare step on this political live rail.

It will use up vast amounts of political capital to get a national care service off the ground. He hardly needed Tuesday’s Mail front page (“Burnham’s £18bn ‘death tax’ nightmare”) to remind him. But he has already fought on the battleground that is social care reform. “I do have some of the scars,” he said. How good to also hear him take a firm swipe at media attackers, who will now redouble their efforts. “You can’t create scare stories when people are already scared by what they’re seeing anyway through their own eyes in their own homes or in care homes,” he said. This is no grasp at low-hanging fruit, no search for a quick win. It’s a cause of deep conviction.

In his speech from a north London care home, the prime minister told of his father with dementia, and of the struggle for families to get any help, the poor quality of much of it, the astronomical costs for some and the profiteering of private equity firms buying up care homes. That will have resonated with many, but his challenge now is to win the attention, hearts and minds of those who know nothing of social care. Making people care about care is the first vital step.

A survey last year found 33% of people in England believed care was generally free at the point of need, like the NHS, and another 18% didn’t know whether it was. Many get a nasty shock when they need it for their family and find they must pay if they have savings above £23,250. Only 4% listed social care as a top priority for the country; its political salience is low because at any one time, few people are using it – and they put it out their minds afterwards. In England, this unseen service uses up a phenomenal 78% of local council funds: no wonder people think they get bad value for their council tax, as visible services keep shrinking to pay for it. Everything about it is broken.

People need to wake up to what confronts us. They need to know that the roulette wheel of fate decides which families are stricken by dementia: one in three people alive today will get this most dreaded of diseases. Some may live for years in a nursing home: one in seven will pay over £100,000 and some will have to sell the family home.

But still, this nation of gamblers shrugs. People bet that it will never happen to them; that when their time comes, they will just drop dead. Burnham rightly described the UK’s social care system as equally unfair as the US health system: it bankrupts some. Would people rather pay a defined amount or risk losing everything? It’s an insurance offer to protect against the risk of catastrophic loss.

Research by the Health Foundation has found public support for funding reform, but – here’s the catch – “once people understand the current system”. As Louise Casey embarks on her Big Conversation on care, educating people about the system will be her primary task: only then can we discuss which other payment options are least unacceptable.

This is about better care, too. For-profit care is lower quality than voluntary, non-profit or local authority-run care services, the Blavatnik School of Government has found. This chaotic system includes 16,500 care homes: 85% for profit, many small family-run businesses and some private equity big chains that will not be part of the new care service.

Why do we endure this barely regulated, barely inspected patchwork of confusion? This was another disastrous Margaret Thatcher privatisation, of the kind Burnham intents to repair. After a 1988 report by the supermarket executive Roy Griffiths, Thatcher effectively ordered councils to close their own homes and services, outsourcing them to the private sector, and closed NHS geriatric care wards. Crafting a new national care service out of all this would be the hardest of all in-sourcing tasks.

This week, the prime minister warned the NHS could collapse unless social care is repaired. Last month, about 13,600 beds were occupied by people who were there only for lack of social care elsewhere, and delayed discharges cost the NHS £2.7bn last year. Burnham talks of integrating NHS and social care, with a workforce eventually on the same pay and with the same career progression. Currently, a starter NHS healthcare assistant is paid more than a care assistant.

Will people agree to pay up? There are signs they will: when Boris Johnson proposed a care levy, it was surprisingly popular. But it was abolished by Kwasi Kwarteng before it could be implemented. Which was just as well, because the plan added 1.25 percentage points to employee and employer national insurance. That meant workers, not pensioners, would pay. No extra tax would fall on dividends or other unearned income that doesn’t attract NI contributions. What’s more, the highest paid pay the lowest marginal NI rates.

Whatever system emerges from these consultations, one principle must be that not a penny more is paid by the young for the old. Pensioners in the UK are the least likely group to be in poverty (though, of course, some are). They generally have the most wealth and property, alongside final salary and triple-locked pensions. They are the overwhelming beneficiaries of the NHS. It’s no cliche to say the young are the future, so they must come first, in better early-years education, holiday childcare and schools with a wider technical, arts, drama, sports and design curriculum, while further education gets the funding and status it needs. The old must pay for the old, in one way or another.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

This is a minefield. The politics of social care are fraught beyond all the other great problems Burnham could have chosen at the start. But the tone of his speech suggests the new prime minister really may lift this as a national priority. The wreckers in the Tory and Reform parties may find themselves wrong-footed; the Mail, yet again, out of tune with the public mood.

When Burnham says we need “a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring”, some old hands sigh and say: “Good luck with that!” But Burnham may strike a chord. A public grown hostile to politics may see through Kemi Badenoch’s deliberately impossible conditions for consensus agreement, as she cynically and childishly demands no borrowing, no taxes and no taking from “those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives”. They know someone must pay, and that includes those lucky enough to have “made provisions”.

It has never been the right time to brave social care reform. But it may be now, with a leader driven by personal belief, in his early stages, when he still has substantial amounts of political capital. He has grasped the nettle: will society, politics and the media? If not now, when?

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Goodwood great escape makes Billy ‘the Kid’ and Bow Echo public favourites

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:46:44 GMT

Jockey extricated colt from tricky position to grab glory

France and Breeders’ Cup in America targets for colt

Billy Loughnane threw his goggles towards an ecstatic crowd packed around the winner’s enclosure as he returned after a thrilling, unforgettable success on Bow Echo in the Sussex Stakes on Wednesday. He missed, but it was the only mistake he made all day.

Technically at least, Billy “the Kid” is still a fair nickname for Bow Echo’s 20-year-old jockey. This, though, was a coming-of-age moment for horse and rider that should see the pair of them graduate to the turf’s established elite.

Loughnane was brilliant on Bow Echo: cool, confident, patient and then decisive as he extracted the three-year-old from a scrum of horses at the two-furlong pole and launched him down the middle of the track. Ryan Moore and Gstaad, the runner-up behind Bow Echo in the 2,000 Guineas and St James’s Palace Stakes, grabbed a useful lead while his old rival was stuck in traffic, but Loughnane had total confidence in Bow Echo’s finishing speed and they chased him down, amid a huge roar from the stands, with a few strides to spare.

Bow Echo is now unbeaten in six starts and the first horse since the incomparable Frankel to complete the milers’ triple crown of wins in the 2,000 Guineas, St James’s Palace Stakes and Sussex Stakes. His jockey, meanwhile, is swiftly becoming the public face of Flat racing – an heir to Lester and Frankie whose first name is enough, and a showman who enjoys the winning moments every bit as much as his backers.

“We have watched millions of these races back,” Loughnane said of himself and George Boughey, Bow Echo’s trainer, “and we always felt that the closer would almost certainly get up.

“We knew there would be plenty of pace. Once I found Ryan’s tail, I was happy enough, but then Christophe [Soumillon, on Puerto Rico] appeared on my outside, so I knew I was going to have a bit of a challenge getting him out. Once he did, he really motored home.

“Today was a tough race for him. There were plenty of runners and we ended up a long way back, but he has got a proper engine.”

After a slightly scrambled short-head defeat of Gstaad at Ascot last month, this half-length success, in Bow Echo’s first race in all-aged company, cemented his status as the best miler in Europe, with the strong possibility of further improvement to come.

“He has been in a couple of scraps recently and he’s shown fight today,” Boughey said. “He’s shown his turn of foot and it’s a career-best. A lot went wrong again but he was still able to win, and win well. I know it sounds mad, as he is unbeaten, but he is improving. He is learning to race and learning to get in a scrap.”

Bow Echo may head to France for his next start, in either the Prix Jacques le Marois at Deauville or the Prix du Moulin at Longchamp, while his long-term target is the Breeders’ Cup Mile at Keeneland in Kentucky on 31 October.

For Loughnane, it could be another career high, and on a global stage, at just 20 years of age. “He is a real showboy, is he not?,” Boughey said. “He loves it. I was pretty nervous today going into the paddock, and he was just chilled out. He has got an amazing head on young shoulders, he has got every attribute and is the consummate professional.”

The market is firmly behind the unbeaten Prix de Diane winner, Diamond Necklace, in the Nassau Stakes at Glorious Goodwood on Thursday, but Aidan O’Brien’s filly faces a couple of strong older rivals on her first try in all-aged company and Friendly Soul (3.35) is an interesting bet at around 7-2 to upset the odds-on favourite.

John & Thady Gosden’s mare is just 1lb behind Diamond Necklace on Timeform’s ratings and remains lightly raced for a five-year-old, having missed the 2025 campaign after getting off the mark at Group One level in the Prix de l’Opera at Longchamp in October 2024.

Friendly Soul endured a horrible start to her five-year-old campaign when she put her foot in a hole when leading a Listed race at Haydock in May, but showed she was none the worse for the experience when finishing third behind Blue Bolt, a subsequent Group One winner, at Royal Ascot last month.

That race was over a mile and the return to 10 furlongs – the Opera trip – on Thursday is another positive as Friendly Soul (3.35) attempts to reward the sporting decision to keep her in training with a second Group One win.

Goodwood 1.50 The lightly raced Ciarrai Abu would have been a more convincing winner at Ascot last time had he not drifted left in the closing stages and he looks sure to progress further stepping up to a mile-and-a-quarter.

Goodwood 2.25 This is a significant rise in grade for Flann Sunna but Simon & Ed Crisford’s colt looks up to the task after a near five-length success in a strong time at Ascot earlier this month.

The Guardian view on funding social care: building consensus requires candour about taxes

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:30:38 GMT

The prime minister is right to want to change the political culture, but aversion to honesty about the funding options runs deep in Westminster

Andy Burnham is well qualified to speak on the subject of what can go wrong with social care policy. As health secretary in 2010, he proposed reforms to be funded by a 10% inheritance levy. This was called a “death tax” by the opposition. It was never introduced.

Where Mr Burnham failed, none have subsequently succeeded. David Cameron accepted the recommendations of the 2011 Dilnot commission, which proposed a cap on the amount any individual would pay for care, but the cost to the exchequer thwarted implementation. Theresa May suggested plugging the money gap with a revised means test and no individual cap. This was branded a “dementia tax” by opponents and never saw the light of day.

Boris Johnson planned a “health and social care levy” alongside a means test. That fell foul of the Tories’ ideological allergy to tax rises. Labour’s 2024 election manifesto promised a “national care service”. Sir Keir Starmer then commissioned a review, led by Louise Casey, to explore reform options and report back in 2028, a timetable that made change before the next general election unlikely.

Mr Burnham has retrieved the Casey review from the long grass. It will now report next year. The prime minister has also called for a “national conversation” with a view to finding cross-party consensus on social care in England. He has invited the leaders of the Liberal Democrats and Conservatives (but notably not Reform UK or the Greens) for talks. Dame Louise will oversee a wider consultation exercise, taking views from the public. Lessons can also be learned from Scotland and Wales, with their devolved care models. This process is intended, in the prime minister’s words, to enable “more problem solving, less point-scoring” in the politics of social care.

The idea is laudable. In his speech on Wednesday, Mr Burnham was eloquent on the subject of what has to change in Westminster culture: the need to foster a climate where hard issues might be debated in good faith, without long-term national interests being sabotaged for short-term partisan advantage.

The prime minister was also refreshingly generous in his praise for care workers, recognising the technical and emotional challenges they meet for inadequate reward. He is right to say that they deserve higher wages and to make explicit the debt that all of Britain owes to a section of the labour force that is substantially staffed by immigrants.

Generosity of spirit is easier to dispense than money. Mr Burnham is new enough to Downing Street that he can afford to set out broad principles without being pinned down to specifics. That privilege will not last long. He admits that a commitment to grapple with an issue that is notoriously destructive of political capital is a gamble. Cross-party consensus will remain elusive if any revenue-raising mechanism is liable to be denounced as an unconscionable tax raid. The Conservatives and Reform UK, forgoing the opportunity to appear broad-minded, have already indicated that this is their position.

Mr Burnham has enough Labour MPs to enact change without opposition support. Reforms, and the contributions that pay for them within the fiscal rules, will form the basis for a future consensus if enough voters are persuaded they are necessary and fair. There is a long road to travel before that campaign begins, but the prime minister’s first steps are the right ones.

The Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni Infantino

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:25:38 GMT

Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted

Like a sporting Dr Pangloss, Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, would like to persuade football followers that they are living in the best of all possible worlds. Maddeningly for him, many disagree. On Monday, Mr Infantino published a 15-page Instagram rant in which he bemoaned the “hate and false rumours” in circulation during the recent men’s World Cup. White House interference over a crucial refereeing decision, prohibitive ticket prices, unnecessary but lucrative hydration breaks; it was all, as his best friend in politics, Donald Trump, would say, “fake news”.

But where the president of world football’s governing body sees haters, others see lovers of the game rightly concerned over where he is taking it. On Tuesday, Fifa confirmed that it hopes to sell stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors who may include Joshua Kushner, the brother of Mr Trump’s son-in-law Jared. The investors would buy into a new $20bn company, Fifa Forward Enterprise, which would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights, including ticketing, and take charge of “operational delivery” of World Cups.

Members of the extended Trump family do not generally contemplate business ventures out of a desire to spread “joy and happiness” in the world (which the egregious Mr Infantino presents as his mission). If the plans go ahead – sweetened by offers of a $30m windfall for national associations – investors’ desires to maximise revenues would undoubtedly accelerate the hyper-monetisation of the World Cup that is already taking place.

Almost certainly there would be pressure for more frequent and bigger tournaments at both club and national level, distorting the international game’s calendar to the detriment of domestic leagues. Mr Infantino has already indicated that he would look favourably on such an expansion, despite objections from bodies such as Uefa, European football’s governing body. Innovations such as the widely loathed hydration breaks – which by breaking games up into four quarters, US-style, allowed extra advertising slots – would no doubt proliferate.

The prospect revives fears generated by the failed European Super League proposals, which were furiously opposed by football supporters in 2021. During this summer’s World Cup in the US, Mr Kushner and others will have seen at first-hand the vast commercial possibilities of an event that unites a global audience in an age of fragmented media. As the highest-level steward of the game, Fifa’s primary job is to protect football from forces that might be interested in exploiting its appeal by selling its soul; instead, under Mr Infantino, it appears happy to do their job for them.

Angry opposition to the plans from Uefa and Concacaf (the equivalent body for North and Central America) suggests that the governance of the game may be at a crossroads. Mr Infantino’s tireless self-promotion, and shameless efforts to curry favour with the Trump administration, have long grated. But placing the planet’s most-watched sporting competition at risk from predation by private capital is of a somewhat different order of magnitude.

The visionary creator of the World Cup, Jules Rimet, hoped that it would help foster unity and solidarity between nations. Mr Infantino routinely pays lip service to such ideals, and did so again in his Instagram screed. In reality, though, he is dragging the world’s favourite sport further and further away from its roots, as he relentlessly follows the money wherever it leads.

‘The breath just went out of us’: people return to their homes after wildfires near Madrid

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:25:31 GMT

Residents struggle to take in the devastation five days after El Morro was evacuated as fires burned across countryside west of Spanish capital

The handwritten sign taped to the front gate of a house in the mountains an hour west of Madrid offered as succinct a summary of recent events as you will find.

“EMPTY,” it said. “No people or animals here.”

The quiet streets of El Morro, a hamlet on the outskirts of the town of Navas del Rey, held further evidence: two burnt-out cars barely identifiable as an Audi and a Seat; blackened gnomes atop a gatepost; charred hedges whose leaves had crumbled to a fine ash; and, everywhere, the smell of burnt, or still smouldering, wood.

On Wednesday, almost a week after the area was one of many evacuated as firefighters rushed to contain the blazes that have consumed tens of thousands of hectares of land west of the Spanish capital, the returning residents of El Morro were trying to process what had happened. Some phoned their insurance companies, some swept up the debris in and around their homes, and some were still too deep in shock.

A man led his elderly father out of a house that had been gutted by fire, telling him it was time to go and get a change of clothes. “We’re all doing so-so,” said the son, which seemed brave but unlikely.

Towards the outskirts of El Morro, a couple in late middle-age walked around what had been their garden. The house had survived bar some smoke staining, but the garden and the patio furniture had been chewed up by the fire.

“We came back to the village, saw what had happened and the breath just went out of us,” said the woman.

Mercedes Merino, who has lived in El Morro for 35 of her 70 years, apologised for being able to offer visitors nothing but lukewarm water – the electricity was still off – as she pointed to her blackened garden, with its flame-twisted cypress, dying loquat and sooty swimming pool. Still, at least her house had been spared.

“We’ve had fires here before, but nothing like this,” she said. “I knew what we were coming back to because lots of videos of the village have been going round. We’re all feeling really low. Some people are crying and some people have lost their houses, like the guy next door.”

Like the burnt-out cars, next door bore little resemblance to what it had once been. Rather than a house, it was a tangle of warped and burnt building materials, its roof collapsed into ripples of tile and its chimney absurdly horizontal.

“The firefighters have been amazing,” said Merino. “But how do you stop fires like these when you live in mountains covered with pine trees? We must have a guardian angel who was watching over us and protecting our house.”

Across the road, Javier Herraiz and his family, who had just returned to El Morro after fleeing south-west to Cáceres, were sitting down to a tortilla and counting their blessings.

The smoke that rose over the mountains towards the end of last week, combined with a visit from the Guardia Civil to warn them that an evacuation order was imminent, had persuaded them to leave sooner rather than later.

Although the damage that greeted them when they returned home on Wednesday morning was minimal, the state of the mountains and the hamlet had shaken them.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

after newsletter promotion

“What we saw when we got here was just Dantesque,” said Herraiz, 68. “It’s such a beautiful place but all of a sudden, it had come to look like hell.”

The damage to the family home amounted to little more than a warped pipe and the loss of a rainwater tank, which had probably helped protect the property as it melted and disgorged its contents over the terrace beneath.

“We’ve been so lucky,” said Herraiz. “Some people have lost their houses and some of them still have mortgages to pay.”

Eva Manso, whose home backs on to steep, wooded hillside, credited a sturdy brick wall – and probably a large measure of luck – with protecting her house from the flames. The wall had certainly done its job; the hills on the other side were black, its trees naked and clawed by the heat of the flames.

“We’ve never been through anything like this,” said Manso. “Yes, we had the Covid lockdown and Storm Filomena, but they were nothing like this. I don’t think anyone thought this would happen.”

That sense of bafflement, shock and fear was as evident in El Morro as it must be across the swathes of Spain that have been affected by another year of wildfires, from Madrid and the neighbouring province of Ávila to the eastern region of Valencia.

“I never cry over life’s difficult moments, but I sometimes cry over silly little things like a mosquito being squashed,” said Merino as she sat on her porch and looked over her ruined garden.

“Maybe I’ll find myself crying in a week’s time and I won’t be able to stop.”

Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaos

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 17:09:36 GMT

Players held banner after semi-final against England

Paredes and Molina investigated over brawl after final

Fifa has opened disciplinary ­proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner ­displayed after their World Cup semi‑final win against England in Atlanta.

As Argentina celebrated ­reaching the final with their dramatic 2-1 ­victory, several players held a sign ­proclaiming “Las Malvinas son ­Argentinas” – the ­Malvinas are Argentinian – in ­reference to the ­British overseas territory in the south Atlantic.

The dispute over the islands, which have been ruled by Britain since 1833, is long running and led to a 74-day conflict in 1982, during which more than 900 people – 649 Argentinians and 255 Britons – lost their lives.

Fifa’s disciplinary code ­prohibits “using a sports event for ­demonstrations of a non-sporting nature” and the banner prompted political debate on both sides of the ­Atlantic. A spokesperson for the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, said: “The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands ­definitely are.” Andrew Giuliani, the head of the White House Fifa taskforce, defended Argentina’s players, saying the US believed in free speech.

The incident was not the first time an Argentina team had expressed such sentiments. In 2014, Fifa fined Argentina £20,000 for a far larger banner held ‌up by players before a friendly with Slovenia in La Plata.

Fifa’s full World Cup charge sheet against the Argentinian Football Association also includes ­“discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, failure to comply with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators and the throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches”.

Several players are also under investigation in relation to the ­chaotic scenes that followed ­Argentina’s 1-0 extra-time defeat by Spain in the final. As Spain attempted to celebrate, ­altercations broke out across the pitch at New York New Jersey Stadium.

The Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes, who was seen wrestling Spain’s Eric García to the ground, faces three counts of assault under the Fifa disciplinary code, while the defender Nahuel Molina faces two counts of assault (one completed and one attempted) and one count of unsporting behaviour.

The assistant coach, Roberto Ayala, faces one count of assault, and Thiago Almada, an unused substitute in the final, one count of unsporting behaviour. Spain’s Gavi also faces an unsporting behaviour charge.

“In accordance with the Fifa ­disciplinary code, the respondents have now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the Fifa disciplinary committee in due course,” said Fifa.

Revealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UK

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:34:47 GMT

Exclusive: Sources say Fiona Cottrell told bankers the transfers, received 24-72 hours before her donations to Reform, came from her son

The convicted fraudster George Cottrell transferred a total of more than $2m to his mother, Fiona Cottrell, in the days before her 2024 donations to Reform UK, the Guardian understands.

Financial industry sources told the Guardian that Fiona received one deposit of $1.4m and two tranches of more than $300,000 each – money she attributed to having come from her son, George, when bankers asked about the deposits.

On each occasion, the Guardian understands transfers were made 24-72 hours before Fiona made a donation either directly to Reform, or via Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle for the political party.

According to sources, the lump sums went through US-based cryptocurrency exchanges before entering Fiona’s account. These platforms allow crypto-assets to be changed for hard currency, such as US dollars or British pounds. Some were routed to Fiona via money exchange services.

The Metropolitan police are investigating the funding of Reform UK, with a focus on scrutinising whether there were attempts to disguise the ultimate source of donations.

The new disclosures will add to the questions facing Reform and its leader, Nigel Farage, whose finances have been under the spotlight since the Guardian revealed he received a £5m gift from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Fiona was one of the most important donors to the party in 2024, making secret as well as public donations. She gave two lots of £250,000 in May 2024, which were disclosed transparently to the Electoral Commission. It can be revealed that these donations were preceded by transfers of $318,878 and $328,815 from her son.

As first revealed by the Guardian, she also gave more than £1m to Britain Means Business, a company controlled by the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, in June 2024. That cash transfer was not declared officially at the time, and was routed via the bank account of Oneify, an Australian money exchange service. Half that sum was transferred directly to the party days later by Tice, with no declaration that it originated from Fiona Cottrell.

It can now be revealed that sources have told the Guardian that $1,400,000 was deposited into Fiona Cottrell’s account by her son before she gave the £1,075,000 to Britain Means Business on 10 June 2024, just weeks before the general election.

In total, George Cottrell deposited $2,047,693 into his mother’s account, the Guardian has been told. Taking into account her 2024 donations to Britain Means Business and Reform UK, Fiona gave a total of £1.5m that year. These amounts are roughly equivalent, based on exchange rate data from May and June 2024.

Two Reform UK sources who were involved in party fundraising before the 2024 vote told the Guardian that George had assured senior party figures that some money would be on its way into the party’s coffers in the weeks leading up to the vote.

“He was acting as a sort of shadow treasurer, saying he would find a way to get more money in,” one of the sources said.

Asked about the transfers, lawyers for George Cottrell said their client had no further comment.

In previous legal correspondence, George has not denied giving his mother – who is understood to be of relatively modest means – large sums of money. Instead, he said via lawyers that “any political donations his mother has made have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.

Fiona Cottrell has not responded to several attempts by the Guardian to contact her.

George Cottrell, a convicted fraudster whom Farage has described as being “like a son to me”, lives in Montenegro and has said he is resident there for tax purposes. He has been described as Farage’s chief of staff by Reform insiders, even though the party maintains that he is only a volunteer.

His lawyers have said he is a permissible donor, despite living abroad, but have not explained how he meets the criteria or when he first met them. The only declared donation George Cottrell made to Reform in 2024 was £15,000 to part-fund Farage’s trip to Florida that December, where he met Elon Musk.

It comes as pressure mounts on Reform’s leadership to explain the lack of transparency, and apparent overlap, between personal funders and political backers.

The Guardian revealed in recent weeks that Tice had received an undisclosed loan of £80,000 from George Cottrell, who has also donated to Reform UK.

In April, this newspaper revealed that Nigel Farage received an undisclosed gift of £5m from the party’s most important donor, Harborne.

Several of these transactions caused bankers to raise potential money-laundering concerns with the UK’s National Crime Agency, via suspicious activity reports (SARs), according to financial industry sources.

After the Clacton byelection, Farage faces investigations by the parliamentary standards commissioner into whether he should have declared the £5m and also over benefits in kind given by George Cottrell.

In an interview with the Telegraph last week, Farage appeared for the first time to acknowledge that he should have declared the £5m on the register of MPs’ interests: “All right, perhaps I should have filled in a piece of paper. If that’s the worst thing I’ve done in life – not filling in a form – I would say that’s not too bad.”

Tice has failed to engage with questions about his loan from George Cottrell and decision to transfer £500,000 to Reform UK from Britain Means Business despite bankers raising concerns with him about the origin of the funds. He has accused the Metropolitan police of being involved in a smear campaign against him and briefing the media.

He posted on X: “The Establishment are playing dirtier than ever to try to smear & discredit Reform leaders.”

The Met investigation into Fiona Cottrell’s four donations in 2024 has been continuing for more than a year.

The Met issued this statement on its investigation in recent weeks: “An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election.

“Detectives from the Met’s special inquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000. Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.

“An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”

Asked whether Reform had been assured that George Cottrell would find a way to provide funds, and was regarded as a shadow treasurer, a spokesperson said: “We deny this completely. Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”

We must fix social care before allowing assisted dying, says Burnham

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:32:44 GMT

Introducing the legislation would be ‘very challenging’ until care system improved, PM says

Andy Burnham has said the assisted dying debate needs to wait until palliative care and social care are fixed, as he set out his path to resolving one of the most intractable problems in British politics.

The prime minister said he was not opposed to having the debate on assisted dying, but told reporters it would be “very challenging” to introduce the controversial legislation until the care system was in a better place.

The new prime minister’s remarks came during a speech at a care home in north London about social care reform, an issue on which he has repeatedly said he was ready to expend his political capital.

Although as Greater Manchester mayor Burnham said he would probably vote in favour of a private member’s bill going through parliament, he said he now thought the priority should be to improve end-of-life support.

His caution may give some Labour MPs pause for thought when the latest version of the bill – which has divided backbenches across the usual party lines – comes before them for a vote in September.

“I take the view that that debate – and I don’t say that there shouldn’t be a debate at some point about those issues – personally, I think there’s something that needs to happen first,” Burnham told reporters.

“That is the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care. I think it is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care.”

When Burnham was previously an MP, he abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

But when the issue came up again, in 2024, he said that his family experience in the nine years since – with his father, Roy, in a care home with dementia – had changed his view. “I think we do allow people to suffer and families to suffer too much,” he said.

At the time, he caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying, saying he would want a requirement, before any new law was implemented, that hospices would be “properly funded and sorted out”.

The bill’s proponents, including the MP Lauren Edwards, who is the new sponsor of the private member’s bill, have said they will press ahead with the vote in September.

But Burnham’s caution about returning to the issue of assisted dying has cheered Labour MPs who opposed the bill. Jess Asato, a vocal opponent, said many shared the PM’s concerns about the practical implications rather than the principle.

Several MPs who backed the most recent assisted dying bill – which was blocked by the House of Lords – have expressed unease about reopening old divisions in the party by returning to the issue and forcing the bill through using the Parliament Act to override the Lords. Among those who wrote to constituents to share that concern was Louise Haigh, a close Burnham ally.

Burnham indicated that his plan would probably require tax rises – though making the NHS and care system more integrated and therefore more efficient would help initially – and he repeated his promise to stick to Labour’s manifesto on tax for this parliament.

“I think more is possible from within existing resources. And the things that I’ve talked about today, particularly around the workforce, will be fully funded. I think it is possible from existing budgets to do much more,” he said.

“Some of what we would want to [do] in the fullest sense will require difficult decisions … But we will be honest with people about those. We will put them before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people’s consent.”

However, the prime minister said life had “moved on” from when he last tried to achieve social care reform as health secretary under Gordon Brown in 2010 – when options had included a 10% levy on inheritances – suggesting that a “more voluntary approach” may work better now.

Burnham has invited the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats for talks in Downing Street as he attempts to find common ground on the issue, saying he accepted that he may need to make some compromises.

“We are in a difficult world from a financial point of view. I can feel whatever I want to feel, but if I want to persuade others and get a cross-party consensus, you don’t just go in and say: ‘It’s got to be my way, and that’s it,’” he said.

“I think there are ways of looking at this that could include a more voluntary approach initially, or could include a roadmap to a reformed social care system.”

Burnham added that “in an ideal world”, nobody would have to sell their home to pay for care, and that his 2010 proposals had been designed to address that, because if everybody contributed a little, most of what they had worked for would be protected.

“I think the whole thing is horrendous for those who live through it. They see everything that their parents have worked for just whittled away in front of them, paying for care that often isn’t good enough. The system isn’t right. And in an ideal world, no, I wouldn’t want to see that.”

Burnham said he would never forgive himself if he allowed “screaming headlines” in the media to deter him from trying to reform the system, after 22 failed attempts over the last three decades.

“On this issue, please can we have a factual debate? Can we allow people to weigh up the different options … and then just come to a considered view based on those facts?

“I don’t think it should be too much to ask, because I think the public will give us their view. They’ll make it really clear what they feel they can accept and what they can’t.

“We won’t get to that point if there’s all of this stuff swirling around, and everyone frightened about everything. That just won’t get us there.”

He announced that Louise Casey would bring forward her independent review into social care options by a year, to summer 2027, and that the fair pay agreement for care staff would be the start of bringing the sector closer to NHS standards. Yvette Cooper, the new health secretary, will appoint a dementia adviser this summer.

Jonathan Freedland recounts how when he was 14 years old, Greater London council, led by Ken Livingstone, reduced child fares on the buses to 5p in a scheme called Fares Fair (Scoff at cheaper bus fares and No 10 North if you like, but Andy Burnham knows what he’s doing, 24 July). In 1950s Liverpool, the corporation had a scheme for schoolchildren in the holidays whereby they could buy a “penny return” to anywhere on the tram network. You could, for example, travel from the Pier Head by the Mersey on the number 10 tram to Prescot, almost 10 miles inland, and back again. Or you could use your ticket to transfer from your first destination to a different one rather than using it as a return. Sadly the last tram ran in 1957.

I remember on one occasion being on the tram when a rather tall boy asked for a penny return. The conductor obviously suspected that he was over the age limit. He gave him his ticket, but asked him: “Why didn’t you bring the missis?” And by the way, this was of course the old penny, of which there were 240 to the pound sterling. Jonathan Freedland is admiring of leaders who make the big statement that defines their term. Those he mentions are a mixed bag. Nye Bevan was right with the NHS, as was Harold Wilson with the Open University, but was Margaret Thatcher with right to buy? All that happened was house price inflation, unfair property windfalls and many of those properties ending up in the avaricious hands of private landlords.

As for Gordon Brown’s Bank of England independence, all that happened was that monetary policy and fiscal policy got separated into ghettoes with no effect on boom or bust. In the 10 years from 1997 to 2007, high Bank rates had no effect in damping down the party, while in the decade from 2010 to Covid, the Bank rate at 0.5% or lower had absolutely no effect in getting the economy anywhere near to normal levels of growth. Shameful treatment of vulnerable families in heatwave

How did London get here (Families in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioning, 27 July)? Your report says homeless families, including young children, were placed in a glass tower during a heatwave and told they could not use the building’s air conditioning because it had “not been offered as an amenity”. London proudly markets itself as one of the world’s greatest cities: a global financial capital overflowing with luxury developments, billion-pound property portfolios and record-breaking real estate values. Yet, in the shadow of that wealth, children are being expected to endure dangerously hot flats where the very system designed to make the building habitable is effectively treated as a luxury.

When a city reaches the point where vulnerable families are housed in buildings that become ovens, while the solution exists but is deemed off limits, something has gone profoundly wrong.

This isn’t an administrative oversight. It is the triumph of bureaucracy over common sense and, ultimately, over compassion. Politicians have spent years telling us London is thriving. Thriving for whom? It certainly isn’t thriving for the record number of families trapped in temporary accommodation or the children growing up without a stable home.

History teaches us that great cities are judged not by the height of their skyscrapers, but by how they treat those with the least power. On that measure, London should be deeply ashamed. A city where air conditioning exists but compassion is switched off is no longer a world-class city. It is simply a dystopia. Fernando Quintana MarreroLondon
