Making proportional representation work in Britain

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:09:54 GMT

Readers respond to Guardian analysis examining what Britain would look like under an electoral system of PR

Antonio Voce and Ashley Kirk’s excellent article (How could Britain look under proportional representation?, 22 July) provides a helpful view on how Britain’s electoral landscape could look under different voting systems.

Perhaps most striking is that whichever the proportional representation (PR) system used, when compared with first past the post they all make a good job of producing a parliament that reflects how the nation voted. There is not as much difference between them as enthusiasts of each PR system might expect, in terms of each party winning its fair proportion of seats, and in terms of voters therefore getting a fair say in who governs us.

It is also important to emphasise that the numerics of the systems proposed do not have to be as they are in the article’s examples. So using the additional member system does not mean we need to increase our parliament to more than 1,000 MPs. Using a single transferable vote does not mean we have to have constituencies any bigger than, say, four to seven MPs. And party list districts do not have to be as big as the official English regions or the whole of Scotland. PR for Westminster can be designed with MPs much more localised, if that is what the people want.

The much-needed new Westminster election system coming our way of course needs to be as good as we can make it. This requires both expert design and legitimacy with the public. If Andy Burnham is as good as his word to date, he will set up a National Commission on Electoral Reform, as already proposed by the all party parliamentary group for fair elections. Michael BursillReigate, Surrey

Antonio Voce and Ashley Kirk note that voters may resist replacing a system they understand. Yet, do they truly understand its absurd outcomes of first past the post? For instance, both Margaret Thatcher in 1983 and Theresa May in 2017 secured exactly 42.4% of the vote. Under first past the post, this gave Thatcher a landslide majority of 144, but left May with a minority, reliant on the DUP to form a government.

While the additional member system is often touted as a British compromise, it introduces its own flaws. If we are to reform our democracy, the only sensible choice is the single transferable vote (STV). By providing a choice of several constituency MPs, STV forces politicians to compete for our votes, effectively eliminating safe seats and complacency. Crucially, it delivers a truly representative parliament where parties must work together in coalition to govern. Tom BeardWorcester Park, London

Your worst fears about cultural collapse might be true – here’s what you can do about it

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:00:37 GMT

Writer Sarah Wilson argues we’re hurtling toward the same end as ancient Rome and the Mayan civilisation – but there’s plenty to fight for

In Sarah Wilson’s new book, one page is mostly blank. It’s intended as a reprieve, a neutral space “for you to stare at for a minute while your feelings catch up”.

You will need it. In I Eat the Stars, Wilson argues that the world as we know it is in collapse – and that we are too late to avoid the worst.

This is not just about the climate, but civilisation buckling under the weight of its own complexity. Given worsening inequality, political polarisation, falling fertility, resource shortages and global conflicts, Wilson argues that we are hurtling towards the same end as ancient Rome, the Mayan civilisation and every other sophisticated society before us.

Wilson, an Australian journalist, has often been ahead of the curve, writing bestselling books about quitting sugar, anxiety and the climate crisis before those topics were mainstream. I Eat the Stars was serialised on Wilson’s Substack newsletter before being published by Penguin.

It is an intensely sobering read, seeming to confirm all our worst fears about the future. But it also delivers clarity. Yes, things are that bad, but there is still plenty to fight for and much we can shape – if we are willing to confront reality.

I spoke to Wilson, who lives nomadically, shortly after she arrived in Greece. “A life skill I’ve developed over the years is finding wifi,” she jokes. Our conversation has been edited and condensed.

You’ve written about sugar, anxiety, the climate crisis and now collapse. What do you see as the common line?

My first book, I Quit Sugar, was contentious back in 2009. Can you imagine, our biggest enemy being big sugar? There were headlines: “Sarah Wilson’s telling us to get rid of a food group.” It was very hard for people to understand that there could be a different framing. From there I moved on to anxiety, tackling big pharma and the hold it had on the narrative – not saying that there isn’t a place for medication, but again treading in the grey area.

What I do is feel what people are thinking and wrangling with internally, but hasn’t yet been expressed as a public narrative. My dad says: “If there’s an elephant in the room, Sarah will just scream it out.” I’m not claiming to be the expert – I’m just bringing the complex science into the public realm.

What’s the difference between climate crisis and collapse?

We’ve been dealing with the climate as an isolated, almost linear concept, where it’s a problem with a fix. But not a single nation stuck to the Paris agreement. People are getting solar panels, but we’re all using more carbon-emitting fossil fuels as well – our habits aren’t changing. We’re still trapped in the mindset that caused the problem in the first place: believing in infinite growth, and that we don’t have to change our ways of being.

A civilisation is a complex system of complex systems. Eventually all complex systems, without exception throughout history, have collapsed under the weight of their complexity. A small crisis like a heatwave can be enough to tip the whole thing over, so the climate crisis is a really powerful node in this whole thing, because it is dictating the buildup of tension of all these other complex systems – while those, of course, are also adding to the climate crisis.

We’re used to glimpses of this, in headlines, reports, expert warnings – you bring them all together, and the outlook is dire. What’s actually at stake right now?

I think we are in a liminal moment: we know the present set-up can’t hold, but we don’t know what’s going to come next. We are basically at the top of this very sharp bell curve, just in the moments before it tips down the other side. Everything that has been going up and up and up – population, wealth, the price of oil – are about to dip.

It’s a terrifying moment, I’m not going to pretend otherwise, but it’s also a moment of stunning possibility. These periods of transition historically have been times of incredible human flourishing. Existentialism, communism and fascism were established between the two world wars. The Axial Age was another liminal time that produced Judaism, Buddhism, Confucianism, the market system and great art. There’s a threshold, and an opportunity.

What does collapse look like?

We do not know: uncertainty is the main characteristic of all this. Anyone who tries to tell you when and how collapse is going to happen, I wouldn’t believe them. We know that certain models are going to decline, but how that plays out will depend on how those things interact together, and also where you live. I would argue that there are parts of the world, such as Sudan and Gaza, that already know what collapse looks like.

What I would say is that, for anyone alive today, things are not going to keep improving. Particularly around the climate crisis, we’ve been hoping that if we just get solar panels and recycle and vote in a good government, then we can go back to the way things were – that ain’t going to happen. Collapse is going to basically look like things being shit and, instead of improving, getting shittier still. At a bare minimum, life is going to get extremely uncomfortable over the coming decades.

If everything is only going to get worse, why should we try to change or care about the future at all?

The reason I wrote the book is that there’s an opportunity here: what’s collapsing is the post-industrial, colonialist, extractivist, growth-based system. If we tether ourselves to that system, we will go down with it, but if we start to distance ourselves, see what’s happening and refuse to take part in its worst excesses, the better chance we have. The way it’s going, the ultra-rich and the tech bros are going to take everything anyway. The market is going to collapse, the millionaire set will suddenly be without assets, and that’s when revolution happens.

Many feel angry that this is our lot, and that people in power aren’t doing enough. How can we avoid turning on each other?

I go into detail explaining these complex systems concepts so that people can see there isn’t a cabal of bad dudes plotting; the government isn’t out to get us. We’re all part of this system … no one is to blame. Yes, there are people who are responsible, and opportunists who are taking advantage of this chaotic time – Trump, the technofascists and so on – but saying “They’re doing it to us” is a very binary thing. I think that by talking about the layers of crises, we can actually resolve the dissonance in our brain, relax and start thinking expansively.

When I started writing about what was happening in this brutal, upfront way, the response was relief. Once you’ve absorbed all that, you want to understand more. The next layer is realising, “hey, this is what’s happened to other civilisations, because they got too complex”. This is not because people are horrible, or it’s “us versus them”. It’s all of us.

You’ve said you have no hope. None?

I have no hope that it’s all going to be OK if we just recycle, or that we can return to the way things were, when everything was comfortable and we didn’t have to take responsibility. But I still have hope that the natural systems of life are going to force us into being the best versions of ourselves.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Basically I see what’s happening as a correction: we’ve gone in the wrong direction, we took individualism too far, capitalism no longer serves us and the centre cannot hold. Nature will recalibrate and find balance again. That’s what’s happening now. In the process, we are being forced to return to everything that makes us human.

AI, for example – it’s going like a bull out of a gate, and we were not consulted. It’s terrifying, but it’s actually forcing us to ask: if it can take our jobs, and become a lover, what is left? It’s art, poetry, messiness, all that juicy human stuff.

What collective action should we be prioritising?

Not everyone has the capacity to comprehend all of this. Those of us who do, need to get sturdy in our nervous systems, become islands of sanity and use whatever privilege we have to fight for things we want to hang on to.

The pathway into the new world will be based on ideas that exist now. I would argue that we need to be fighting for democracy, and our rights to protest, which are being eroded everywhere.

Researchers have found that the two determinants of the speed and likelihood of collapse are basically levels of inequality and polarisation. We have the capacity to actually do something about those two things. That will steer how fast and how bad things are, and how much time we have to adjust.

On the individual front, are there practical things we should be doing, to prepare?

One way is starting to simplify your life, make consumer choices that are based on the smallest amount of trade routes and supply chains.

Another is going analogue – building that muscle and normalising it with your children. There’s a whole generation who don’t know how to get across their suburb without their phone, but at a bare minimum, we’re going to be experiencing outages of power and internet.

Knowing how to ride a bike, use a compass – I would go as far as saying they’re survival skills. People in Europe have already been advised to put together survival kits, whether for world war three or heatwaves. Having water and food for three days, a battery-operated torch, pen and paper ready to hand – it’s not so fringe.

So do you think we should all be preppers?

People often ask me this. I say absolutely not, because if things get so bad that you need to be off in the hills with a stockpile of tinned corn and batteries, then you’ll need to be able to defend it with weapons and violence. I myself am not prepared to do that, and I think it is absolutely the wrong direction.

We need to be going collectivist. Our strength as a species is in collaboration and communication. That’s when we flourish. Studies have shown that less than 5% of “intentional communities”, which are set up away from the usual systems in an assumed “self sustaining” fashion, last longer than five years. What does work are organically formed communities of roughly 20 to 30 families, or an apartment block. We need to be forming stronger bonds where we are now: joining food co-ops, getting together in groups, sharing tools and assets and skills whenever we can.

You write that there’s joy to be found from going through this transition. How?

The title of the book, I Eat the Stars, comes from a poem written by Rebecca Elson, an astronomer who was diagnosed with terminal cancer, as an antidote to fear of death. Once we’re pushed right up against the prospect of things ending, then we go: well, let’s max the hell out of this. There’s an urgency to live fully.

Neoliberalism has taught us that we don’t live for the moment; instead we save up, build a nest egg, retire, play golf and then we die. What we’re talking about here puts a bomb underneath all of that. I see a lot of people putting off what really matters to them, because they’re caught up in a system that is now going down.

We don’t know what’s going to happen – so live beautifully regardless. That’s what these aphorisms and parables are essentially saying: you’re still allowed to have a beautiful life. In fact there’s an imperative now.

I Eat the Stars: How to Live Fully and Beautifully in a Collapsing World by Sarah Wilson is out now through Penguin Life

Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoir

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 16:00:36 GMT

Dominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the author

For all the drugs and punch-ups, this is an unexpectedly sentimental coming-of-age story – or maybe origin myth – about the formative youthful kitchen experiences of legendary badass chef Anthony Bourdain. It is taken from the opening chapters in his bestselling memoir Kitchen Confidential; Canadian film-maker Matt Johnson directs and Dominic Sessa (the callow kid from Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers) plays the conceited, smug yet lonely and vulnerable young college student Tony. “Anthony” is in the future.

It is the mid-1970s and Tony effectively runs away from home after failing to get a residential summer writing scholarship that he had assured everyone was in the bag. He shows up nearly penniless in the seaside vacation resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts – a place that is pretty similar to Amity Island in Jaws, which is showing at every drive-in. The reason is that he has a desperate crush on Nancy (Emilia Jones) who is there for the summer too and whom he desperately wants to impress with his smouldering intellectualism.

Then, having got drunkenly thrown out of a bar serving seafood, pathetic Tony gets hired there as a humble dishwasher by its kindly-stern chef (Antonio Banderas). He finds he kinda likes the heat in the kitchen, and gets to know louche, coke-addled womanising chef Sal (Leo Woodall) who shows Tony the ropes of being a tough guy and a player, but who is, in the time-honoured manner of films like this, Tony’s sacrificial mentor: inspirational figure and awful warning.

This is a strange film in some ways. It is watchable and entertaining, but its feelgood trajectory is compromised by what we know of the author. In 2000, when the book came out and Bourdain was approaching the height of his celebrity, these anecdotes would have felt simply warm, wry and funny. If he was still alive now, Bourdain would assuredly have an ironic cameo, perhaps as one of the greybeard authority figures that obstruct the rake’s progress. But we are watching the film in the knowledge that Bourdain took his own life in 2018 after a painful breakup, having suffered from instability and depression. All the sadness, all the emotional danger that this film gestures at, all the crises that the drama suggests are just obstacles to be surmounted … they are all very real.

How exactly, for example, do we take the moment in this movie when Banderas’s character tells Tony about François Vatel, chef to Louis XIV, who killed himself in shame when the key ingredients didn’t arrive for a banquet? (It’s not in the book, though Bourdain spoke about it in interviews as an example of extreme perfectionism.) The scene is presumably there tacitly to acknowledge Bourdain’s heartbreaking fate. It sits oddly.

As for Sessa himself, Johnson gives him plenty of shots looking silently stricken, or hungover, often sporting a black eye. In a way, Tony is the author, the narrator who just bleakly sees it all, but for a writer he sometimes doesn’t have much to say about the situation in which he finds himself. There’s some nice support from Rich Sommer and Dagmara Dominczyk as Pierre and Gladys, Tony’s parents, and Banderas always has gentleness and charm. A bittersweet dish.

Tony is out on 7 August in the US, 14 August in the UK, and 20 August in Australia.

Nelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishes

Nelly Korda is the likeliest winner of the Women’s Open, but there is no question who would be the most popular. Charley Hull’s brushes with major glory – she has five runner‑up finishes – have only intensified a widespread desire for the 30‑year‑old to break through the tape. Royal Lytham & St Annes provides the latest opportunity for the flamboyant Englishwoman.

Korda arrived in Lancashire with half her four major triumphs having come in 2026. Perhaps the Floridian can afford to be generous and she has endorsed Hull’s prospects. “She’s such a great personality,” Korda said. “It would be great for her to do it on home soil, too. She’s an amazing player. I enjoy playing with her. It would be great for the game.”

Hull does not seem the type to be dispirited by close shaves. A year ago she was pipped by Miyu Yamashita. Hull finished a shot adrift of Korda, the champion, in the US Women’s Open last month. “That’s sometimes how she goes,” Korda said. “It’s about putting yourself in that position. You can’t control what others are doing, but she’s doing something right to always be there and be relevant, to be in the hunt.

“It’s like Sam Burns. He’s been in the hunt a lot during major championships, hasn’t got it done. Eventually he will. You can’t get discouraged, it has to be encouraging.”

History is in Hull’s favour. The last time the Women’s Open visited here, in 2018, England’s Georgia Hall claimed her maiden major victory. A scorched links will render this a wonderful test. Korda estimates she will employ her driver five times per round at most, instead adding a four-iron to her armoury.

This is also something of a trial run, with the men’s Open due to make a long-awaited return in 2028.

Korda is more comfortable than ever at being the name on everyone’s lips. Early in her career, the world No 1 struggled with fame and attention. Having parents who were professional tennis players, a brother who still competes in that domain and a sister who is also on the LPGA Tour has helped with her mindset. So, too, has a frustrating 2025.

“My family always make sure my batteries are recharged,” she said. “It’s a funny conversation; my dad and my mum are always telling me to take more days off. I’m like: ‘No, no, I don’t want to. I want to grind on my craft.’

“There gets a point in the season where I’m really tired. It’s not just golf. It’s not just like the travel. It’s kind of a combination of everything people don’t really see behind the scenes.

“My parents are people I go to all the time for advice. My sister, too. She has been at a lot of majors this year. Those are my people. I’m so comfortable and vulnerable with them. They’ve seen every side of me and know me the best.

“I decided I need to stop getting so frustrated with everything. I hit a great shot, it goes in a divot and I would get frustrated. What is going on? Why am I getting these bounces? It’s draining having that attitude. I just told myself: ‘I’m not going to have this attitude.’”

“He’s very humble and I would say he’s your typical Kiwi guy that happens to be a freak athlete,” Ko said. “I went to work out and everywhere I went I was like: ‘Please turn on the Open.’ It ended up not working on the TV so I had my trainer turn it on my cellphone. I can’t remember my workout at all because my whole focus was there.

“I took an Uber ride back home. As soon as I got home he was on the 18th and when I saw that drive I was so relieved, but so excited, super pumped.

“I screamed when his winning putt went in. I closed the door and I screamed. My husband ran out and was like: ‘What’s happening?’ Ten seconds later, I was crying.”

Drinkflation: why British booze is getting weaker

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 15:31:21 GMT

While the sizes and prices are staying the same, brands are reducing the alcohol content in their beer

Name: Drinkflation.

Age: The current round started in 2023.

Appearance: To the naked eye, no appreciable change.

But drinks are getting bigger? Drinks are staying the same size.

Then the price of these same-sized drinks is getting higher? Prices are also staying the same.

So what is happening? The drinks are getting less alcoholic.

Which drinks? Specifically, beer. Even more specifically, Carling Original, which is being reduced in strength from 4.0% alcohol by volume (ABV) to 3.4%.

I hadn’t noticed. You won’t have done, because the change doesn’t come into effect until October.

And also because I don’t drink Carling. Or indeed beer. Good for you.

Anyway, if they’re actually reducing the alcohol, why is it called drinkflation? It’s a coinage based on shrinkflation: the practice of reducing food portion sizes – putting fewer crisps in the bag, say – while keeping prices the same.

Sneaky. Are any other beer brands considering doing something similar? Lots already have: Foster’s has gone from 4.0% to 3.4% ABV over the last three years; Sol went from 4.2% to 3.4% in 2025. Carlsberg, Grolsch, John Smith’s, Coors and Amstel have also reduced their alcohol levels.

Is this because drinkers prefer weaker beer? Or is it a bid to curb the nation’s alcohol consumption on the sly? Neither. It’s a bid to save money and maximise profits.

How much money can you save by reducing the level of alcohol by a few measly percentage points? A lot. But it’s not the alcohol that costs money, it’s the tax.

I have no idea what you’re talking about. The move could have something to do with the changes to alcohol duty in 2023, under which packaged beer between 3.5% and 8.4% ABV attracts a levy of £22.58 per litre of pure alcohol.

I don’t know what that amounts to. For a 4.0% beer it’s about 41p a pint. Whereas a 3.4% beer is subject to a duty of just £9.96 per litre of pure alcohol, or about 19p a pint.

That’s quite a difference, but what if people don’t like Carling’s new weak beer? The company claims the 3.4% version actually ranked “higher for overall taste” in consumer tests. It also laid the groundwork for the reduction by introducing a stronger and more expensive Black Label version in February, at 4.7%, creating a “value-premium price ladder” within the brand.

Do say: “Alcohol duty must strike a difficult balance between raising revenue and improving health.”

Don’t say: “3.4%? My urine is stronger than that.”

Prince Harry and co-claimants face huge legal bill due to insurance shortfall

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 15:17:28 GMT

Claimants’ cover might not meet Associated Newspapers’ costs for defending phone-hacking case, high court hears

The Duke of Sussex and his co-claimants could be millions of pounds out of pocket after losing their privacy case against the publishers of the Daily Mail, the high court in London heard.

The seven claimants, who include Prince Harry, Doreen Lawrence and Elton John, sued Associated Newspapers Limited over allegations of unlawful information gathering.

Their claims were dismissed in their entirety by Mr Justice Nicklin on 7 July and now their insurance may not cover the costs incurred by ANL in defending the case.

In a two-day hearing beginning on Wednesday to determine how costs should be paid, the court heard there was a shortfall between the £16.2m insurance cover the claimants had, and ANL’s reported costs of £34.5m.

Lawyers for ANL say the claimants should pay its costs on an indemnity basis, under which the losing party covers the other side’s costs without the need to show that those costs are proportionate.

ANL is asking for an interim £9,950,624.37 payment. The claimants have offered an £8m interim payment.

Antony White KC, for ANL, argued that the claimants’ conduct justified costs on an indemnity, rather than standard, basis, and said the allegations were “of the broadest scope and utmost seriousness”.

They alleged misconduct including “serious wrongdoing amounting in many cases to criminal conduct” against no fewer than 77 journalists, editors and executives, although only 23 were involved in the claims. Some allegations were unceremoniously abandoned at trial “without any apology or even acknowledgment”.

White said the legal action was part of a “campaign” to demonstrate ANL had “misled the Leveson inquiry”, using high-profile individuals to persuade the government to implement the second part of the inquiry.

The allegations were pursued to the “bitter end”, with the proceedings seen as the “vanguard”, or first wave of cases, before a “banquet of litigation” in a strategy to swamp ANL with other potential claims, he said.

The strategy was such that, even if the full panoply of allegations were not proved, any finding against ANL would be a “catastrophe” for the Daily Mail publisher, White added.

The claimants, who included David Furnish, Sadie Frost, Liz Hurley and Simon Hughes, cast a “strikingly wide” net for their claim “in the hope of catching some fish”.

White said he was sad to say that Lawrence, the mother of the murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, was recruited to the case by Harry as a “national treasure” to garner public sympathy and give the claims the necessary degree of credibility. “That is a matter of regret for my client, but it is not to be shrunk from,” he said.

White pointed to the statement, issued by Harry and Lawrence after the 11-week trial, which attacked the judge and called the 426-page ruling a “complete and obvious whitewash”.

Nicholas Bacon KC, for the claimants, said in written submissions that the judge should not award ANL its costs on the stricter, indemnity basis, adding that the incurred costs as of this month were nearly £34.5m, which “exceed its approved budget” by more than £18.6m.

It reflected “an astonishingly high legal spend” by ANL and an “entirely cavalier” and “no expense spared” approach, overriding the principle of proportionality that seeks to ensure parties are on an equal footing.

The claimants had obtained insurance cover of a combined £16.2m. “At that level of cover, the claimants would reasonably expect to be insured for the total of Associated’s incurred costs and approved estimated costs.”

He told the court ANL had increased its legal spend “without telling us”, and had previously told the court its spend would be £20m.

He said that the group had “conducted themselves honestly and in good faith”. Referring to the post-trial statement by Harry and Lawrence, he said “The costs to be ordered at this hearing concern the action itself, not the reaction to it.”

ANL argued the costs had been incurred during the four-year legal battle and 11-week trial.

Bacon said ANL knew what adverse costs the claimants had insured themselves for, and there was no suggestion its costs were anything like what it was now seeking until it disclosed last Friday that its total spend was £34.5m. “They have left us in a world where we are uninsured,” he told the judge.

All the claimants had entered the litigation in “good faith”, Bacon said. While the court dismissed their claims, it did not make any findings against them of “dishonesty or lack of sincerity in belief”.

“They accept they have lost and costs should follow the event.” Bacon said. But ANL wished to take that further and had stated publicly that it intends to “go for the jugular” in the costs hearing, he added.

The hearing continues.

‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandal

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 14:41:46 GMT

Laughter, disbelief and outrage over video appearing to show Saltburn player tricking umpire into giving batters out

At the Saltburn over-60s ukulele club there was a unanimous reaction to news that the town’s cricket club were being compared to the Argentina football team: laughter. Then a spirited rendition of I Love to Boogie.

On the seafront, a litter-picking volunteer was looking forward to the Wednesday night quiz just to get the gossip. But she had her own view. “All I would say is it’s just not cricket, is it?”

Bill Peters, a retired steelworker on a day out from Middlesbrough with his wife, Janet, reflected on what would have happened in St Lucia where he played cricket growing up. “There would have been a big fight,” he said slowly and purposefully.

Saltburn-by-the-Sea is a lovely Victorian town in north-east England whose usual claim to fame is the cliff lift, the oldest water-balanced funicular still in operation in Great Britain, although currently out of operation.

This week it has become the centre of a cheating story that has made headlines all over the world.

It began after a video was posted online of Saturday’s game between Saltburn second XI and Norton second XI.

The video appeared to show a fielder clicking his fingers as the batter swings for the ball. The fielder has been accused of trying to trick the umpire into thinking the ball clipped the edge of the bat before being caught.

The bemused batter can be seen protesting to the umpire as Saltburn players celebrate.

It has been called ‘Clickgate’ and the fielder dubbed ‘Clicky Ponting’, although his name is Brian.

Ponting, a former Australian cricket captain, is, it should be emphasised, entirely blameless and not a character in the affair beyond his name Ricky rhyming with Clicky.

The clip has been viewed more than 7m times and has made headlines around the world including, as would be expected, in Australia. One wit on Facebook remarked: “It’s official, Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket.”

Neither Saltburn nor Norton have commented on the affair, which is being investigated by the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

When the Guardian visited the cricket club no one wanted to talk. Tennis players arriving for games on the adjacent courts just burst out laughing.

In town, Pete Welsh, part of the litter-picking posse, was struggling to get his head round it. “It must have been a very loud click,” said the retired teacher. “If he was doing it and cricket is a gentleman’s game, it wasn’t very gentleman-like. I reckon if the lad has anything about him he will come forward and say yes, it was me.”

Just how someone managed to click his fingers so loudly that the umpire heard it is baffling a lot of people. The commentator Jonathan Agnew, told BBC Breakfast: “I can’t wrap my head round it. Can I hear someone click his fingers from 30 yards away? That umpire … must have incredible hearing. They call it a gentleman’s game, but it’s not really.”

The story has prompted many jokes but if you play cricket in the league then it is less of a laughing matter.

In Saltburn’s previous match, against Shildon Railway second XI, the wicketkeeper made an incredible eight catches in his team’s 22-run victory. The men’s Test record for catches by a keeper in an innings is seven.

Shane Rowley was playing for Shildon Railway and is sure he was a victim of clicking. When he was judged out, he said to the umpire: “Come on, please. You know I haven’t hit that one. I was miles away from it. I wish I was somewhere near it!”

He didn’t hear the ball hit his bat – “but everyone else did,” Rowley told the Guardian. Or did they?

After the game and the eight catches behind, Rowley said they raised complaints about poor umpiring. After Clickgate footage emerged on social media, Rowley said he rang an umpiring official to apologise.

“I said, can I just retract what I said earlier in the week and apologise and please extend apologies to the umpires.”

Rowley said three players did get a nick on the ball before they were caught. The others were adamant they did not and were “absolutely fuming”. Including him, his team’s last man out.

“It is absolutely unbelievable,” said Rowley. “I’ve never been involved in a game where I’ve seen anything like it and I’ve been playing for 30 years, since I was eight.”

To say other clubs are annoyed might be an understatement. Ian Palmer, chair of Newton Aycliffe Cricket Club, said, if true, it was “scandalous”.

He added: “These are lads giving up all of their Saturday to play a game of cricket and if they are being cheated it is just not on really.”

The “Clicky Ponting” player has been identified as Brian Devine, a 38-year-old company secretary who has lost sponsorship from a local Indian restaurant. Unconfirmed reports suggest he has been suspended by his club. Devine did not respond to an approach for comment.

For Neal Toulson, a former chair of Thornaby Cricket Club and someone involved in the game for more than 50 years, the allegations are a reflection of a wider malaise.

“I think cricket in general has gone down the pan a little bit with regards to gamesmanship,” he said. “When I was a lad – and it’s a while ago now – you never even appealed unless you thought it was genuinely out. Now everybody’s shouting for everything. And then there’s the sledging.”

Sledging, the dark art of trying to put off a batter with insults or teasing, goes on all the time in lower league cricket, Toulson said.

He added: “You’d think they were playing for money. It’s crazy, right? I always took cricket seriously, I competed as hard as I could but at the same time – you play fair.”

Toulson said he hoped there would be a full investigation and if cheating was found then a ban should be the consequence.

“It has come across as a bit of a joke but it’s not. It’s cheating. If the guy is found guilty he should be punished. I’ve seen players banned for swearing to themselves and it is a lot worse than that.”

Australian runner Olli Hoare clarifies he did not witness murder in Glasgow

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 14:26:21 GMT

Hoare confirms he was ‘six miles away’ on training run

Josh Kerr books place in Saturday’s men’s mile final

It is not every day a reigning Commonwealth Games champion is asked whether he witnessed a murder in Glasgow. Then again, it has been quite a few days for the Australian 1500m runner Olli Hoare. After competing on Wednesday in the heats of the men’s mile – when he finished with bloodied knees after being tripped – the 29-year-old was asked about reports that he had come across a murder scene while out training with his teammate Ky Robinson.

“No, no, I didn’t see a murder,” Hoare said. “The murder that was reported was six miles away and also at a different time.”

Hoare and Robinson were heckled as they ran, though, with at least one of those shouting at the pair holding a knife and, as a result, the Australia team have been told not to wear their kit in the city.

It was thought initially the pair had witnessed the aftermath of the murder of Paul McMinigal, in the east end of the city, on Friday. “I don’t know how that came about because Ky and I were running in the afternoon,” Hoare said. “We’re running on the river. Somehow these Chinese whispers have come in.”

Hoare’s good friend Jake Wightman, the Scotland 1500m runner who is staying in the same hotel as the Australians, said: “I am sure I am allowed to say it, he saw someone with a knife. That was it. And now they were saying he was in a murder scene. They’re two stories put together. But we’re joking that he ran out on the track with a stab-proof vest.

“Glasgow is like any city. There’s good and bad parts and you see some things you don’t necessarily want to see. Unfortunately, he ran into the middle of that and I hope it didn’t affect him.

“We were having a laugh about it, just because of all the weeks you want Glasgow to look as best, on his first run that happens.”

Hoare was determined to move on. “We came across a police dispute,” he said. “There were people walking around saying things. But I was never threatened.

“There was nothing heinous about what was happening. We were just running through, and there were some characters, and that was it.”

Asked whether they were carrying knives or not, Hoare said: “They looked like they were carrying something, but they weren’t threatening us. There was police there. They were breaking up a dispute when Ky and I ran past and we didn’t even think to report it.

“When we came back, all of a sudden I had Jake Wightman and all the boys coming up saying ‘you’re in the papers’, and I was like: ‘For what? Did I offend somebody wearing an Aussie beer T-shirt?’”

‘It hurts to lose a job you love’: Starmer loyalist Bridget Phillipson fights on despite cabinet demotion

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 13:24:16 GMT

Exclusive: The former education secretary on her new role as Labour chair and continuing as the minister for women and equalities

If Bridget Phillipson is angry at losing a job – one that, in the brief honeymoon period at the start of Keir Starmer’s Labour government, she called the “honour of my life” – she is doing a good job of hiding it. “It hurts to lose a job you love,” she says. “Being education secretary was amazing … and I’m really proud of what we achieved in that time.”

Phillipson was removed during the clearout of Starmer’s cabinet when Andy Burnham took office last week, and was replaced by Lucy Powell, an ally of the new prime minister. But unlike some spurned colleagues, Phillipson didn’t walk away from government, instead accepting the brief of women and equalities minister – now a cabinet standalone position – which she had previously held alongside education.

Her visit to a Rape Crisis centre in Cambridge this week highlighted why retaining the women and equalities brief may prove a canny move. On Monday, Burnham appointed Phillipson as the new chair of the Labour party – an apparent olive branch to Starmer allies, and a not entirely subtle attempt to restore some sense of unity to the party.

The role of Labour party chair is a nebulous one. Part election planner, administrator and party cheerleader, the chair’s importance rests heavily on the backing of the PM. On Monday, Burnham said Phillipson would play a “vital role” in getting Labour “match fit for the next election”.

With the subtlety of a sledgehammer, Labour’s communications stressed that the appointment showed Burnham’s commitment to building “one united team”. Phillipson echoed that it was by “uniting together” that Labour would “bring hope back to communities and strengthen British society against those working to divide us”.

Unity will involve working harmoniously with Powell, who defeated her in October’s deputy leadership contest and has now replaced her as education secretary. “That contest was almost a year ago. It’s in the past, and Lucy’s a great colleague,” Phillipson says. “We’ve worked together for many years, and she has my full support in the role.”

Phillipson hopes she can act as a vital bridge between bruised Starmer loyalists – many of whom are making no secret of their anger behind the scenes – and Burnham’s team.

“I know how people will feel, those who’ve lost out – I know it hurts. It hurts to lose a job that you have loved and put heart and soul into,” she says. “But I know that however people feel at the moment, they want to win the next election as much as I do, and they know how high the stakes are.”

Despite being a gentler character than some of her predecessors in the chair role, including Angela Rayner and Tom Watson, Phillipson insists she won’t pull her punches. She points to her record in developing the government’s fraught issue of reforming special educational needs provision in schools and pushing Starmer and Rachel Reeves to eventually lift the two-child benefit cap.

“I’m my own person, and I’ve always believed that there are different ways of being effective,” she says.

The fight against Reform UK, which slipped into second place behind Labour in a voter intention poll for the first time in more than a year this week, is a message she returns to repeatedly.

Phillipson insists that Labour’s manifesto commitment to halve violence against women and girls in a decade still stands, despite Burnham making no reference to it so far. Making her role a standalone cabinet position “demonstrates his commitment to equality and advancing women’s rights in our country”, she says, adding that ministers will be tracking VAWG crimes reported in the crime survey for England and Wales to hold themselves to account.

A week and a half into Burnham’s government, after a blitz of new policies, social media videos and a bounce in the polls, Phillipson says the new PM has brought “a real sense of hope, optimism and energy”. But she adds that he is building on the “good work” of the last two years under Starmer. “I am very sad at how things ended for Keir because he has achieved something that very few Labour leaders ever do, which is going from opposition into government and winning a landslide victory,” she says.

But she makes it clear that her loyalties lie with the new man in No 10. “I supported Keir from opposition to government because I believe it is right that you support the leader of your party and you support your prime minister,” she says. “It is therefore now right that Andy commands that loyalty from all of us.”

Andy Burnham wants to fix social care. It’s personal for him and for a lot of us too

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 13:21:03 GMT

Finally a grownup is in charge who speaks to voters as fellow adults. If he fixes this, he’ll achieve more than most other PMs

UK politics live – latest updates

It feels like the UK has a prime minister again. Not the Maybot paralysed with indecision. Not the clown-like Boris Johnson who crumbled under the weight of his own narcissism. Not the ridiculous Liz Truss. Not the steamrollered Rishi Sunak for whom everything was impossible. Not the automaton-like Keir Starmer who was never entirely sure what he wanted to do.

But a prime minister who is emotionally intelligent. Who understands the country and can connect with it. Who is prepared to expend political capital to get the things done that other politicians were too weak to go near. You can almost feel the sense of relief in a UK that has become almost accepting of decline and failure. It’s the return of hope over grievance. Where once more we have an adult prime minister prepared to speak to voters as fellow adults. It could catch on.

This was Andy Burnham’s first big set piece since taking office. And he went straight for social care. An issue that previous governments over the past 30 years have done their utmost to avoid. A royal commission, 22 reviews and absolutely nothing has changed. Too difficult, too many hard choices. Far simpler to keep on with a system that’s failing. Let the next government deal with it. They can take the hits. Just concentrate on trying to win the next election.

“This is personal to me,” said Andy, as he addressed a small audience of care workers and the media at Jewish Care in north London. Personal because his father has dementia and needs daily care.

It’s personal for a lot of us. It’s personal for me. My mother had Alzheimer’s and needed to be in a care home for seven years before she died last year. My sisters and I had to sell her home to pay for the care she got. We didn’t resent it. It was just what needed to happen and the care she got from a mostly overseas staff was superb. We couldn’t have asked for more. But my mother would have been bitterly upset had she been aware of what we had done. Before she got dementia she had always been so proud she would be able to leave her house to us children. It was to have been her last gift to us.

Here’s the thing. No one wants to pay for social care until the point when you find you have no choice. It’s a lottery. Some people just drop dead of heart disease. Others die of cancer. By and large they have no need for a social care system. But then one day you find an elderly relative is beginning to behave differently. Their personality begins to change. They start forgetting things. You try to explain it away. Maybe they are anxious and depressed. The doctor puts them on antidepressants. Old people’s memories do fail. It’s only months later you accept it’s dementia.

Then the choices become harder. You find a carer to make daily visits to their home. To get them dressed. To make sure they are still eating. Then you up the care so there’s someone with them at night. Next there comes a time when the carers say your loved one’s needs have become too much for them to be looked after at home. And all the while you are having to make the financial calculation. How can I give them the best care when I have no idea how long they are going to live. When they might die within a year or live for seven. It’s a nightmare.

And Burnham gets that it’s a nightmare. That hard choices need to be made. No one wants to pay extra for social care, but how can it be fair that some families are left with next to nothing just because they can’t choose the manner of their own death? Here was Andy talking human. Talking unscripted from the heart. Accepting that some people will be cynical about his intentions as they’ve heard warm words that have come to nothing before. But putting his political career on the line. He had no idea how long the public would give him in No 10, but he would make it his mission to reform the system.

First the good bits. The men and women – paid and unpaid – who deliver quality care day in, day out. But there was so much that didn’t work. The 15-minute care packages. The emergency calls. The bedblocking. The care homes that profited from others’ misfortunes. The random nature of who could afford what level of care provision. A system that was ultimately unsustainable. Every bit as unfair as the US health system, where time and again it’s the vulnerable who are left to pick up the tab.

So there would be three changes. Bringing forward the review to be completed next year. Converging the social care and NHS workforce. And, most importantly, starting cross-party talks. Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey had written to Burnham at the weekend so he had invited them to be part of the consensus. Presumably Nigel Farage had not written, preferring to snipe from the sidelines about a death tax. One day he might discover that even Reform supporters may need social care at some point. There again, this was probably a politics that was a little too grown up for Nige.

Then we got to the questions. Here, Burnham was also a revelation. Some media outlets have been moaning for the past week about how Andy was avoiding being interrogated. Running scared. Running a totalitarian socialist state. But he answered everything. No rambling. No answering questions he wished he had been asked. Just straightforward responses. Grownup to grownup.

Yes, it was going to be difficult. That’s why no one had tried to do it before. Yes, he did believe in consensus. Doing the big stuff involved dropping the political point scoring for the bigger picture. He hoped Ed and Kemi would be up to the challenge. He seemed to have given up on Nige already. And, yes, though some of the costs could be met from efficiency savings, there would inevitably be some hard choices on tax to be made. Do you feel lucky that no one in your family will need social care? Maybe you do. But it’s coming for most of us.

Andy left with a smile. Maybe this had been the easy bit. Starting the ball rolling. But it was better than ignoring it. And what a relief to have someone in No 10 who talks human. We should enjoy it while we can. Just think of the prize. If Andy were to do nothing in his time in office but fix social care, he would have achieved more than most other prime ministers.

Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: the secret to summer layering? Sheer bravery

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 13:00:33 GMT

Adding layers doesn’t have to leave you a hot mess – think sheer scarves and crochet with flashes of colour to elevate your look

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Perhaps I shouldn’t admit this, but I’m in two minds about summer dressing. Part of me believes summer is about joy, sunshine and good times, and clothes should embrace all of that. This woman loves Pucci and owns not one but two silver kaftans. The other part of me believes summer should be uncomplicated, laid-back and earthy. This woman never checks in luggage and has worn the same black beach cover-up for so many years it’s too threadbare to cover anything much.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The thing is, either approach looks absurd if taken to extremes. Candy swirls, cherry prints and strawberry bag charms are delightful, but pile them too high and you look like a walking knickerbocker glory. And while white linen shirts and simple black sandals are chic, you risk looking a bit like you’re on a meditation retreat where the dress code is “wealthy disciple”. Know what I mean?

Which is why I want to talk about layering, even though we are bang in the middle of summer. This tactic can be the key to landing your look in the sweet spot between the two extremes. A way to give your summer wardrobe some chat, without making it shout.

Summer layering isn’t about keeping warm. It’s about adding interest and hinting at skin without necessarily baring it. For a summer layering starter pack, all you need is a shirt that isn’t entirely opaque – sheer silk works, but so does fine linen – and then, crucially, something underneath that is visible on purpose. So instead of instinctively reaching for nude tones, choose a neon pink or black.

Whether this just-visible under layer is a lace bra or a sturdy vest top depends on how sheer the shirt is and how much sauciness you are comfortable with. But maybe try to be a little bit brave? An odd quirk of British dressing is that we don’t bat an eyelid at wearing a tight spaghetti strap vest, with its accompanying expanse of bare skin, but we consider it risque to wear, say, a billowing sheer shirt with a peekaboo hint of bra underneath. Yet sheer coverage is the more sophisticated option, as well as the sexier one.

Next: crochet. Left to its own devices, crochet has a tendency to look more beach or festival than real life. You know the look: floppy hat, enough anklets to start a percussion section. But treat crochet as a translucent top layer rather than the main event and it suddenly feels sharper. An open-knit jumper thrown over a tomato-red swimsuit gives you all the texture without the boho baggage. The flash of saturated colour makes the holes in the knit feel graphic rather than homespun, and the open weave does something clever with colour, softening a hot coral or an acid green bottom layer.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

When one piece is visible under another, your outfit looks instantly less basic. Clothes that are in conversation with each other is what style is all about. A sheer skirt can look sensational over black knickers as a party look, or intriguing worn with ballet flats and over cycling shorts for daytime. I see a lot of gen Z women with sheer scarves round their waists over trousers – a DIY nod to the sheer skirt. It sounds counterintuitive to add a layer in the heat, but silk weighs almost nothing and has an old-school glamour that elevates everything.

Summer layering asks you to think less about buying new clothes and more about wearing the clothes you already own differently, which is always a good thing. It’s also a way of reconciling those two women I mentioned at the start. The Pucci-loving magpie gets her colour and sparkle, but it’s softened by a sheer shirt or an open knit. The linen minimalist gets her simplicity, but with a kick that stops the whole thing becoming monastic. Why choose between maximalism and minimalism when we can spend summer in the happy, sun-dappled space in between?

Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret review – the tales of abuse are utterly disturbing

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 12:54:47 GMT

Four women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?

Jared Leto has long been a person with something of a reputational issue. The public-facing side of this was bad enough – while playing The Joker in 2016’s Suicide Squad, he reportedly sent rats, dead pigs and used condoms to his cast mates – but for years there have been upsetting rumours about what he does in private. After a lengthy investigation, the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret has finally brought at least some of them to light.

This is, as you might imagine, not a fun thing to watch. The film documents allegations of what are said to be decades of systematic criminal misconduct against teenage girls. The women interviewed here allege sexual assault, threatened sexual assault, sexualised grooming and statutory rape. They are backed up by anonymous male former co-workers who claim to have witnessed the machinery that Leto set up to procure underage girls from concerts.

What is particularly galling about Hollywood’s Dark Secret is that this is not the first time someone has tried to investigate these claims. As far back as 2005, the New York Post was running gossip columns that claimed he was “aggressively pursuing” what were described as “underage objects of desire” at a New York hotel. By 2018, actor Dylan Sprouse and director James Gunn were trading jokes about Leto’s interest in teenage girls online. Last year, Air Mail’s Elena Clavarino spoke to nine women who variously claimed that Leto pursued them, engaged in sexually explicit telephone conversations with them, exposed himself to them and masturbated in front of them – all while they were underage.

When that report was published, Leto’s representatives issued a denial. It seemed that everything continued as normal. He promoted his movie. He toured with his band. For a while it seemed that the world had blinked and moved on.

However, something with the heft of Hollywood’s Dark Secret will be harder to ignore. Released on YouTube as well as the BBC to ensure maximum impact, it is a disturbing look at what is alleged to be a skin-crawling pattern of behaviour. Jessica Sartenaer and her team have put together a case that bears the unmistakable smell of shoe leather. Clearly, it often takes a long time for allegations like this to see the light because of a culture of silence. People are often scared to go public for fear of shame or reprisal, and it is in the financial interests of many people to keep the Jared Leto machine running as long as possible.

That Sartenaer was able to find four women, and allay their concerns enough to let them show their faces onscreen, speaks volumes. We should let their testimonies speak for themselves (this really is a documentary that deserves to be seen, rather than simply read about), but their bravery deserves to be commended.

Although historical – these women are now all in their 20s, 30s and 40s – it is difficult to watch them recount what they experienced while they were underage. Some of their stories are straight from the Hollywood predator playbook, with them being procured by Leto’s team and led to dingy hotel rooms. Others are more baffling, like the woman who found herself receiving sexually explicit calls from Leto as a 16-year-old girl, only to then receive further calls of a similar nature from a man she believes was Leto in character as somebody else.

Cumulatively, when these stories have been added to archive footage of concerts where Leto has his arms draped around young girls, and talkshow appearances where he brags about sleeping with fans, and one particularly unnerving clip where he quotes the old Dazed and Confused line about high school girls – “I keep getting older but they stay the same age” – the effect is completely disturbing.

So far, Leto has been bulletproof against allegations like these, but you can’t help feeling that this film will land a blow. Of course, it should be noted that the timing of the documentary might help. Leto is no longer the box office draw he once was. Last year’s Tron: Ares reportedly lost somewhere in the region of $130m, and his latest film – Masters of the Universe – is among the biggest flops of the year so far. It isn’t the best reflection of Hollywood that it will only choose to round on alleged sexual predators once the bottom line has been weakened, but better late than never.

Leto declined to comment to Sartenaer and her team, unlike the robust denial he gave after the Air Mail investigation. Maybe it’s a sign that the floodgates will finally open?

Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret is on BBC iPlayer and YouTube now

Braiding used to be low maintenance and budget-friendly. What happened?

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 12:00:32 GMT

Every time I get my hair done, I find myself confronted with rising costs, and dizzyingly long maintenance regimes

Don’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up here

This week, I tried to book in for some knotless braids at the last minute. I knew I was going to be writing about how the simple pleasure of getting a head of box braids is starting to feel increasingly complicated, and thought that it would be good to get some pictures of the process. Then, I found myself getting wound up as the subject of this newsletter began to play out on a sort of meta-level.

When I decided to get my hair done for this piece, I knew that booking a next-day braiding slot would prove to be a kafkaesque task. My usual place asks that you schedule around a month in advance. My second option says that we’d need a “private room” to bring a photographer, bumping the bill up to £600. While trying to write an immersive report on the difficulties that come with getting braids, I suddenly realise that I am living the report.

None of the salons seem to care about my journalistic endeavour. They don’t need the publicity, or have time for it. As one salon tells me: “We have a high demand for braids, which is why it is hard to be super flexible.”

The lack of supply is causing tension. Braided divas frequently bemoan the power stylists have to set increasingly high prices. New Yorkers can pay around $450 (£339) for knotless braids, a more expensive style that has become the standard in the city in the past five or so years. In London, I’ll pay between £150 and £250 for the same. It wasn’t always like this.

Navigating an elaborate affair

With braiding you’re paying for every inch of labour – with waist length costing £20 more than bra length, small braids costing about £40 more than medium, and so on. If your hair isn’t pre-stretched, add another £20. Want your hair washed and blow dried? That’ll be an extra £20-35. For boho or goddess braids, a newer trend where wispy tendrils cascade out of your plaits, that could be, say, £50 more. If you’re using synthetic hair, it’s going to matt over the one to two months that you wear the style, so it’s better to use human hair bundles. But these can cost upwards of £250. Each of these decisions fills me with a moment of micro-dread.

When The Long Wave’s lead writer, Nesrine Malik, tells me that the Dutch braids she just got in Nairobi were the equivalent of £2, and that a full head of knotless only costs £20, I get a bit hot and itchy.

Obviously, London is its own economy. But I can’t simply opt out of the dizzyingly expensive process. Having your hair done isn’t exactly a choice, with one in five Black American women aged 25-34 having been sent home from work for their hair. To make matters worse, shifting beauty standards have completely normalised (if not mandated) these boho, knotless and butt-length styles, which take at least five hours to install.

“Braiding used to be a matter of convenience and low maintenance,” Nesrine tells me. “Branded as a ‘protective style’, it felt like something that could deliver you from the hamster wheel of washing and drying and curling or straightening. Now it is its own elaborate stressful affair.” And even once they’re done, the pressure doesn’t end. “Many of us are told that we’re doing it wrong: not washing them enough, keeping them in too long, getting braided too tight, too heavy.”

Anna Gifty Opoku-Agyeman, economist, Harvard PhD student and author of The Double Tax: How Women of Color Are Overcharged and Underpaid, agrees. “This is a topic that’s significantly understudied,” she tells me. “But we do know that the cost of beauty has gone up over time. That’s due, in part, to inflation, but also to ever-growing beauty standards.”

Victimised by similar forces

Still, Opoku-Agyeman believes that it’s shortsighted to solely focus on the experience of the consumer. “[Black hair stylists] are expected to know how to do everybody’s hair, and you get penalised if you can’t,” she says. “So you might have to just get more products, in order to accommodate all the different hair types that might come through your door.”

Opoku-Agyeman, who is Ghanaian-American, says you also need to factor in the spiralling rent in places like the US, and that shipping synthetic hair from China is no longer as cheap as it was. “When tariffs entered the picture, I was telling folks that this was actually going to hit black women very hard.”

Other specialised products like conditioners and gels made by Black-owned businesses may be more expensive, because they can struggle to gain investment, leading to low levels of supply. Opoku-Agyeman believes that the costs customers complain about aren’t resulting in massive profits for braiders. I still feel a little uncertain about the extra costs: I’ve heard stories of customers being charged extra for being a new client, or for having long or thick hair. Opoku-Agyeman gently checks me on these annoyances. “You have your sort of corner case type people, who will charge you just for parting your hair, right?” she says. “I think [this] is preposterous, but I don’t know how frequent they are.”

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

And I don’t want to undervalue Black women’s labour for, not only a specialised skill, but an art form. Perhaps as consumers we’re directing our ire towards victims of the same forces. “The folks who own the means of production around hair braiding are not the folks who are typically using hair-braiding services,” Opoku-Agyeman says. Most braiding products are not sourced from Black-owned businesses.

“Back in the day, people used to braid outside, braid in their houses, but now people are trying to build out a business.” They also are tending to you for the five to eight hours that you’re in the chair, often without a lunch break. Braiders need to be trained, which can be expensive. It’s hard work.

Paying the societal cost

What Opoku-Agyeman, Nesrine and I agree on is that Black women feel an intense pressure to be “presentable”, which comes from within and outside Black communities. “There is a real societal cost, and literal cost, to not getting your hair done,” Opoku-Agyeman tells me. “People are willing to spend $500 to get their hair done, because if I don’t, I’m not going to get the job … you could get suspended. You could get expelled.” Maybe when we get angry at add-ons, we’re really feeling anger at a lifetime of having to pay luxury prices for something that feels like a necessity.

This doesn’t only apply to braids. You could say the same for “wash and go” routines, the “straight natural” movement, locs, relaxers, fades and other Black hairstyles that have been subject to similar creeping policing and commercialisation. No matter what style you choose, the restrictions are tight and only seem to get tighter: with numerous steps, products and services deemed “essential” to keep you looking neat and professional.

The hair discrimination that forms part of this pressure is something that we can address in our own schools and workplaces. But it is also only one symptom of a longer, knotty history in which Black women’s hair has simultaneously been a site of expression and oppression. For many of us, going to the salon can feel like both of these things at the same time.

So what are we to do? As I admire my French curl braids, topped off with scalp-slick canerows, all I can think about is where I might channel my resentment at these rising prices. After six hours in the chair, it’s not toward my braiders. The beauty industry that profits from our social and economic anxieties? That’s a different question.

Trump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nasty

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 11:01:04 GMT

The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters

Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto

Though many hate to admit it, Canadians have long wished for more attention from the US. Well, we’re getting it now. And it turns out that President Trump and some of his top supporters in the Maga movement don’t much like us.

The first big hint was when he started talking about annexing us, saying we couldn’t survive without American support. But the most recent example of Trump’s dislike for Canada can be seen in his latest tariff policies. Canada was largely spared the impact of his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025 by its pre-existing free trade deal with the US (and Mexico), but earlier this month, as expected, the US declined to extend that deal for another 16-year term. It’s now subject to annual renegotiations. Then, last week, the White House announced tariffs as high as 50% on a selection of Canadian products including, for the first time, items previously protected by the trade agreement. The US called it retaliation for Canadian trade practices.

It’s true that the US announced tariffs against dozens more countries just days later, but there has been something odd about the lopsided attention paid to Canada, which most US presidents tend to politely ignore. Most of the tariffs Trump recently announced were in the range of about 10%, but Canada was hit by 50% tariffs (albeit on a narrower range of exports). The president, it seems, wanted to send a message to Canada, but without hurting US consumers too much.

The tariffs also land differently here, given Trump’s stated desire to annex Canada as a 51st state. The president has ruled out using military force to accomplish that, saying instead that he would use “economic force”. Tariffs would meet that definition.

There may have been little sign that the talk of annexation is anything more than typical Trumpian bluster, but even the suggestion, along with the tariffs, has been a shock for a Canadian political class that has long taken a friendly America as a law of nature – and has let Canada grow shockingly dependent on the US for defence and trade. An unfriendly, potentially even hostile US is a staggeringly consequential change. It’s hard to overestimate how huge a shock this has been.

And it’s having a massive effect on our domestic politics, thus far to the benefit of the Liberal party and the prime minister, Mark Carney. The return of Trump to the White House upset an election last year that the Liberals had been set to lose decisively. Canada’s Conservatives were cruising to an easy win with a campaign focused on public safety and the cost of living, but once Trump began musing about annexation, the Liberals dumped Justin Trudeau, replaced him with Carney, wrapped themselves in the flag, and won decisively. Carney remains popular, largely because Canadians see him as the right choice to deal with Trump.

US pressure is complicating Canada’s increasingly fraught internal politics in other ways. Canada does not have a true national economy, but a series of regional ones. Ontario and Quebec, the most populous provinces, are heavily dependent on manufacturing. In western Canada, particularly the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the economies depend more on exporting natural resources, including oil. Most of this goes to the US, as Canada lacks the transportation infrastructure to readily export it elsewhere (there’s that dependency).

The response has therefore been more fragmented than unified. Ontario has pursued a strategy of confrontation; the western provinces have preferred to appeal to shared interests with the US. These are obvious fissures that the US could choose to exploit. It was strange to see, when the most recent round of tariffs was announced, that most of the economic damage landed on Ontario and Quebec and the province of British Columbia – three jurisdictions that have taken stronger anti-Trump positions. The economies of Alberta and Saskatchewan were relatively spared.

Trump’s administration was probably hoping to mete out some punishment to provincial leaders it finds irritating. But it would have given Canada a much more challenging problem had it targeted instead the western provinces, where scepticism of rule by “eastern elites” and separatist movements are intensely divisive issues (Albertans will vote in a referendum this fall on whether to pursue independence). Carney must consider domestic blowback from any possible retaliation, such as an export tax on oil, lest he further inflame existing regional tensions.

Trump’s new tariffs aren’t due to take effect for several weeks, and Canada has not yet given any signal of how it will respond. To date, though, it has generally retaliated against US levies – Carney, whose political success rests on public belief that he will stand up to Trump, would find it very difficult not to retaliate this time.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This, more than anything else, is what the White House has failed to understand about Canada. The US has some legitimate gripes with us, including trade barriers and Canada’s chronic underinvestment in defence. It’s reasonable to be angry about those things. But the nature of Trump’s actions has made resistance the only plausible Canadian response: caving in to the US president is toxic for Canadian voters. Some provincial resistance is likely due to unpopular regional leaders seeing salvation in battling Trump – and although Carney has made some concessions since becoming prime minister, including scrapping a planned digital tax that angered US tech companies, he dare only go so far.

Trump has often complained that dealing with Canadians is unpleasant and nasty. He should expect us to get nastier still. Whether he knows it or not, he’s left us little choice.

Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto, and co-editor of The Line, an online magazine

Uefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenable

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 10:22:19 GMT

European football has shown an increased willingness to talk tough with Fifa but words can only be wielded so many times

FA joins criticism of Fifa plan to sell off World Cup stakes

As the World Cup neared its conclusion, one leading figure in European football pondered how Gianni Infantino might attempt to rinse away the damaging stain of the Folarin Balogun scandal. It all came down to money. “He will just announce more funds for everyone,” was the gist, although the tournament passed without any explanation of how Fifa would carve up its record $15bn (£11.2bn) haul.

That was the tip of the iceberg. Infantino’s plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, announced on Tuesday, nine days after the final, has sent shock waves around the sport and left senior personnel scrambling. There is little time for a coordinated response given Fifa, at the height of what passes for football’s holiday period, has given FAs until 19 September to decide whether to accept the initial $20m payment that would effectively count as endorsement of the new scheme.

The reaction must come quickly. Perhaps, when Uefa assesses its next move, it will look back to 2021 and remember the credit it happily banked in blocking the proposed European Super League. Fifa’s plan, which could allow private investors a say in how and when its tournaments are run, is potentially more seismic and global in scale. If football’s future has been on a ticking clock under Infantino, the time is one minute to midnight.

Uefa’s speed in responding to the plan was of a piece with its renewed appetite, honed over a number of run-ins over the past 15 months, to stick the boot into Fifa. “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” it said, although anyone feeling a sense of deja vu needed only to scroll back three weeks. On 6 July, another Uefa statement said the shelving of Balogun’s suspension “crossed a red line”. These are strong, accurate words, but they can be wielded only so many times.

Infantino can rush his proposals through by counting on votes from the overwhelming number of FAs, primarily based outside Europe, who pledge fealty to his administration. But a show of backbone from football’s most powerful continent, a sporting behemoth that has eaten up any competition on the pitch and through the financial clout of its institutions, would be a major blow to Fifa. It would only take concrete action from a few of Europe’s major nations, with their governments in lockstep, to render any plan to sell off football’s crown jewels untenable.

Who will put their heads above the parapet? This is a moment to remember that, as the Guardian revealed in mid-July, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 members have already submitted letters in support of his candidacy for re-election early next year. Most of those resisting significant pressure to offer backing are from Europe, with Germany the highest-profile holdout. But England’s FA, which is hoping to rubber-stamp its hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, was quick to offer its endorsement well before this summer.

Then there are cases such as Finland, whose FA president, Ari Lahti, said in June that his country aimed “not to be an eyesore” by refusing to back Infantino. It is a common stance, even among federations who are vocal in private about their disgust for Fifa’s trampling over norms and proximity to the Donald Trump administration. Countries of all sizes have a duty to put the beauty contest on hold.

Any talk of boycotting future World Cups, which would surely have to include the women’s edition in Brazil next year, is complicated by a section of Fifa’s statutes that says its members are obliged to take part in its competitions. The only way to avoid financially prohibitive sanctions may be to threaten the most radical step of all: a withdrawal from Fifa and the creation of a new governance model for football.

Uefa’s position may be made trickier by its close relationship to the thus far taciturn European Football Clubs (EFC), which would like to set up a joint venture with Fifa to run the Club World Cup. EFC and Uefa already run a joint venture, UC3, that operates the commercial aspect of Uefa competitions, but one of the key differences from Fifa’s proposal is that it does not involve private capital.

Somehow, everyone must be corralled together if Infantino is to be tackled. Another way would be to remove some wind from Infantino’s sails by putting up a serious electoral opponent. After the Balogun affair, conversations with figures at all levels of the sport speculated whether Uefa might endorse its own candidate to run for the Fifa presidency in March. Consensus suggested it would be too soon; that this will be a period of positioning for 2031 when, according to Fifa’s current rules, Infantino must stand aside.

But there is no time to play a long game when Infantino plans to carve up football’s future among private interests in rapid order. Nor is there the opportunity to wait for any European Commission response to the complaint by FifPro, the global players’ union, and the European Leagues organisation about Fifa’s grip on the international match calendar, which was lodged in October 2024. A favourable outcome could place obstacles in front of any plans by Fifa, or its friends in private investment, to expand its tournaments, but no resolution appears in sight.

Uefa and Europe must take a lead and reject the status quo. Doing so might reveal friends in unexpected places. There are certainly countries in Asia, among other confederations, that would be open to clear suggestions of a better path. The fear is that a rush of nebulous statements such as that by the Danish FA, which responded to Infantino’s plan by emphasising the need to “gain a complete understanding of the proposal and the process behind it” will result in nothing bar the standard procrastination and tacit acceptance.

Bravery and sturdy spines are required now, more than ever, if football is to survive in anything resembling its present form.
