Even Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse …

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 10:00:29 GMT

The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world

There’s something a bit off about JD Vance. And I mean that literally: the vice-president has been snacking on sauerkraut and other fermented foods as part of a weight-loss regime. Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr got a number of Trump officials, including Vance, on to the diet, and is thrilled with the results. “Within 20 days I lost 20 pounds,” Kennedy said at an event in Michigan last month. “JD Vance is also on the diet and you can see how different he looks.” Dunno about that: still looks like a naked opportunist to me.

If you want to get into Donald Trump’s good books, improving your looks is a surefire way to do so. According to MS Now, the president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure; it’s helped propel him back into Trump’s good graces. Which is lucky for him because he doesn’t have many other fans. They may be full of beneficial bacteria, but everyone around Vance seems to hate his guts.

That includes a member of his protective detail, who is now under investigation for revealing to the media the Vance family’s lavish travel requests. The Hillbilly Elegy author reportedly asked for one of his sons to be dropped off at a golf lesson via helicopter, and demanded last-minute chopper trips to Virginia to go house-hunting. With help like that you can understand why Vance is so pronatalist. I’d be popping out kids too, if I could get the taxpayer to fund helicopter trips to their extracurriculars.

It’s not just the help he has angered. On Friday the Washington Post reported that Vance has faced a barrage of attacks from within his party “unlike that faced by other vice-presidents in decades”. Vance’s allies told the Post that the attacks, which seem largely driven by his mild criticism of Israel and the Iran war, are a “coordinated” attempt to poison his 2028 presidential chances. Over the weekend a Fox News panel criticised Vance for a recent appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast where (in a brief moment of good judgment) he questioned putting troops on the ground in Iran. “[Vance] seems to be going off base a lot, and contradicting the president a lot in public lately, and it’s not helpful,” Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen said.

I can’t say it’s not fun to watch Maga infighting. Nevertheless, it’s hard to take too much satisfaction from Vance’s troubles considering they only really benefit his rival for the 2028 Republican nomination: the odious war hawk Marco Rubio, who is now narrowing the gap with Vance in the polls. A setback for one awful politician always seems to spell a career boost for someone even worse. It’s really quite the pickle.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 09:08:57 GMT

Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago

‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing

“There was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.”

Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake in southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks.

At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured when the earthquake struck the island of Kyushu. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday: “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time. We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”

Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke.

Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.”

In April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead.

At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast.

A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke.

A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the mall told the Nikkei newspaper that he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said.

Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing.

In nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts.

A woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” she told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun from Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in.

On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside.

“The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.”

As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park.

In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.”

Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 09:00:29 GMT

Five years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out against fossil fuels. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to act

France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins

Such is the astonishing scale of the wildfires burning at the gates of Bordeaux and Madrid, that if they had happened 20 – even 10 – years back, they may well have shocked the world into taking action on the climate crisis. But like the proverbial frog in a pot of slowly heating water, we have become inured; not only to the ever more devastating impacts of climate breakdown, but increasingly to the actions needed to bring global heating to heel.

Even as more than 35,000 wildfires rage across the surface of our world, and as we continue to rewind our planet’s climate so it resembles hotter episodes from its distant past, governments and trading blocs are very deliberately turning away from climate action.

The latest evidence that we are not only doing too little but actually doing less as time goes by is provided by the climate action media platform, We Don’t Have Time. It reported last week that the 12 months to July this year saw the reversal across the world of 45 climate policies. The retreat on climate action is global, but Europe – previously seen as a leader in emissions reductions – is in the vanguard, weakening measures across the board, including in the areas of carbon pricing, methane emissions and the phasing out of petrol and diesel vehicles.

This isn’t yet an apocalyptic reversal of the majority of climate commitments, as the continuity of countless other climate policies testifies. We are, however, at an especially critical period: if we don’t want backsliding on climate action to continue, we have to act now.

We Don’t Have Time lays the blame squarely at the foot of lobbying by the fossil fuel sector, and other industries antagonistic to climate action, making the point that as long as the usual suspects continue to make the most noise in the meetings where decisions are made, they will get what they want. What we have to do, then, is to make even more noise – on the streets, via the ballot box and in the media – putting pressure on politicians and governments so that they don’t cave in to vested business interests.

We must force those in power to join the dots between the fires raging across Europe and the El Niño building in the Pacific, and the activities of the fossil fuel corporations and others who choose not to do so.

But we need our own lobbyists too – those qualified and in positions to speak truth to power about the dire straits we are already in, who can add credence to the noisy debate. Cue the world’s climate scientists. At this critical moment, the science has a duty to out-shout and out-shine corporate weasel words and government irresponsibility. The problem is that even now, at a time when the rate of global heating has doubled, this is just not happening.

Sure, there are climate scientists out there telling it like it is, making a lot of noise and often putting their livelihoods and career prospects on the line, but they remain the exception rather than the rule. Far too many individuals, for one reason or another, still keep silent, heads below the parapet, fears and frets internalised.

In 2021, I wrote an open letter to all climate scientists, reminding them that they had a duty to speak out, to come down off the fence and to force those who need to know to listen to the truth. Sadly, five years on, little has changed. For far too many, fears about funding, academic advancement, prestige, and the contempt or ridicule of colleagues, still trump speaking out.

As the heat continues to ratchet up, this cannot go on. If we want to have any possibility of drowning out the bogus claptrap of those determined to prevent serious climate action, then climate scientists – all scientists for that matter – need to wake up now and make themselves heard.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Climate science is a vast tent that incorporates aspects of geology, chemistry, physics, oceanography, meteorology, economics, social science and many other fields, so that one source putting the number of climate scientists at 18,000 worldwide is almost certainly an underestimate. When it comes to scientists of every ilk, the global figure comes out at not far short of 10 million. Just imagine how much racket the scientific community could make if it spoke with the same voice – demanding the reinstatement of climate-friendly policies, arguing for more rapid emissions cuts, and at the same time overwhelming the perfidious calls for inertia from those lobbying for business as usual.

This may well be our last chance to turn things around; to help politicians grow the backbones they need to stand up to vested interests. At this crucial time every scientist needs to examine their conscience, take on board the reality that there will be no research grants on a dead planet – and act accordingly.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London and author of The Fate of the World: a History and Future of the Climate Crisis

What makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castle

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 07:00:25 GMT

Modern weddings seem to have become all about the spectacle – although, if you do take the opulent route, I still want to come

Am I allowed to start a column about weddings by saying I don’t know exactly what I think about weddings and marriage in general? Well let’s see.

One thing I do know: I really like attending weddings. I love to go as a valued guest, to see close friends in love and watch dads I have known for many years gruffly and fearfully breach the dancefloor. But I also love to go as a totally minor guest (the better for people-watching) and collect anecdotes about who, from the various overlapping families, hates who. People will just tell you these things, especially if your presence is quite random. I like to see the freshly single sporting their revenge dresses and haircuts and physiques. I like to witness and partake in the abundance of flirting. I don’t think I’ve ever had a bad time at a wedding.

I asked friends their views on weddings while writing this. One of them said: “In general, I feel like weddings bring out behaviour we could use more of. For example flirting, dancing, and making plans, getting dressed up etc.” I agree completely. In fact, I have always dreaded getting the call to write about weddings precisely because I don’t want to compromise my cherished status as a frequent guest. But the truth is, I do feel some ambivalence about the contemporary execution, and I do consider my generation’s approach to weddings, and even marriage, a little odd.

I started thinking about this after former rugby player Danny Cipriani and his fiancee, the actor Annalynne McCord, launched a “tacky and distasteful” (as one source had it) crowdfunding page asking guests to help pay for their wedding. The total amount they are asking for is £10,660. It seems fair to say that their combined earnings considerably outstrip those of your average newlyweds.

And yet, unexpectedly, I find myself feeling sorry for them. I feel wary of the spectacle that weddings have become. I don’t think it was always like this. Talk to older people and you’ll hear stories of a family dinner and then a dance in the local pub. These days – even for non-celebrities – they are often big, flashy affairs, perhaps in exotic destinations, sometimes over several days. I hear so much about arguments when people don’t get invited, even though we all know space is usually limited. I wonder why people feel it has to be like this. I wonder, too, if the opulence makes the whole thing even more emotionally charged.

Admittedly my own views on weddings and marriage, as these things might apply to me, make no sense at all. On the one hand, I’m an Irish Catholic who has been in a heterosexual relationship for a while. On the other hand, the institution of marriage feels odd to me. I wouldn’t argue my own lifestyle is radical, but I am sometimes surprised that big white weddings are still such a widespread norm.

I never imagined my own wedding as a child. And when I try to picture a wedding for myself now, it would have to be in a Catholic church. The version of Catholicism I subscribe to could absolutely be described as “one I just invented in my head”. I stop into churches all the time to light candles and pray, meanwhile I pay attention to basically nothing the church has to say. Some would say that a humanist wedding might allay my discomfort with the institution of marriage, and I would agree. Still, the idea of being married in a humanist service by someone wearing, say, skinny jeans and a black T-shirt gives me willies. Why is this? Logically, it makes no sense. But that’s how I feel.

And actually, I think that’s the core of it. Weddings seem governed not by logic but by random yet passionately held whims. Maybe that is what causes people to have their names monogrammed on to hundreds of napkins, or to demand hundreds of people traipse to a country that even the two people getting married have never visited. It is precisely this sense of heightened and crazed emotions that makes weddings fun.

So much deranged behaviour occurs. I myself have been asked out several times over the years, at weddings I have attended with my boyfriend. Once, memorably, a man with swept-back hair (a doctor no less) sort of charged up to me and said: “Look how are things going with your boyfriend? It seems like they’re going well. But if not …”. Then he gestured at himself, to present the alternative option. You have to admire it.

I’m not deluded enough to interpret this as proof of my startling beauty or charm. Instead, I see it as evidence that the sentiment and nostalgia that suffuse every wedding does something strange to us all. Picture the kind of man who’s spent a decade or so juggling situationships arriving on the dancefloor as the music of his misspent boyhood floods the room (a Calvin Harris song or Mr Brightside, say). He thinks: “God, I’m tired!” And then, casting frantically around: “Look, just pick somebody, anybody! Well she would do, would she?” Time comes for us all.

All the money in the world wouldn’t make up for this kind of experience. The atmosphere at weddings exists all by itself. There’s no need to book a French castle for a memorable day. Having said that, if you have cash to burn, why not? I wouldn’t turn down the invitation. Which is all to say: please continue to invite me to your weddings.

Rachel Connolly is a writer and the author of the novel Lazy City

Suddenly the British right feels a political chill. It’s getting cold in Andy Burnham’s shadow

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 05:00:23 GMT

The Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has become

Andy Burnham’s recollections of Britain in the 1970s must be pretty hazy. He was nine when the decade ended. Kemi Badenoch, born in 1980, can remember nothing. Lacking first-hand experience, the Conservative leader evokes the turmoil of a bygone era with cautionary zeal borrowed from an older generation. In a speech last week, she accused the new prime minister of pining for “endless strikes, rubbish not being collected, bodies not being buried, inflation at 25% and a chancellor going cap-in-hand to the IMF”.

This is more incantation than argument, a ritual fondling of beads on the Tory rosary. It is a symptom of a leader under stress, affirming her faith in Our Lady Margaret Thatcher and warding off socialist devils. Burnham has done nothing to support the claim that his government is a 70s tribute act, unless you count the appointment of a man named Healey as chancellor and the imposition of price controls on buses.

What the prime minister has done is trace Britain’s present malaise to choices made in the Thatcher era. From the threshold of No 10 he delivered the verdict on that legacy: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, large parts of the country de-industrialised, and they still haven’t recovered.” That statement has become the foundation stone for an edifice of neuralgic conservative commentary, bemoaning Britain’s capture by anti-market, pro-state fanatics.

The right of British politics seems to be disoriented by the appearance of a Labour prime minister whose message isn’t crafted as a preemptive flinch at the accusation that he might come from the left, believe some leftish things and gamble on them being popular. Nigel Farage is playing it safe with the predictable but flimsy complaint that Burnham lacks a mandate. The Reform UK leader knows that isn’t how British politics works and, given that his personal ratings are on a downward drift, he doesn’t want a general election anyway.

Badenoch’s reach back to the Seventies is a default setting in the absence of better ideas. It isn’t totally irrational, given the hint of nostalgia in Burnham’s tone. His ascendancy to No 10 relied on him being acceptable to a coalition of disputatious Labour factions. Lamentation over the death of a proletarian way of life, killed by Thatcher’s hand, is a hymn the party can sing in harmony. The new leader is a skilled choirmaster – in contrast to his predecessor, who knew the words but couldn’t carry a tune.

But Burnham has also just spent nine years as mayor of Manchester, leaving it an enterprising capitalist city. He argues that its success is a function of pragmatic partnership between government and business, and that this model can be replicated on a national scale. It is hardly wild dogma to suggest that a strategically minded state can guide the hand of the market. The prime minister believes devolving power will give that hand a defter feel for local needs.

Conservatives might disagree, but it takes wilful denial, or maybe intellectual laziness, to pretend that Burnham’s Manchester blueprint is retro-socialism, plain and simple. The prime minister could hardly be more explicit in rejecting the 20th-century central planner’s adage that “the gentleman in Whitehall knows best”.

It is normal for oppositions to take time to get the measure of a new prime minister, and vice versa. Leaders need to make a few mistakes before their weaknesses form a pattern that can be woven into an effective political attack. Keir Starmer was a slippery target in opposition. But in government he made life easy for his enemies by shedding what modest popularity he had accrued almost immediately. Badenoch didn’t have to develop an argument against a prime minister who struggled to explain what he was trying to do and was easily bullied into doing something else.

The Tories were bystanders while Starmer’s government self-immolated, mostly to the benefit of Reform UK and the Greens. Badenoch’s personal ratings have picked up over the past year, reflecting perhaps growing squeamishness on the right about Farage as a prospective prime minister. But the Conservative vote share has yet to climb as high as the giddy depths it fell to in July 2024, when the party suffered its worst ever general election defeat.

Disillusionment with Labour rule has done nothing to revive public interest in a Conservative alternative. Badenoch has done nothing to make her party interesting. She wasted her first year fretting perversely that the Tories had been too leftwing in office, thereby endorsing the case for defection to Reform UK.

She then switched to a focus on fiscal parsimony, hoping to occupy electoral terrain between public wariness of Labour’s tax-and-spend instincts and suspicion that Farage was a bit spivvy where money is concerned. But having scoped out a desirable patch of political real estate, Badenoch isn’t building anything. She has no theory of public service reform. To read her speeches is to inhabit a parallel universe where the obvious causes of dissatisfaction with the state are chronic overfunding and infestation by militant leftwing civil servants.

It is a vacuous analysis, coloured by excessive consumption of radical US conservative content online. British politics has always been shaped by trends across the Atlantic, but the radicalisation of the British right through exposure to Maga influence (both cultural and financial) in recent years amounts to cognitive surrender. Political fandom has usurped judgment; craving validation from a foreign power takes precedence over loyalty to the national interest.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

A Labour prime minister has the excuse of realpolitik, being obliged to show deference to a despotic US president who despises democratic allies but remains indispensable when it comes to their defence needs. Even then, Starmer found the courage to distance himself from Donald Trump’s disastrous military adventure in Iran. Not so, Badenoch. She turned squeamish only when she realised how far her initial gung-ho instincts had carried her from British mainstream opinion.

What British conservatives either fail to observe or refuse to acknowledge in their mindless orbit around Planet Trump is that Maga politics contains more heresies against the sacred Thatcherite creed than anything Burnham proposes. The US president hates free trade. He admires single-party regimes where a supreme ruler directs economic activity. He imposes arbitrary tariffs. He uses his office to extort money from private companies or coerce them into giving equity stakes to his government. And he acquired the power to do all of this by skilfully manipulating economic and social grievances caused by deindustrialisation – the alienation and dislocation felt by working-class communities that felt their security and dignity washed away by cold global market tides.

It is the same trend that Burnham identifies as a cause of British discontent and economic stagnation. The difference is that the UK prime minister talks about healing wounds, while Trump keeps them salted with partisan spite. It should be obvious to anyone who cares about democracy and the rule of law which model is preferable. Maybe the new prime minister’s methods will not work. Perhaps his prescriptions are flawed. At least his diagnosis belongs in 2026. It is the leader of the opposition, craving reenactment of a battle that was won before she was born, who is stuck in the wrong century.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Organic eggs have worse impact on climate than eggs from caged chickens

The Guardian Wed, 29 Jul 2026 04:00:24 GMT

Adopting organic free-range model in UK could lead to greenhouse emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2, study suggests

Organic eggs are twice as bad for the climate as eggs from chickens living in cages, research suggests.

According to the study, switching the UK’s entire egg production to an organic free-range model would lead to greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2 (tCO2e), while production through a fully caged system would emit 1,184,000 tCO2e.

This is because organic free-range models need more chickens for the same number of eggs produced, as birds living in cages tend to be more efficient.

Organic free-range production also scored worst in its potential for water eutrophication, acidification and land use. Chicken mortality was also highest in organic free range farming, the researchers said.

However, the study used data from 2009-2010, which the researchers acknowledged as a limitation as it did not capture more recent developments in egg production. The research also did not take into account other environmental impacts such as pesticides or biodiversity.

Laying hens are the largest group of animals kept in cages across the world, and global egg consumption is going up, making their treatment an important welfare consideration, said Dr Harriet Bartlett, one of the authors of the study.

“I’d say perhaps it’s also a little bit of a blind spot when we talk about sustainability,” she added. “Meat and dairy get a bit more attention, talking about environmental sustainability, whereas [egg production] hasn’t been as researched.”

Bartlett is the senior research associate at Oxford University’s Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, and has previously studied factory farming methods.

The latest study, published in Royal Society Open Science, involved Bartlett and colleagues examining data from UK poultry farms to calculate environmental impacts such as greenhouse gas emissions, land use and types of pollution. They also looked at welfare indicators such as mortality and the number of hens needed to produce a given number of eggs.

“Then we did some some modelling to work out these environmental and welfare outcomes,” she said.

“We found an important trade-off,” Bartlett added. “It’s that, the types of farms that are generally regarded as being better for animal welfare, like organic and free-range, can actually require more birds to produce the same amount of eggs because they’re less less efficient and they can have higher environmental impacts.”

However, Bartlett said the research did not show the whole picture regarding factory farming. “Organic could come out better on pesticide toxicity, maybe biodiversity on farm as well,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

Lee Holdstock, the head of regulatory and trade affairs at Soil Association Certification, who was not involved in the study, said the research “highlights some important trade-offs” but gave an “incomplete picture of environmental impact”.

“While intensive systems can have lower emissions per unit of output because birds use feed more efficiently, this reflects only one part of the picture,” Holdstock said. “A truly sustainable food system must also consider impacts on nature, soil health, water quality, the use of synthetic inputs, and animal welfare.”

The researchers estimated that 1,439,000 tCO2e is emitted under the current regime, in which egg production is split between caged, barn-housed, free-range non-organic and free-range organic systems.

One of the Soil Association’s standards for organic eggs is that chickens must have continuous and easy daytime access to an outdoor range covered with suitable vegetation.

Connections Coach

OpinionNicholas Kristof

A woman showing the tattoo of one of her traffickers. Credit... Tamara Reynolds for The New York Times

Supported by

By Nicholas Kristof

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Oklahoma City.

Kanisha Hamilton became an expert on sex trafficking in the most unfortunate way, beginning at the age of 12. So whenever she heard talk about the Jeffrey Epstein case, “it triggered me bad,” she recalled.

“I would wake up in the mornings and think about something that had to do with it, and just start crying uncontrollably,” she told me. “Because I knew there are thousands if not more women, children and even men suffering at that moment. And everyone else in the world is just going about their business acting like they can’t do anything.”

“That’s how people like that get away with sex trafficking people,” she said.

One of the paradoxes of the moment is that there is intense outrage at Epstein and his enablers — as there should be — but almost no effort to protect the girls or boys who continue to be trafficked all around the country and the world. We are rightly appalled at the general indifference that powerful figures showed toward Epstein’s assaults, yet collectively we show a parallel indifference to the predation that continues to unfold in cheap motels everywhere. The upshot is that exploitation of girls and boys continues daily at thousands of times the scale of anything Epstein did.

Hamilton’s pathway began when she was around 6 months old and her mother, who was addicted to drugs, was murdered, she said. Her grandmother then traded her to a child molester for heroin, she said, and after enduring abuse she ended up in the dysfunctional world of foster care. At 12 she joined her dad, a pimp who began selling her as well as the other women he controlled, she added.

We sometimes imagine that traffickers jump out of bushes, grab teenage girls and drag them into vans, to be chained to radiators. But I’ve been writing about trafficking for more than 25 years, and mostly the traffickers prey on girls who are already vulnerable. In need of housing, food or love, these girls are too often invisible to society — but not to pimps.

“There’s just an overall misconception of what trafficking is, what it looks like,” said Felicia Bowman, who was trafficked at the age of 7 by a friend’s brother who was also a drug dealer. “People think that it’s a white van, it’s the zip ties on your car at Target.” She was referring to an urban legend that traffickers drive white commercial vans to kidnap girls, and mark kidnapping targets with zip ties.

“How do we hold the fact that it’s all these vulnerabilities that we’re not addressing?” she added. “Because then we’re all accountable, and we’re all responsible, and a lot of the problems that lead to that are so big.”

Bowman had those vulnerabilities. A female family friend who watched over her took advantage of them and sold her for sex, she said. “She was making me sleep with people for money for drugs,” Bowman recalled.

It’s not just that we don’t try to help these children. Often, we scorn them. We see them as bad kids, as troublemakers, as runaways, and we are lenient to those who abuse them.

Bowman says that when she was 12, a man was arrested for sexually assaulting her. “He was found guilty,” she said. “He got 30 days.” Records document that.

I asked her if any mandatory reporters — teachers or doctors, for example — had seen evidence of her abuse and reported it to the authorities. On the contrary, she said, authorities who should have been looking out for her also abused her. One was caught and convicted, but his only punishment was house arrest.

It’s no wonder that Bowman didn’t trust authority figures. All they did was exploit her.

I met Bowman and Hamilton through an impressive nonprofit called Dragonfly that serves trafficking survivors in Oklahoma. These local initiatives, offering everything from therapy to medical care to removal of pimp tattoos, are invaluable — but they are starved of resources. When a girl leaves a pimp, it can be a scramble to find a bed for her.

When help comes, it can be transformative. Both Hamilton and Bowman are now thriving and helping other survivors of human trafficking.

“We’re underfunded, and the demand is insane for our services,” said Whitney Anderson, a founder of Dragonfly. “What keeps us going is that these are individuals who have survived the worst of the worst. That they have seen things done to them that humans should never do, and they are in front of us. And so we owe them the very best.”

If we were serious about confronting trafficking, we could boost support for these programs around the country. We could shut down websites where pimps advertise girls (and sometimes boys), as prosecutors did with Backpage, which once dominated the field. We could insist that social media platforms crack down on traffickers who recruit on their pages using coded language (if 14-year-olds understand it, the companies can as well). We could make much greater efforts to prosecute pimps. And local D. A. s could prosecute johns to suppress the demand that keeps traffickers in business.

Most of all, we could do more to help families and children so that they’re not in the pipeline to be trafficked. Girls in foster care are at particular risk; there are no statistics on this, but after decades of these interviews I wouldn’t be surprised if a girl in foster care is more likely to end up trafficked than to graduate from a four-year college.

Yet instead of helping these vulnerable children, we’re magnifying the risks. President Trump’s cuts in social services, such as for mental health and addiction treatment, may lead to more disadvantaged and chaotic homes and more trafficked children.

I’m on my annual “win a trip” journey, in which I pick a university student to travel on a reporting trip with me — this year, it’s Brunella Tipismana of Yale — and in Tulsa, we visited an outstanding pre-K system called Educare serving the neediest families. Educare seems to me a tool to build resiliency, improve outcomes and reduce addiction and trafficking, yet America has never been willing to invest in high-quality pre-K for the kids who most need it.

In Kentucky, we visited Freedom House, which helps moms overcoming addiction. If we were serious about trafficking we would make such programs much more broadly available. But addiction treatment is underfunded in America, and Trump’s Medicaid cuts next January will make the problem worse.

My quarrel with conservatives is that they defund programs that can, imperfectly, reduce the number of children vulnerable to exploitation. My quarrel with liberals is that they sometimes are so nonjudgmental that they favor legalizing sex work in ways that would also permit pimping (anyone who thinks pimps are business partners of girls doesn’t understand the trade). My quarrel with the public is that our fury at Epstein’s friends seems performative if in effect we shrug at children being sold for sex down the street.

Consider Cassidy Husband, who grew up in a dysfunctional home and ran away at the age of 13 into the arms of a pimp who said he loved her — and then started selling her. Now 29, she recalled working for many different pimps over the next 14 years, and they always kept the money. They often assigned her daily earnings quotas, and she risked a beating if she fell short. Her body is marked by tattoos from pimps trying to establish their ownership over her.

In her years on the street, Husband said she regularly recruited girls for her pimps. She looked for girls with broken sandals, or unkempt clothes or hair, who lacked confidence. “Come on,” she would tell the girl, “and we’re going to take care of you.” It was emotional manipulation of desperate, vulnerable young women, but it was not the kind of kidnapping that the public associates with human trafficking.

“It’s really hard to bring awareness, I think, about child sex trafficking,” said Husband, who is now off drugs, getting her tattoos removed and rebuilding her life. “Because a bag didn’t get put over my head. I didn’t get shoved into a van, that kind of thing.”

If we truly think that Epstein was a monster, then what’s needed isn’t shaking our fists at his corpse. It’s a real effort to help the girls and boys who, in cities around the country, are struggling in chaotic homes, desperate for help and not getting any at all.

Readers, a question for you: We as a society fulminate against sex traffickers. So why don't we show more compassion for actual girls being trafficked? If we're so horrified by Jeffrey Epstein's abuses, why don't we do more to help stop kids from being sold?

With Blanche Nomination at Stake, Payouts to Trump Allies Continue

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A seven-figure settlement is announced two days before a scheduled Senate committee vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general.

By Devlin Barrett and Alan Feuer

Devlin Barrett reported from Washington, and Alan Feuer from New York.

Two days before Senate lawmakers were scheduled to vote on advancing Todd Blanche’s nomination to serve as attorney general, a million-dollar payout was announced for an anti-abortion activist he has called a victim of government weaponization by the Biden administration.

The settlement given to Paul Vaughn, who was convicted by a Tennessee jury in 2024 of conspiring to prevent access to an abortion clinic, shows how the goal of a $1.8 billion fund announced in May can continue, despite a public retreat by Mr. Blanche. An already existing avenue for disbursing taxpayer money could allow him to assuage skeptical Republicans while fulfilling President Trump’s desire to pay people he believes were wronged by the Justice Department.

Mr. Vaughn will receive a seven-figure settlement from the government, his lawyers said, making him among those aligned with the administration who have received a payout by an alternative means.

Since 1870, the Justice Department has handled claims for civil compensation against the federal government. Such claims can be filed through public lawsuits, or privately through forms sent directly to the department.

Mr. Vaughn, whom the president pardoned last year, has insisted he is innocent and accused the Biden administration of misusing a law meant to ensure women and health care professionals have unobstructed access to reproductive services.

The settlement was reached by his lawyers at the Thomas More Society, which often represents anti-abortion activists, in April. But it first disclosed the payment on Tuesday in a statement that said their client had been prosecuted for political reasons and as part of a government weaponization effort against people who oppose abortion rights.

The continuing ability of the department to make such payouts with or without a formal fund structure is one of the sticking points between the Trump administration and Republican senators as they weigh the nomination of Mr. Blanche, currently the acting attorney general.

A single “no” from a Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee could stall or sink his nomination, and Thursday’s scheduled vote was in doubt after some crucial holdouts expressed skepticism.

In May, the Justice Department announced that it would resolve a lawsuit from Mr. Trump demanding at least $10 billion from the I. R. S. by establishing a fund intended to compensate his supporters, raising the possibility that taxpayer money could be funneled to Jan. 6 rioters. A related provision barred the I. R. S. from pursuing audits of past tax returns of Mr. Trump and his relatives.

Senator John Cornyn of Texas has voiced the loudest concerns on the committee, saying on Wednesday that he would not support the nomination of Mr. Blanche unless he provided written assurances about the end of the fund and the tax provision.

Mr. Blanche publicly defended the fund as necessary for “victims of lawfare and weaponization to be heard and seek redress.” Democrats called it a brazen slush fund meant to steer huge sums of taxpayer dollars to the president’s supporters.

Despite his public retreat, Mr. Blanche has resisted providing a written guarantee to the courts or Congress that the fund will not come back in some form.

Two weeks ago, Judge Kathleen M. Williams of Federal District Court in the Southern District of Florida, wrote that she was “extremely troubled” by Mr. Blanche’s answers to the Senate about the fund.

In testimony in May, Mr. Blanche told the senators there was “no mechanism” for a legal review of the agreement creating the fund. He argued that documents had never been submitted to a court for scrutiny because the case from which it emerged, a lawsuit Mr. Trump filed against the I. R. S. over the leak of his tax returns, had been dismissed.

“This answer is, at best, misleading and, at worst, disingenuous,” the judge wrote. “The court was available to review any pleading by any party at any time during this lawsuit.”

Another federal judge, Leonie M. Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia, has left alive a lawsuit seeking to dismantle the fund. She said the case remained open because Mr. Blanche and the Justice Department had refused to file an affidavit under penalty of perjury “that they will not take any action to create or operate” the payout fund and that it “will not proceed in any manner, under any name.”

Mr. Blanche has pushed back against such demands. Even as he promised lawmakers in June that the fund was dead, “I’m not committing to putting anything in writing.”

The reason for creating the fund, he also told lawmakers, “remain as important as they were before.”

The fight over the fund is the most consequential instance of Mr. Blanche’s singular management style since he became the No. 2 Justice Department official in March 2025. Far more than his predecessors, Mr. Blanche has publicly taken direct control over key decisions in politically fraught cases, often prompting criticism that he continues to act like Mr. Trump’s personal defense attorney, rather than a senior law enforcement official with responsibilities to taxpayers, the rule of law and the public.

Federal judges have repeatedly singled out Mr. Blanche by name, highlighting the direct role he has played in a wide array of what judges have cast as prosecutorial missteps. But Mr. Blanche has in some ways invited the censure by repeatedly taking on responsibility in high-profile cases that would typically have been left to his subordinates.

In May, for instance, a federal judge in Nashville put Mr. Blanche at the heart of his decision to dismiss a human smuggling case against the Salvadoran immigrant Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia as a vindictive “abuse of prosecuting power.” The judge, Waverly D. Crenshaw Jr., found that Mr. Blanche had led a “tainted investigation” and sought an indictment not because the facts and law demanded one, but rather to give the department “cover” for doing what it said it would never do: bring Mr. Abrego Garcia back to the United States from his wrongful deportation to El Salvador.

The next month, a federal judge in Minnesota also took aim at Mr. Blanche, saying that his aggressive statements about Gov. Tim Walz and other Democratic leaders had paved the way for the Justice Department to issue a raft of improper grand jury subpoenas during an investigation into whether elected officials in the state had interfered with the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The judge, Patrick J. Schiltz, pointed out that Mr. Blanche had accused Mr. Walz and Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, of “encouraging violence against law enforcement” and vowed that he would stop their “terrorism by whatever means necessary.”

Judge Schiltz ultimately quashed the subpoenas. He ruled that they were “part of a broader campaign to coerce” officials in Minnesota to help with Mr. Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda and came at a moment when the administration had used “criminal investigations to retaliate against and pressure the president’s political and personal adversaries.”

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

What We Really Learned From the Fauci Hearing

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Rachael Bedard

Dr. Bedard, a contributing Opinion writer, is a geriatrician and a palliative care doctor.

Senate hearings are always theatrical. Even still, Wednesday morning’s Senate committee hearing to interrogate Dr. Anthony Fauci on, among other things, the origins of Covid-19 was a shocking performance: Dr. Fauci barely spoke, while everyone else spent some three hours projecting their emotions onto him.

Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the committee chair, has cast himself as a contemporary Joe McCarthy intent on ferreting out the truth about one man’s supposed crimes against his country. The Covid lockdown “could never have been inflicted without you aiding and abetting the crime,” he said to Dr. Fauci during his opening statement. And “you have for years avoided responsibility.”

Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden took the remarkable step of providing Dr. Fauci with a blanket pardon covering all of his activities from 2014 to early 2025. This pardon would not protect against new accusations of perjury if Dr. Fauci were found to have lied during sworn testimony after Mr. Biden left office in 2025. On the advice of his lawyers, the 85-year-old Dr. Fauci made the extraordinary choice during Wednesday’s hearing to plead the Fifth Amendment. As Republican senators peppered him with often hostile questions, he repeated over and over again that he respectfully declined to answer.

By doing so, Dr. Fauci became the speechless cipher to whom committee Republicans and Democrats argued their irreconcilable stories — about the pandemic, but also more broadly about science and public health in America. The effect was a useless drama that offered zero insights to a public desperate for them.

Mr. Paul personally and directly accuses Dr. Fauci of: funding dangerous gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China, that may have resulted in a lab leak, releasing SARS-CoV-2 into the world (which Dr. Fauci denies); promoting mitigation policies that infringed on civil liberties; profiting off his pandemic-era fame; and hiding the truth about what he knew about the virus’s origins and when.

Dr. Fauci has faced congressional grilling numerous times, before both the House and the Senate. In the days before this event, Mr. Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Dr. Fauci’s diary entries. (Dr. Fauci apparently wrote them on computers associated with his government account; they were retrieved by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his staff, who provided them to Senator Paul.)

Excerpts from Dr. Fauci’s private writings, including his reflections on his conversations with celebrities and his growing award collection, seem to affirm the right’s portrayal of him as a self-regarding operator who was flattered rather than humbled by the attention he received during a national crisis.

But many of the entries being cited as evidence that Dr. Fauci lied to the public or deliberately withheld information are really reminders of how uncertain the context was for pandemic decision-making. Some of the entries, in fact, give a useful glimpse into how decisions were hashed out among experts with different perspectives and concerns, with Dr. Fauci often playing the role of convener or informal chair. On Jan. 26, 2020, he wrote that the virus may have originated in animals and jumped to humans; later, he dutifully noted conversations he was having with other scientists who were discussing alternative possibilities.

In an interview with The New York Times’s David Wallace-Wells in 2023, Mr. Wallace-Wells pushed Dr. Fauci on the lab leak hypothesis and his role in funding research in Wuhan. When Mr. Wallace-Wells suggested more thorough responses that Dr. Fauci could’ve offered when questioned on the subject, he became irritated. “David, have you ever testified before a congressional committee?” he snapped.

Dr. Fauci seems to have concluded years ago that the more he says, the more his character and actions become subject to debate. And so, on Wednesday, he took abuse — and some praise — and stayed silent. Another Republican senator, Josh Hawley of Missouri, in a particularly aggressive performance, accused him of wanting “to be the sun god of science.” Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, demanded to know, using an expletive, who Dr. Fauci thought he was for doing what he did.

Democratic senators, including Gary Peters from Michigan and Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut, commiserated with Dr. Fauci over his ordeal, and used much of their time to argue that the committee ought to be discussing all of the ways President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have ruined public health.

Only Senator Andy Kim, a Democrat from New Jersey, said anything insightful — and that was about what the hearing represented about the state of politics in America, and the implications for trust and a functioning democracy. “Right now, I feel the hyper-partisanship growing in this country in dangerous ways,” Mr. Kim said. “People calling our public servants criminals,” he lamented, is “undermining the very nature of the work of governance.”

He’s right, of course; show trials are bad for democracy and do nothing to get us closer to either truth or consensus. Hanging over every conversation about what happened during the pandemic of the recent past is anxiety about what might happen should we face a pandemic in the near future. In projecting all of a difficult era’s conflicts onto Dr. Fauci, Republicans evade the harder work of figuring out what we actually should learn from his, and our, mistakes.

Dr. Fauci is a complicated man who has been both elevated and reduced to a symbol. His legacy after a decades-long career at the intersection of science and politics is now defined by incompatible, contested accounts of his pandemic-era impact. There is little hope of resolving that contest any time soon.

Theater, at its most powerful, refracts truth through fiction so its force can be viscerally felt. This hearing was a performance that only entrenched the mistrust that increasingly defines Americans’ relationship to their institutions. Dr. Fauci, the ultimate institutionalist, has become that mistrust’s enduring target.

Rachael Bedard is a contributing Opinion writer, a geriatrician and a palliative care doctor.

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The Silicon Valley company’s costs rose more steeply than revenue growth, as it continues to invest heavily in artificial intelligence.

By Eli Tan

Reporting from San Francisco

Meta has bet big on artificial intelligence. On Wednesday, it said that bet would not let up.

The Silicon Valley company, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, increased the lower end of its capital expenditure forecast for the year to at least $130 billion, up from $125 billion that it had projected in April. Much of that investment will go to building data centers, the computing facilities that power A. I.

Meta also said that its costs and expenses rose faster than its revenue growth for the second quarter. Revenue was up 28 percent to $60.8 billion from a year earlier, while costs jumped 55 percent to $42 billion. Profit was $18.3 billion, down 14 percent from a year ago.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, focused on how A. I. was aiding his company’s businesses, including its digital advertising.

“We are now at a point where our investments in A. I. are accelerating every major part of our core business,” he said. He added that “potentially selling compute directly,” which refers to computing power, could be a new business opportunity.

But investors appeared to be spooked by Meta’s rising expenses. The company’s stock fell more than 9 percent in after-hours trading.

Meta’s continued spending follows Google’s announcement last week that it would raise its capital expenditures. Big tech companies are expected to pay $1.5 trillion on building data centers this year and next year. The enormous sums have raised questions about whether such spending is justified, with the stock market gyrating over concerns about the outlays in recent weeks.

Mr. Zuckerberg has previously said that Meta was considering selling computing power from its data centers to other companies. In June, Anthropic offered to buy computing power from Meta in a deal that could be worth up to $10 billion; the talks are ongoing.

Unlike Google, Amazon and Microsoft, which are also spending on A. I. data centers, Meta is without a business that lets companies rent computing power and A. I. tools.

People think A. I. spending “is supposed to slow down, but who’s going to be the first company to blink?” said David Wagner, the head of equity at Aptus Capital Advisors.

Meta’s shift from a social media company to an A. I. firm has not been smooth. This month, it removed a feature that let people make A. I. images of each other on Instagram just days after its release because of a backlash over privacy concerns, among other snafus.

But the company has made progress developing its own A. I. models. This month, Meta released the latest version of Muse Spark, its most advanced A. I. model developed under Alexandr Wang, the company’s chief A. I. officer. It also introduced an A. I. image generator called Muse Image and plans to release a video generator in the coming months.

Muse Spark still trails other A. I. models in benchmarks that measure coding, reasoning and writing. Meta plans to release a more powerful model, code-named Watermelon, this fall.

In recent days, Mr. Zuckerberg has also gone on the attack against companies like Anthropic and OpenAI in defense of open-source A. I. models, which are freely available for others to build upon. In an interview with The New York Times on Tuesday, he said that tightly controlling A. I. development would be “abandoning our values” and would stifle innovation.

Meta also faces ongoing litigation over claims that its social media products are addictive and said it spent $2.4 billion on legal fees in the second quarter. It lost the first of nine bellwether addiction trials in March but gained a reprieve this month after the plaintiff in one lawsuit, a 15-year-old teenager from Florida, dropped his suit.

Meta’s A. I. smart glasses continue to be a bright spot. Its Reality Labs division, which develops those glasses, generated $431 million in revenue in the quarter, up 16 percent from a year earlier. The division lost $4.6 billion, about the same as a year earlier.

Meta’s family of apps grew to 3.6 billion users, up 3 percent from a year earlier.

Eli Tan covers the technology industry for The Times from San Francisco.

The New York Times July 29, 2026

An explosion at a port on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast set fire to two ships, including a U. S. gas storage tanker, according to maritime tracking firms.

By Zane IrwinPeter EavisFarnaz Fassihi and Pranav Baskar

Two ships, one of them a U. S.-owned natural gas storage tanker, caught fire after an explosion at an Egyptian port on Wednesday, broadening the conflict in the Middle East.

Three marine tracking companies reported the incident. One of the companies said the explosion, in the Egyptian Mediterranean port of Damietta, had been caused by a drone attack, though there was no official confirmation from Egyptian authorities or the ships’ owners.

The attack isn’t likely to affect global energy markets as much as those elsewhere in the Middle East because Egypt is not a big exporter of natural gas.

Kpler, a maritime tracking firm, said both vessels had been moved away from the Damietta Port, which is near the Suez Canal on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. There were no confirmed injuries or deaths, Egypt’s ministry of petroleum said on social media.

Joshua Hutchinson, the chief commercial officer of Ambrey, another maritime tracking firm, said in an interview that the explosion was believed to be caused by a drone attack, which hit at least one of the ships. Ambrey has not identified the source of the attack.

Two Iranians, who asked not to be named to discuss security matters, said the explosion was a drone attack designed to show that global shipping and energy supplies could be more deeply disrupted if Iran chose to escalate. The individuals did not say whether Iran or an Iran-allied militia in the region had launched the attack, or from where.

President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that he had been briefed on the explosion and implied that Iran was responsible, without offering details. He said the incident was “more of the same” and that the United States was “going to be hitting them very hard, because it’s our turn to hit them.”

By attacking ships in the Mediterranean, Iran could further disrupt trade. Shipping companies would have to assess the risks of using Egyptian ports. Since the Iran war began at the end of February, many ship operators have avoided the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The Energos Winter, the U. S. storage tanker that caught fire, belongs to Energos Infrastructure, a U. S. company based in Stamford, Conn. Jonathan Chia, a representative for Energos Infrastructure, said the company had not been able to determine whether Energos Winter had been hit by a drone. Mr. Chia said that all the crew members had been accounted for, and that none of them had been injured.

Footage circulating on social media and verified by The New York Times showed tugboats hosing down the Energos Winter with water at the Damietta Port.

Energos Infrastructure’s website says the company is owned by investment funds managed by Apollo Global Management, a large Wall Street firm. Apollo declined to comment. The Energos Winter is being leased by Egyptian Natural Gas Holding Company, Egypt’s government-owned gas company.

The other ship, a liquefied natural gas carrier operated by a Greek shipping company, was struck by at least one drone, according to Ambrey.

The vessel, the GasLog Salem, caught fire after an explosion, said Marina Leonidhopoulos, a spokeswoman for GasLog, the operator of the vessel. Ms. Leonidhopoulos said the cause of the explosion was being investigated.

Attacks on ships in two crucial Middle Eastern shipping routes — the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea — have disrupted the passage of oil tankers, jolting global energy markets.

Since March, the war has made it much more dangerous to travel through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow portal to the Persian Gulf. That has forced Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, to rely more heavily on exporting oil through the Red Sea, which was also recently threatened with a blockade by the Iranian-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen.

Those attacks and threats have deterred shipping companies from sending vessels through the region’s waters. The number of vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab in the Red Sea has decreased by one-fifth since July 20, according to Windward, a maritime data agency. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains at less than one-tenth of prewar levels.

Rebecca F. Elliott and Erica L. Green contributed reporting.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Peter Eavis reports on the business of moving stuff around the world.

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The project would make the airport easier to navigate and include a new United lounge, officials said. It’s part of the president’s plans to remake the Washington area.

By Karoun Demirjian

Reporting from Washington

President Trump unveiled plans for a $22.5 billion redesign of Dulles International Airport at the White House on Wednesday, characterizing the reconstruction as part of his broader efforts to remake the Washington region.

“This transformation is another step in our ongoing efforts to make Washington, D. C., safe and beautiful again,” Mr. Trump said, adding that the project would have bipartisan appeal, because “whether you’re Republican or Democrat, you don’t want to go and be subjected to this airport.”

Dulles Airport, which opened in the Virginia exurbs of Washington in 1962, has long been celebrated as an architectural landmark, thanks to the sweeping glass features of the main terminal, designed by the Finnish American architect Eero Saarinen. Mr. Trump called that terminal “iconic,” and he said that it would be spruced up but preserved as part of the redesign.

But the expansion of the airport in the years since it opened made navigating it an awkward experience for many, due in large part to the separation of the various concourses and the airport’s reliance on a fleet of buses, known as people movers, to ferry passengers between the concourses and the main terminal.

“It’s an impossible airport: You go off a bus, you get into a train; you get off of a train, you get into another bus,” Mr. Trump said to reporters, expressing a frustration common to many travelers through Dulles.

In the redesign, which officials said would not require federal spending, the concourses would be connected by a central walking tunnel and a new air train, Mr. Trump and his transportation secretary, Sean P. Duffy, explained. A new hotel would be built on the airport campus, the C and D terminals would be replaced, and the airport would be outfitted with new restaurants and shops, as well as a large United Airlines lounge.

United Airlines and the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority submitted the design that Mr. Trump ultimately settled on after reviewing more than 30 proposals, according to a Transportation Department spokesman. Dulles Airport is one of United Airlines’ main hubs.

The airport redesign also includes plans for a 32,000-space parking garage, which Mr. Trump repeatedly bragged would make it the largest in the world. The added capacity would come as the airport had sought to ease vehicle congestion, having recently connected to the metro transit system that serves the nation’s capital.

In all, the project would encompass more than five million square feet of new and renovated space, Mr. Trump said, and take about two years to complete. Mr. Duffy said that administration officials “think we can start construction in the spring of next year."

But there are financial and regulatory hurdles left to clear, even as officials said the project would not need federal spending.

Mr. Trump told reporters that “cost was no object” in finalizing the design, and Jack Potter, the president and chief executive of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, said that it could be completed “not requiring federal dollars.”

“This is going to be airport-generated dollars, airline contributions,” Mr. Potter said.

While the project is bonded at $22.5 billion, there are still certain permissions that the administration must secure from Congress before forging ahead, Mr. Duffy noted. The Airports Authority operates Dulles under a lease from Congress, which, according to the authority, is not set to expire until 2100.

It is also not clear whether Mr. Trump would try any further personal intervention in the project as it proceeds.

Earlier this year, White House officials tried to pressure Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, into helping Mr. Trump rename Dulles Airport after himself, dangling billions in frozen funds for a rail tunnel under the Hudson River as leverage.

As Mr. Trump showed off an architectural model of the envisioned changes on Wednesday and boasted about the details of “a modernization of Dulles that’s sorely needed,” he made no mention of potentially changing the name.

There is at least one Republican-sponsored bill pending before the House to affix Mr. Trump’s name to the airport.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

Families Face Anxiety, Angst as Loved Ones Are Deployed to Fight Iran

The New York Times July 29, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

As the war with Iran has continued, some are finding that the stress is bringing back old anxieties.

By Bernard Mokam and Georgia Gee

Bernard Mokam reported from Florida and New York. Georgia Gee reported from New York.

A 4-year-old child began having behavioral problems when his father left for war.

A wife whose husband works in Army intelligence is already dealing with heightened anxiety, even though he hasn’t been deployed yet.

A woman found this year that she is struggling to cope with the news of conflicts at home and abroad, nearly 20 years after she lost her fiancé in combat.

More than 80 percent of military families have reported elevated stress from the war with Iran, driven by safety concerns, deployment changes, and the fear of escalation, according to a March poll of an estimated 200 families by Blue Star Families, one of the largest nonprofits supporting active military and veterans.

As the war with Iran persists, mental health counselors say they are attending to more military families who are reporting stress and anxiety about a conflict that has taken the lives of at least 18 service members and wounded more than 400.

“We have tripled our caseload,” said Hannah Simms, the founder of Rise Alone Therapy, a tele-therapy provider that caters to the military and their families. “Everybody is kind of on edge.”

“There was this understanding that this was going to be a short-term deal,” Ms. Simms added, noting President Trump’s declarations at the beginning of March that the war could last four to five weeks.

Five months later, the war has flared again, following the end of a cease-fire agreement and then two weeks of bombing. The Strait of Hormuz has again been closed, sending gasoline prices over $4 a gallon, diplomatic efforts are at a standstill and the latest round of U. S. attacks do not seem to have deterred Iran.

A Pentagon spokesman declined a request seeking details about how the military helps the families of service members cope with the stresses of war. But military officials have said that there are a variety of counseling and support services available, including a 24/7 service called Military OneSource that provides free and confidential support.

In interviews, military families said the war has triggered grief once thought to be healed. Some cope with feelings of guilt brought on by the conflict, a common emotion among military families, counselors said. Others lamented the lack of transparency and communication that has left them not knowing when their spouse, child, brother or sister will come home.

“I don’t know where he is,” said Elisha Puente, a mother of four, whose husband deployed in February as part of Operation Epic Fury.

Ms. Puente’s husband, who is in an artillery unit in the Marine Corps, calls home about every three weeks, she said. He does not have access to his personal device and must use a satellite phone on base to make the call, often waiting in a line of Marines doing the same.

The communication lapses have roiled her children, who range in age from 11 months to 12 years old.

But Ms. Puente, 34, has developed strategies for her children to manage the absence. She keeps dolls and stickers of her husband at home. Her children love watching videos of their father, particularly those of him swimming with turtles.

Still, Ms. Puente, who has been in therapy to help with her husband’s deployments, said she has sought counseling for her four-year-old, who is currently on a wait list.

“I just knew that it was time to maybe ask for some more help for him,” she said.

Last month, Kelsey Smith, 35, started counseling to help cope with the stress caused by the war, even though her husband is stateside. She had struggled to control her emotions recently — blowing up over small things, she said.

“It’s better,” she said, adding that the therapy has helped. But overall, she said, “I’m not better.”

Her husband is an intelligence officer for the Army and supports the Middle East campaign from a base in the Northeast. Since he started working around the clock, Ms. Smith began completing a tuxedo cat Lego set, about 1,700 pieces, to calm her nerves, she said.

“I know how hard my husband’s working and the amount of stress he’s under,” said Ms. Smith, who used her maiden name because of her husband’s work in intelligence. “So there’s a level of guilt of just feeling like I’m not doing enough or not working as hard as he is.”

For veterans whose children are now in the military, a deployment can trigger anxiety as they recall their own deployments.

Eric Dorner, who lives in Mountain, Wis., is a veteran whose 27-year-old son Brenden just returned home after an extended deployment, serving 13 months as a sergeant in the Middle East. His contract officially ends at the start of August, but he could be deployed again anytime in the next three years.

“It is difficult because I knew he had already seen and been through traumatic things,” said Mr. Dorner. “I did struggle myself as a veteran, even though he went through way more than me.”

Kyle Harper, who is a communications adviser for Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors, a service that connects people who have lost loved ones in the military, restarted trauma therapy three months ago to help process her own grief.

In 2007, her fiancé, Army Staff Sergeant Michael Hullender, responded to a vehicle that had been struck by a roadside bomb in Iraq. As a medic, Staff Sergeant Hullender approached to offer aide. Leaving his vehicle, he stepped on an I. E. D. and died as a helicopter rushed him to the nearest military hospital.

For almost two decades, Ms. Harper said she has been healing from the loss that has partly defined her adult life. She wears the engagement ring Staff Sergeant Hullender gave her on her right hand. She has completed two full Ironmans in his honor.

When she learns of military casualties, in combat or in training, Ms. Harper always feels a pang of grief — knowing how difficult it may be for those families.

“I look at the faces and read the names of people who served and died because I wanted someone to do that for Mike,” she said.

Ms. Harper said she returned to therapy to work with someone who understands “the layers of loss.”

“It felt strange to go back and talk about some of this stuff,” she said, adding, but “the world seemed really overwhelming again.”

Bernard Mokam covers breaking news.

A man who stabbed the author Salman Rushdie more than a dozen times was found guilty on Wednesday of aiding a foreign terrorist group and carrying out the orders of the Iranian government, which had called for the luminary’s death more than three decades ago.

Hadi Matar, a young man who had been enraged by Mr. Rushdie’s work, rushed onstage at a retreat in western New York in August 2022 and stabbed him repeatedly. Mr. Rushdie survived the attack, but was left with severe nerve damage and blind in his right eye.

The judgment, which was reached by a federal jury in Buffalo after just two hours of deliberation, means he could spend the rest of his life in prison.

Canada’s Answer to Trump’s Tariffs: More Energy Deals With Europe

The New York Times July 29, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The Carney government’s agreement with a German natural gas company will also reduce Europe’s dependence on a Qatari supply made more uncertain by war.

By Ian Austen

Reporting from Ottawa

Canada announced a second major deal on Wednesday to export liquefied natural gas to Europe, part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s effort to reduce the country’s economic dependence on the United States.

The announcement came a week after President Trump signed an order imposing 50 percent tariffs on a range of Canadian exports, excluding energy, and amid global energy upheaval caused by the American and Israeli war against Iran.

Canadian natural gas and oil exports have historically gone almost entirely to American customers. In a briefing note on Wednesday, Canada said it now aims to sell 55 percent of its natural gas exports to customers other than the United States by the middle of the next decade. In 2024, the year before the opening of Canada’s first L. N. G. terminal, other countries accounted for just 0.01 percent of Canada’s natural gas exports.

The deal comes as some politicians, including the leader of Canada’s most populous province, have called on Mr. Carney to use energy and mineral exports to the United States as leverage against Mr. Trump’s trade measures, which include tariffs of up to 50 percent on cars, steel and aluminum introduced last year.

The Trump administration also recently refused to renew the free trade agreement between Canada, the United States and Mexico for another 16 years, leaving it to be reviewed annually instead. Mr. Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st U. S. state, and said last week, “without us, there’s no way they can survive.”

Tensions peaked last week when Canada canceled a joint ceremonial opening with the United States of the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, whose cost of 6.4 billion Canadian dollars, about $4.5 billion, Canada funded entirely.

American guests were uninvited and the event moved to the Canadian end of the bridge after Mr. Trump imposed his latest tariffs and delayed the bridge’s opening. The president relented only after the United States, which played no role in building the bridge, was granted a share of its tolls for the first 15 years.

In the new energy deal announced on Wednesday, Uniper, a German gas distributor and electric power company, will buy up to 2 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas a year starting in 2032 from a proposed project in British Columbia led by the Nisga’a Nation. Uniper supplies gas to customers in Germany, Britain, Sweden and the Netherlands.

The contract is twice the size of one announced in May, between the Nisga’a Nation’s Ksi Lisims L. N. G. project in northern British Columbia and Securing Energy for Europe, or SEFE, which is owned by the German government.

Tim Hodgson, the natural resources minister, said in a statement that the deal shows “that by working with allies like Germany, Canada can strengthen its economy and sovereignty and support global energy security.”

While Canada’s manufacturing sector has been battered by Mr. Trump’s tariffs, those losses have been more than offset by gains in oil and gas, mineral and agricultural exports.

Europe has grappled with natural gas supply issues since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, a problem compounded by the closing of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran. As tankers have been blocked in the strait, a growing number of countries are now looking for alternatives to liquid natural gas from Qatar, which with the United States is one of the dominant suppliers of L. N. G. globally.

“This agreement is about far more than L. N. G.,” Michael Lewis, Uniper’s chief executive, said in a statement. “As a trusted partner, Canada helps diversify Europe’s energy supply and strengthens resilience against future disruptions.”

Dominic LeBlanc, the Canadian minister responsible for trade with the United States, said in a statement that the contract would “reinforce Canada’s position as a global energy superpower.”

Mr. LeBlanc was in Washington on Wednesday. In a social media post he said that he and Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator with the United States, met with Jamieson Greer, the United States Trade Representative, but offered no further details.

A poll today suggests that some Canadians have become uneasy with Mr. Carney's emphasis on expanding fossil fuel exports, a contrast to Justin Trudeau's focus on mitigating climate change. I'm interested hearing how Canadians feel about the current balance between economic measures and the environment.

Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes. com.
