The New York Times July 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A lifeguard with a relentless grip on a young boy brought him to safety amid enormous waves that ripped across a Santa Cruz beach over the weekend.

By Sejal Govindarao and Pooja Salhotra

As relentless, crashing waves pummeled the shores of Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz, Calif., over the weekend, churning up sand and turning the surf into a salty foam, a teenage lifeguard with an unrelenting grip pulled, dragged and lifted a young boy from the water to bring him to safety.

A video captured the save and showed bystanders rushing into the surf in an attempt to help as violent waves sent the lifeguard and the boy under the water multiple times. Claps broke out as the lifeguard, with the help of another person, pulled the boy to the shore.

“You never see panic,” said Tom Gill, president of the United States Lifesaving Association, after watching the video. “He does such a good job maintaining contact with the victim and understanding the situation and what he has to do to maintain safety.”

Mr. Gill, who has been a lifeguard at Virginia Beach for more than three decades, also noted that the rescue involved little to no equipment. Although the lifeguard appeared to have a buoy with him, he does not manage to get the flotation device around the victim.

“This was really simply a human helping a human,” Mr. Gill said. The National Weather Service said storms across the Pacific this summer have resulted in a very active southerly swell season along the California coastline, which can contribute to record high tides.

“The ocean may appear that it’s seemingly tranquil, but know that there’s a lot of energy still moving in the water,” said meteorologist Cynthia Palmer.

In June, two Bay Area college students died after they were swept from a beach near Santa Cruz. A few days earlier, a five-year-old girl died after she was swept into the sea at Laguna Beach.

The video of the rescue quickly spread through social media, drawing the attention of President Trump, who said he wanted to honor the lifeguard at the White House.

“Very brave, he deserves it!” wrote Mr. Trump in a post on X.

Wyatt Werneth, a spokesman for the American Lifeguard Association, said he hoped the recognition would help elevate lifeguards to the status of first responders.

“We sometimes get overlooked,” Mr. Werneth said. “What this young man exhibited is the true ethos of lifeguards.”

A California State Parks spokeswoman said the child who was rescued was knocked down by a wave and swept into the ocean about 15 yards offshore at about 3:30 p. m. on Saturday. The child was pulled from the ocean without serious injuries and released to his parents, the spokeswoman said.

Scott Vander Dussen, who captured the video, said in an interview that it was the thunderous booms of the waves that prompted him to look out at the water and notice the boy drifting. Onlookers were pointing at the boy and screaming. Mr. Vander Dussen said he alerted a lifeguard, who told him someone was already on the rescue.

That day, the National Weather Service warned of elevated surf and hazardous conditions along the Pacific Coast. The agency said beaches across the San Francisco Bay Area faced an increased risk of rip currents and sneaker waves — fast-moving walls of water that can arrive without warning and surge farther up the beach than other waves in a set. Breaking waves could reach up to 10 feet, the service warned.

Lifeguards with the California State Parks’ Santa Cruz District performed 34 rescues over the weekend, officials said.

Sumit Rai, the father of the boy who was rescued, said “it’s a miracle” his 10-year-old son was alive. Mr. Rai, who is separated from his wife and lives in Texas, said his son and 8-year-old daughter were vacationing with their mother in California. Mr. Rai said he learned about what happened in a phone call that night from his children, who he described as “extremely” close.

“To watch her brother go through a near-death experience is not a small thing,” Mr. Rai said.

Mr. Rai said he didn’t sleep for several nights after the phone call and described himself as the “biggest fan” of the lifeguard who saved his son.

Amy Graff contributed reporting.

The kingdom’s defense ministry said airstrikes in Iraq targeting Iran-backed militias were in retaliation for attacks on Saudi oil facilities this week.

By Vivian Nereim and Ismaeel Naar

Saudi Arabia entered the U. S.-Iran war on Wednesday with airstrikes in Iraq. Its delayed entry, six months into the war, illustrated the bind the kingdom faces as it tries to deter attacks without getting sucked into the broader conflict, analysts say.

The kingdom’s defense ministry announced the airstrikes, accusing Iran-backed militias in Iraq of attacking Saudi oil facilities this week. No Iraqi militias have claimed responsibility for those attacks.

Iraq’s National Security Council said in a statement that the strikes had caused the deaths and injuries of “a number of innocent people,” and Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi of Iraq called the strikes “an unacceptable aggression.” The Saudi government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

However, Saudi government statements appeared keen to portray the strikes as a limited reaction to specific attacks, rather than an entry into the wider U. S. and Israeli war with Iran.

“The kingdom confirms that it is not seeking escalation but that it will respond to any aggression,” said a Saudi defense ministry spokesman, Maj. General Turki al-Malki.

His statement invoked the right to self-defense and quoted a line from the Quran calling for believers to attack those who attack them in a similar manner.

His language underscored the dilemma that Saudi Arabia has faced since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, setting off a military conflagration across the region and threatening the kingdom’s security and economic ambitions. While Saudi Arabia has long had antagonistic relations with Iran, Saudi officials had been pursuing warmer ties for several years — viewing them as the most pragmatic way to manage the threat posed by Iran.

The war dashed those efforts at diplomacy. In retaliation against U. S. attacks, Iran launched thousands of missiles and drones at Persian Gulf states that host U. S. military installations, including Saudi Arabia.

This month, the kingdom also entered into a renewed confrontation with the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, which has claimed responsibility for several attacks on Saudi soil and declared a blockade against Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.

Analysts say that while Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman probably saw benefits to the potential weakening of Iran, the war has, in reality, posed major risks for his plans to turn Saudi Arabia into a business and tourism hub.

It has also imposed an economic cost on Saudi Arabia by restricting routes for the export of oil, which provide the lifeblood of the Saudi government budget. As fighting has dragged on, it has strained the kingdom’s relations with the Trump administration, with American and Saudi officials increasingly at odds over how to approach security in the region.

The joint Saudi-American strikes marked the first time the kingdom acknowledged direct involvement in the U. S. war effort, although Saudi Arabia had carried out secret strikes against Iran earlier in the war.

Abdulaziz Alghashian, a senior nonresident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, a Washington-based research organization, said the Saudi leadership likely decided to take overt action this week because it was aware that its reluctance to enter the war “has been misunderstood as acceptance” of attacks against it.

The kingdom is now trying to deliver a message, to its enemies on all sides, that “there are costs to attacking Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Faisal Al-Hamad, a retired Saudi Air Force brigadier general and defense analyst, called it an attempt to “draw clear red lines” to deter further attacks.

This is the first time that Saudi Arabia has acknowledged any attacks against armed groups in Iraq, noted Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The strikes could also be read as a warning to Iran that escalating further could push Saudi leadership to align even more closely with the United States, he said.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Microsoft Increases Spending on A. I. as Profit Jumps 31.6%

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Like other big technology companies, Microsoft is hoping its aggressive spending on artificial intelligence is starting to translate into revenue.

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Microsoft’s spending on artificial intelligence is still going up, even as questions swirl about whether returns justify the cost.

On Wednesday, the company said it spent $41 billion on capital expenditures, including data centers, in the three months that ended in June, up 69.4 percent from a year earlier. Microsoft also said its spending hit $145.3 billion in its 2026 fiscal year, which ended in June.

Microsoft’s profit for the quarter was $35.8 billion, up 31.6 percent. Revenue was $90 billion, up 17.8 percent.

Revenue at Azure, the company’s cloud computing service, which lets companies rent computer power, storage and A. I. tools, drove much of the growth, surging 43 percent. Analysts had expected growth of about 40 percent — a figure investors watch closely as the clearest sign of whether Microsoft’s A. I. spending is translating into revenue.

The results exceeded Wall Street’s projections of $87.6 billion in revenue and $31.5 billion in profit, sending Microsoft’s shares up more than 1 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

The company has said demand for its cloud computing services outpaces its available data centers, requiring more spending to expand.

Microsoft’s shares have fallen since January, as investors have grown anxious about whether the hundreds of billions of dollars that it and its peers are pouring into A. I. development will convert into profit.

That anxiety was on display just last week. Alphabet, Google’s parent, reported that it had quadrupled its quarterly profit to $112 billion, strengthened largely by major investments in other A. I. companies, and raised its expected 2026 spending to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion. Its stock fell roughly 7 percent the day after the earnings call.

Much of the demand filling those data centers traces back to OpenAI. Microsoft’s relationship with the San Francisco company behind ChatGPT was overhauled late last year, when the start-up converted into a for-profit entity and Microsoft took a stake valued at roughly $135 billion. Under the revised agreement, Microsoft retained access to OpenAI’s technology through 2032.

Sales rose 14 percent to $37.8 billion for commercial subscriptions to Microsoft’s productivity tools for businesses, which include Excel, Teams and Word, as well as its A. I. assistant, Copilot. Microsoft’s personal computing business had $12.9 billion in sales, a 4 percent decline.

“This year, Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, reflecting the confidence customers are placing in us to power their A. I. transformation,” Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, said in a statement.

Microsoft has been trimming its other businesses to help pay for its A. I. push. In July, the company eliminated 20 percent of its Xbox work force as part of roughly 4,800 job cuts, and dropped several game studios.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The companies have denied the claims.)

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

Vote on Blanche in Doubt After Senators Express Skepticism Over I. R. S. Provision

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis accused the attorney general nominee of refusing to put on paper his promise to kill aspects of the deal he cut to settle President Trump’s suit against the agency.

By Glenn Thrush and Michael Gold

Reporting from Capitol Hill

Two Republican senators on the Judiciary Committee, who lost their seats after defying President Trump, threatened on Wednesday to block Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general over a deal he cut to settle Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I. R. S.

The senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, accused Mr. Blanche of refusing to put on paper his promise to kill aspects of the deal. In June, Mr. Blanche said he would drop a proposed $1.8 billion fund to compensate purported victims of Biden-era actions by the Justice Department but said a related provision shielding Mr. Trump and his family from tax investigations would remain in place.

Mr. Cornyn scrapped a scheduled meeting with Mr. Blanche on Wednesday morning and told reporters staking out his Capitol Hill office that he was unsure whether a committee vote scheduled for Thursday would take place.

He said he was not “prepared to vote yes” and gave the department until 4 p. m. to produce clear written guarantees on the fund and tax deal. It is possible the vote could be postponed, Mr. Cornyn added.

He reiterated the demand after the Senate Republican lunch. “Why don’t you call over the Department of Justice and tell them they have one hour and 50 minutes to get me what I asked for?” he said. “We actually sent them a red-line strikeout of what we need, and they just need to make a decision.”

Mr. Blanche, who can continue as acting attorney general indefinitely, cannot afford to lose a single Republican vote. He appears, for the moment, to be two short.

Mr. Tillis expressed solidarity with Mr. Cornyn but appeared to be considerably more sanguine that the two sides would reach an agreement that would clear a path for a floor vote on confirmation.

“We’re trying to work just to get the language,” Mr. Tillis told reporters. “I really do believe it’s just a drafting exercise. I don’t believe that we’re apart in terms of the objective.”

He added that he believed the central issue was “the remaining language on the audit” deal with the I. R. S. and suggested that Mr. Cornyn was already comfortable with “language related to rendering the 1776 fund inoperative.”

Justice Department officials have been in communication with Mr. Cornyn’s staff over the past week. An administration official with knowledge of those exchanges was under the impression that Mr. Blanche had addressed many of Mr. Cornyn’s concerns about the exemption, which could result in a $100 million windfall for Mr. Trump and his family.

But Mr. Cornyn, a former state judge who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, Ken Paxton, said he had received no written assurances from Mr. Blanche that the audit shield would not apply to future tax liabilities or be extended to a wide circle of people.

He said he was mystified why Mr. Blanche had not sent him a clearly drafted commitment to “revising” the tax deal.

Mr. Cornyn said he did not know what the holdup was, but he did not rule out that Mr. Trump was intent on keeping a tax-immunity deal in place.

“I can see why he wants it, because it provides immunity from audits no other taxpayer would get,” Mr. Cornyn added.

During Mr. Blanche’s confirmation hearing this month, Mr. Cornyn joined Democrats in questioning Mr. Blanche’s independence from White House control and ultimately refused to commit to supporting his nomination.

While politely praising Mr. Blanche’s public service, he said it was a very difficult position “to be the president’s personal lawyer, and then to end up being a member of the cabinet.”

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Trump Administration Is Repurposing Federal Land for A. I. Data Centers

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

In the latest example, the Energy Department will convert a shuttered Cold War-era uranium enrichment facility into a data center campus and gas plants.

By Brad Plumer

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration is repurposing large chunks of federal land to host enormous data centers and the power plants needed to run them as officials seek to accelerate the development of artificial intelligence and overcome growing local opposition to the facilities.

The Energy Department announced on Wednesday that it would redevelop parts of a retired Cold War-era uranium enrichment facility in Paducah, Ky., to host a large new A. I. data center campus. The site is owned by the federal government and has been undergoing environmental cleanup for years.

The $100 billion project would include construction of 2 gigawatts of natural gas power connected to the local grid and 2.6 gigawatts of battery storage capacity. The Energy Department said the project would be privately funded through a partnership with NextEra Energy, one of the nation’s largest power companies; the investment firm Brookfield; and several local utilities. (One gigawatt of gas can power roughly 750,000 million homes.)

“The U. S. government is leveraging its assets — like our federal lands — to add power generation, create jobs, and ensure the United States wins the A. I. race,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement.

It’s the third time that the Trump administration has detailed plans to redevelop Cold War-era facilities into data centers. In March, the Energy Department announced that it would repurpose parts of a former nuclear enrichment facility in Piketon, Ohio, to host an enormous 10-gigawatt data center, mostly powered by natural gas and financed partly by Japan.

And this month, the Energy Department’s National Nuclear Security Administration said it would work with the engineering firm Amentum to explore a 1-gigawatt data center, potentially powered by gas and nuclear power, in Savannah River, S. C., at a federal complex once devoted to making plutonium for nuclear weapons.

President Trump has been a major supporter of artificial intelligence, which he has called essential to winning the technology race against China. In recent months, he has also tried to confront growing opposition in many communities to the proliferation of giant, energy-hungry data centers, which are driving up electricity demand.

A recent Gallup poll found that nearly half of Americans would “strongly oppose” a new data center in their neighborhood, with many citing concerns about noise, pollution and energy and water usage. In the first quarter of this year, at least 75 data center projects worth $130 billion were delayed or stopped by local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a project by the A. I. research firm 10a Labs.

At a White House event last week, Mr. Trump aimed to address some of those concerns by announcing that nearly 200 companies — including tech giants, utilities and data center developers — had signed a voluntary pledge to prevent A. I. data centers from increasing electricity costs for Americans. Experts said that pledge could be hard to honor in practice, since power prices are often determined by local regulators.

Mr. Trump highlighted examples where new data center projects had helped reduce local property taxes or electricity rates. And he railed against data center opponents, calling them “radical left communists” who “would not lower your electricity bills.”

His administration has moved to encourage data center development on lands owned by the Energy Department, which could offer a smoother path for approval. The Environmental Protection Agency has also taken several steps to make data centers easier to build, such as loosening limits on smog-causing pollution from the gas turbines that often power the facilities.

Separately, the Interior Department recently approved plans for the first-ever data center on federal land near Boulder City, Nev., on a site where a large utility-scale solar array had previously been permitted. The agency said it did not to conduct a new, time-consuming environmental review for the project because the data center would have impacts similar to the original solar facility. The approval was originally reported by Heatmap, a climate news site.

Two environmental groups filed a legal challenge against that decision this week.

“By cutting the public out of the process, they’re trying to hand over Nevada’s desert to billion-dollar tech companies without anyone getting a say,” said Olivia Tanager, executive director of the Sierra Club’s chapter in the Toiyabe area of Nevada.

In Kentucky, the new data center will sit on portions of a 3,556-acre Energy Department site that produced low-enriched uranium for both military reactors and nuclear weapons since the 1950s. The enrichment facility, which used a now-obsolete gaseous diffusion method, closed in 2013.

The Energy Department said the project’s new gas-fired power plants would produce more electricity than the data center needed and could provide the surplus to local communities. The project is expected to be completed in 2031.

The Trump administration has sought to use more natural gas to power the A. I. data center boom while cracking down on wind and solar energy. Natural gas has become the largest source of America’s greenhouse gas emissions that are heating the planet. A report issued on Wednesday by the Rhodium Group, a research firm, found that U. S. emissions declines could potentially slow in the coming years because of faster data center growth and rising gas demand.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

Sanctions Bill Would Give Trump Sweeping New Tariff Powers

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Lindsey Graham (1955-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

A bipartisan bill in the Senate would allow President Trump to impose tariffs on the biggest importers of Russian energy.

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

The sanctions legislation that moved forward in the Senate this week goes beyond enacting new financial restrictions on Russia and Iran. It also gives President Trump broad new powers to impose tariffs on imports from some of the world’s largest economies.

The bipartisan bill, which was designed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican, was intended to demonstrate that Congress is unified in its desire to punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine and to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But tucked inside the legislation are tools that would give the Trump administration sweeping discretion to impose steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy products. The measure would restore some of the trade authorities that the Supreme Court stripped away when it ruled against Mr. Trump’s use of tariffs on national security grounds earlier this year.

It if becomes law, the bill would allow Mr. Trump to impose 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports, which include mostly fertilizers, and tariffs as high as 100 percent on the largest importers of Russian oil and gas. Countries that help Russia evade sanctions could also face tariffs as high as 100 percent.

The policy could lead to additional levies on billions of dollars’ worth of products imported from China, India and European Union countries.

The bill represents the latest move by Congress to cede more of its authority over trade policy to Mr. Trump. It also comes amid bipartisan anger over the president’s provocative use of tariffs, which has led to retaliation from other countries and uncertainty for businesses.

Scott Lincicome, a trade expert at the free-markets-oriented Cato Institute, said that some of the key language in the legislation is murky and that Mr. Trump has shown he will push the limits of his tariff powers.

“The president has demonstrated repeatedly that he is willing to exploit any ambiguity in a tariff statute that lets him impose additional import taxes,” Mr. Lincicome said. “When you’re dealing with Trump, you should be extremely reluctant to give him new tariff powers.”

Despite last-minute changes to reduce the potential impact of the tariffs on American companies, the bill leaves room for the White House to interpret who are the biggest buyers of Russian energy products, which could open the door to a more expansive use of tariffs.

The legislation also gives Mr. Trump, who has at times been reluctant to punish Russia with sanctions, the leeway not to impose them by issuing a waiver and providing Congress with an explanation of why he believes an exemption is in the national interest. The president has argued that he needs flexibility when it comes to tariffs and sanctions when negotiating with other countries.

In a social media post, the Russian Embassy in the United States assailed the sanctions legislation and said it was doing America a disservice.

“Given growing instability in the Persian Gulf and war with Iran, with a looming energy crisis and prices going up at gas stations right on the eve of midterm elections, sanctioning Russia and its trade partners in order to block Moscow’s natural resources exports would be highly counterproductive for the U. S. itself,” the embassy said.

The potential for Mr. Trump to gain more power to unilaterally impose tariffs has rattled industries that were already struggling to cope with the gyrations of his trade agenda. Over the last year, Mr. Trump has continuously added, adjusted and removed tariffs as he sought to gain negotiating leverage with American trading partners. That has left companies struggling to plan how to source the products they buy and how to set their prices.

As they rushed to finalize the bill ahead of Mr. Graham’s funeral on Tuesday, lawmakers met resistance from lobbyists who are anxious about giving Mr. Trump more tariff authority.

“The potential of new, broad, 100 percent tariffs on imports from secondary countries risks raising costs for American businesses, workers and consumers,” a group of nearly two dozen trade associations wrote in a letter to Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the Republican majority leader, and Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader.

“Tariffs of this scale would increase costs for everyday consumer goods, manufacturing inputs and other products while creating significant uncertainty for companies making sourcing, pricing and inventory decisions months in advance.”

The lobbying groups include the U. S. Chamber of Commerce, the Retail Industry Leaders Association and the National Foreign Trade Council. They asked lawmakers to remove the tariff authority in the bill and warned that tariffs were “a blunt tool that can penalize law-abiding U. S. companies.”

The fate of the bill in the House is unclear, as some top Democrats have already expressed opposition to giving Mr. Trump more tariff authority. However, the bipartisan support in the Senate suggests that it could pass. Still, some Senate Democrats have also expressed reservations.

“I do not think tariffs, which are paid for by American businesses and consumers, will help Ukraine win this war,” Senator Maggie Hassan, a Democrat from New Hampshire, wrote on social media following the vote. “ And over the last year, it’s become more clear that President Trump will use any legal — or illegal — mechanism to make families pay his reckless tariffs.”

A White House official said that the bill was the result of months of negotiations between federal agencies, the White House and lawmakers and that it reflected bipartisan national security and foreign policy objectives.

Late changes to the Senate version of the bill were intended to restrict some of the potential impact on America’s trading partners. Only the top five importers of Russian oil or gas are eligible to be hit with U. S. tariffs. Countries that take significant steps to reduce their purchases of Russian oil and gas could have their tariff rates reduced or eliminated.

The Supreme Court invalidated Mr. Trump’s preferred legal tool in February, when it said his use of an international emergency law to impose tariffs was unlawful and ordered roughly $160 billion in tariff revenue to be refunded.

Earlier this month, the president moved to revive his protectionist agenda, imposing tariffs of around 10 percent on goods from more than 80 countries.

Those duties were issued under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to impose tariffs on foreign countries that engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. The administration has cited the failure of foreign countries to pass or enforce laws banning the importation of goods made by forced labor into their own countries, saying that disadvantages U. S. businesses that do follow such laws.

Mr. Trump also said this month that he planned to impose 100 percent tariffs on imported generic drugs starting in 2028.

The president has expressed a preference for using tariffs over sanctions as an economic weapon. Last year, Mr. Trump imposed tariffs on India as punishment for its purchases of Russian oil. However, the tariffs proved to be ineffective at curtailing India’s oil purchases and the Trump administration later rescinded them.

Ben Harris, a former Treasury Department official in the Biden administration who helped design its policy to cap the price of Russian oil, said that he was encouraged to see bipartisan legislation that could compel the Trump administration to punish more Russian shadow fleet tankers and tighten enforcement of existing sanctions.

But with energy prices remaining volatile because of the conflict in Iran and Mr. Trump continuing to express mixed messages about Russia, it is not clear how the president would wield new sanctions and tariff powers if he gets them.

“The Trump administration has a terrible record with respect to sanctioning Russia’s oil industry to date,” Mr. Harris said. “It’s been unclear what their objective has been from the get-go.”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

Connections Coach

The peculiar dynamic is playing out in Texas, where the fate of the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, will help decide which party controls the U. S. Senate.

Ken Paxton, attorney general of Texas, is the Republican nominee for Senate there but has struggled to raise money. Credit... Antranik Tavitian for The New York Times

Supported by

By Theodore Schleifer

In one of this year’s most competitive Senate races, Republicans are refusing to spend money — so far.

That peculiar dynamic is playing out in Texas, where the fate of the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, will help decide which party controls the U. S. Senate. But Mr. Paxton has struggled to raise cash, and no one has stepped in yet to help him.

Mr. Paxton finds himself in a unique situation among Senate candidates, according to interviews with a dozen Republicans with ties to his campaign. Republican donors still hold grudges from a bruising primary. The state, with its 18-plus television markets, is an epically expensive setting. And his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has proved to be a particularly strong fund-raiser.

Perhaps the most striking piece of Mr. Paxton’s money woes is the high-stakes game of chicken that two of the Republican Party’s biggest money committees, along with their allied donors, are playing.

Both of those groups, the Senate Leadership Fund and MAGA Inc., are not so secretly hoping that the other one swoops in to boost Mr. Paxton with tens of millions in spending, the Republicans said. Neither group has reached for its wallet yet.

“Somebody is going to have to spend big money,” said Dan Eberhart, an oil executive who is raising contributions for Mr. Paxton. “We’ll see who blinks.”

In the primary, Mr. Paxton defeated Senator John Cornyn, a favorite of many of the country’s and state’s largest donors. The Republican nominee still lacks enthusiasm from these contributors, who financed ads in the primary repeatedly calling him a criminal and a womanizer. Their opinions largely haven’t changed, especially with the continuing drumbeat of revelations of Mr. Paxton’s world travels with his girlfriend, the Republicans said.

Mr. Paxton is not getting help from Washington, either. National Republican groups are slated to spend tens of millions of dollars this summer and fall in every other top-tier Senate race, including in some states that prominent handicappers think are not as competitive as Texas. They even plan to spend more in noncompetitive Kansas. In most states, Republicans are expected to outspend Democrats — for instance in Ohio, where the G. O. P. commitment totals over $100 million.

A Paxton adviser disputed concerns about his campaign’s financial straits.

“The trajectory is unmistakable: Support is accelerating, not softening. Everyone from grass-roots Texans to large conservative donors are consolidating behind this campaign, and June was the clearest signal yet,” said Nick Maddux, the adviser, touting what he said was $7 million raised last month across Paxton committees.

There’s also the fact that Democratic Senate candidates in the state have not won despite out-raising or out-spending Republicans in the last few cycles.

Republicans say that Texas requires around $15 million a week in super PAC advertising to mount a comprehensive paid-media campaign, making Texas more a drain on resources than cheaper states that could also decide the majority.

The amount of Republican spending planned in Texas from now through Election Day, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm: $0.

So who should pick up the Texas tab?

First, there’s the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC run by allies of John Thune, the Senate majority leader. It backed Mr. Cornyn in the primary and has hardly embraced Mr. Paxton.

During a June trip to Washington, Mr. Paxton met with officials of the super PAC at its headquarters and told them that he hoped the race wouldn’t be so close to warrant a heavy spend, two people with knowledge of the meeting said.

The Senate Leadership Fund is funding polling and candidate research in the race and has told donors it is monitoring the state. Even so, the super PAC conspicuously left out Texas when unveiling a $342 million plan in eight other states. Allies said that the Senate Leadership Fund didn’t have millions lying around to invest in another race, especially given the year’s volatile map, including fresh uncertainty over the Montana Senate race.

Staring across the table is MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by top advisers to President Trump with an extraordinary $400 million cash reserve. His endorsement of Mr. Paxton the week before the May runoff election dealt a death blow to Mr. Cornyn. Some Republican donors close to the Senate Leadership Fund say that MAGA Inc., which has yet to reveal how much it will spend on the midterms, should therefore be on the hook for whatever bill is due in Texas.

MAGA Inc. officials say there is no impasse with the Senate Leadership Fund, claiming they are simply being discreet with their spending plans, which they said last month would be “very soon” and “substantial.” Chris LaCivita and James Blair, two of MAGA Inc.’s top officials, have spoken in recent weeks about Texas with Alex Latcham, who heads the Senate Leadership Fund, according to two people with knowledge of the conversations.

“I think his PAC should help Ken, and I can’t imagine they wouldn’t,” said Doug Deason, whose family has donated $410,000 to Paxton committees this year, of Mr. Trump. “He endorsed him. He wants to keep the Senate. And obviously we don’t want a Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas.”

That Democrat, Mr. Talarico, entered July holding about nine times as much cash in his principal campaign account than Mr. Paxton does in his. Since June, Mr. Talarico has been up on television, airing about $12 million in ads to introduce himself to voters. He is also raising money aggressively, including a high-dollar event near Chicago last Saturday and others in Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket this weekend, according to invitations viewed by The Times.

To some extent, national Democrats are experiencing the same paralysis as Republicans. The Senate Majority PAC, controlled by Senate Democrats, unveiled new spending last week but has not reserved any ad time in Texas.

Still, Mr. Talarico’s own ability to raise enormous amounts of money himself makes him less dependent on Washington than Mr. Paxton is. Plus, last month, a dedicated pro-Talarico super PAC received $10 million from the tech investor Reid Hoffman.

And in private conversations with donors, Senate Majority PAC officials have outlined various potential spending plans for Texas and the trade-offs those might require across the Senate map, giving Democrats the impression that the PAC is preparing to spend in Texas at some point, according to two people briefed on the conversations.

All of this makes fund-raising an urgent priority this summer for Mr. Paxton. Yet his relationships with donors in the state remain frosty, including the Texas network of former President George W. Bush, which he has regularly criticized. Holdouts include moderates like the G. O. P. megadonor Ken Griffin, who is said to have no plans to help Mr. Paxton, and longtime right-wing backers like the oil industry’s Wilks brothers and Tim Dunn.

Mr. Paxton has made individual calls to some Cornyn-aligned givers seeking six-figure checks, a person with knowledge said. But some Cornyn donors have declined even to return calls from the Paxton camp, multiple Republicans said.

Mr. Paxton is hosting a fund-raising dinner this Thursday in Aspen, Colo., according to an invitation viewed by The Times, and one in Jackson Hole, Wyo., later this summer. Senator Ted Cruz formed a joint fund-raising committee with him this month to coordinate fund-raising events, such as a recent one at a hotel in Houston owned by Tilman Fertitta, the owner of the N. B. A.’s Rockets.

Last Wednesday in Washington on Capitol Hill, Mr. Thune more fully embraced Mr. Paxton than previously, throwing him a fund-raiser at the Safari Club International and pledging he would not abandon Texas, according to an attendee. Another Republican senator, Bill Hagerty of Tennessee, predicted that outside groups would in August spend big for Mr. Paxton. He didn’t specify which.

Here’s a jarring stat: Republicans are on track to spend more to win a noncompetitive race in Kansas than they are in Texas, where the outcome could help determine which party controls the U. S. Senate. This story looks at the strategic questions at play in the contest between Ken Paxton and James Talarico, and whether Republicans should be investing more.

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Obama Makes One of His First Midterm Endorsements With a Basketball Video

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The former president is trying to help Josh Turek net a Senate seat in Iowa, which Democrats see as one of their best pickup opportunities of the midterms.

By Tim Balk

Barack Obama, the only Democrat to win Iowa in a presidential election in the last quarter-century, famously loves basketball. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee in the state’s high-stakes Senate race, does, too — he was a two-time Paralympic gold medalist on the U. S. men’s wheelchair basketball team.

So for one of the former president’s first endorsements of the midterm elections, he appeared in an endorsement video shooting hoops with Mr. Turek, a centrist state lawmaker who is seeking to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Iowa in more than a decade.

Last week, Mr. Obama joined Mr. Turek at a gymnasium in Chicago, where they filmed a two-and-a-half minute video while playing a game of IOWA, a variation of HORSE, the shoot-around game.

Democrats are trying to flip the seat held by Senator Joni Ernst, a Republican who decided not to run for re-election. Mr. Turek faces Representative Ashley Hinson, a moderate Republican running with President Trump’s endorsement.

“Let’s go, we playing HORSE or what?” Mr. Obama, who had the White House tennis court modified so it could also be used for basketball, says from the sidelines in the opening moments of the video, released Wednesday.

Mr. Turek replies with a grin, “We’re playing IOWA.”

“I know a little something about winning Iowa,” says Mr. Obama, who upset Hillary Clinton in the Democratic race for president in 2008 and carried the state in the general election that year.

He also won Iowa in the 2012 presidential election. But the state swung sharply in 2016. Mr. Trump carried it by nearly 10 percentage points. Thirty-one Iowa counties pivoted, the most of any state.

Republicans have since maintained a hold on Iowa, and Mr. Trump won it comfortably in 2020 and in 2024.

But Iowa’s farming-heavy economy has struggled under Mr. Trump’s tariff policies in his second term. Democrats see the state as one of their top pickup opportunities in their quest to reclaim the Senate.

Opinion polls show the race between Mr. Turek and Ms. Hinson essentially tied. Mr. Turek has argued that the state is ready to elect a “common-sense” Democrat, and has pointed to his bipartisan record in the Iowa Legislature.

In the video, Mr. Obama asks Mr. Turek how his campaign is going.

“Everywhere we go — urban areas, rural areas — people are ready for change,” Mr. Turek says.

Mr. Obama says that “of all the things I’ve done in politics, Iowa was my favorite thing,” describing “a magic about regular folks showing up in gyms” for the state’s caucuses.

Mr. Turek tells Mr. Obama that people in the state say they are feeling “hope” for the “first time in a long time.”

Mr. Obama replies, “That’s my sense.”

Ms. Hinson’s campaign dismissed the endorsement.

“Another liberal endorses Josh Turek — shocking,” Billy Fuerst, a campaign spokesman, said in a six-word statement.

Mr. Obama has endorsed few candidates in the midterm elections, which are still three months away. But in May, he joined James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in traditionally red Texas, to get tacos at a campaign event that was filmed and turned into a glossy video.

Mr. Obama’s video with Mr. Turek shows a series of swishes by the two left-handed Democrats and the former president badly missing a midrange bank shot from the wing. (“The bank was closed,” Mr. Obama says.)

It includes a discussion of the greatest basketball players of all time. (Both men put Michael Jordan, the Chicago Bulls guard, atop their lists.)

The video leaves some ambiguity about who won the game of IOWA, though Mr. Obama says he was “whooped” and describes Mr. Turek as “somebody who knows how to win.”

A spokeswoman for Mr. Obama, Hannah Hankins, declined to say who won, saying simply that they had fun and had a good conversation.

It was not the first time the former president had met Mr. Turek. Mr. Obama welcomed him to the White House in 2016 to celebrate the U. S. Paralympic men’s basketball team’s Olympic gold medal victory in Rio de Janeiro.

Reihan Salam loves New York. He loves the free market. And he’s very worried.

Reihan Salam, the Manhattan Institute’s 46-year-old president, is a lifelong New Yorker who is worried that his hometown is on the brink of disaster. Credit... Amir Hamja for The New York Times

Supported by

By Eliza Shapiro and Nicholas Fandos

Reihan Salam has a lot in common with the man he is trying to stop.

They went to rival New York City public high schools. Both are South Asian Muslim men with a talent for remembering faces and names. Mr. Salam, the head of the conservative Manhattan Institute, and his democratic socialist foil, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, both favor merch embroidered with the same 1970s cursive City of New York insignia.

They share something else. They are convinced that their beloved city is in crisis. For the mayor, the crisis is affordability. For Mr. Salam, the crisis is Mr. Mamdani.

“You have a couple of decades of prosperity that are slipping away,” said Mr. Salam, 46, who lives with his family in a Brooklyn neighborhood that voted overwhelmingly for Mr. Mamdani. “We are squandering this incredible opportunity to show that urban life can work.”

He fears that many of his fellow New Yorkers have been seduced by what he sees as the mayor’s vilification of the city’s wealthiest residents and misled by Mr. Mamdani’s vision of free buses, free child care and frozen rent. He believes the mayor’s big plans to subsidize the costs of city life for even well-off New Yorkers (“unlimited welfarism for the near-rich,” Mr. Salam calls it) could steer New York City into a financial tailspin reminiscent of the dark days of the 1970s.

To counter all that, Mr. Salam is trying to make the Manhattan Institute, a think tank with a roster of New York City obsessives, the intellectual engine of the resistance.

Slowing down the mayor and his popular movement will be no easy task, as others have discovered. The city’s vaunted business elite spent tens of millions of dollars trying to persuade voters that Mr. Mamdani’s ideas about capitalism and Israel were too radical for New York, without success. The Democratic establishment has largely been cowed by the mayor’s political strength. Elected Republicans are so outnumbered in New York that they have no real power to stop him.

Neither does the Manhattan Institute. Over a half-century, the organization has lobbied constantly for shrinking the city’s sprawling bureaucracy and letting private industry work its magic. The election of a democratic socialist marks a low point for the institute in New York, where its project has never been further from the halls of power.

But Mr. Salam, its president since 2019, sees an opportunity. Mr. Mamdani’s electric campaign has created unusual interest in big ideas about what works, and what doesn’t, when it comes to administering government in the city.

Where some right-wing critics have caricatured the mayor as a communist, a jihadist and a candidate for deportation, Mr. Salam and his fellow conservative urbanists are testing a less hyperbolic approach. They have taken direct aim at Mr. Mamdani’s policy agenda, deploying deep knowledge of city history and policy expertise to try to serve as a voice of skepticism whispering in the city’s collective ear.

Do people making hundreds of thousands of dollars a year really need free child care?

Might a rent freeze cause even fewer people to leave their apartments, driving the vacancy rate so low it could destabilize the housing market?

Could free buses turn the M4 into a daytime shelter for homeless people?

The mayor’s office declined to comment on the Manhattan Institute. Mr. Mamdani has said he believes it is government’s job to deliver excellent services rather than choose who receives those services, especially in the face of the city’s affordability crisis. In his inaugural address, the mayor took on critics of “big government,” saying, “No longer will City Hall hesitate to use its power to improve New Yorkers’ lives.”

Changing the mayor’s worldview may be out of the question. But if Mr. Salam and his group of warrior-wonks can influence other pillars of the New York cognoscenti — activists, nonprofit leaders, city commissioners, journalists — they hope it might be just enough to slow down the big-government bandwagon.

“I vehemently believe that we are defenders of the beautiful mosaic,” said Mr. Salam, using a twist on a phrase coined by David N. Dinkins, a former Democratic mayor, to describe New York in all its glorious complexity.

“But it means that you need to not be an idiot.”

A half-century ago, the mosaic was seriously blighted.

Decades of poor fiscal management had left the city teetering on the edge of total financial collapse, and signs of New York’s imminent demise were everywhere. The subways were covered in graffiti, muggings were common, trash piled up on the sidewalks and streets, some landlords set their buildings on fire for the insurance money and a 25-hour blackout led to widespread looting.

These days, the city is not in pristine financial health. Fiscal experts estimate that New York will face significant budget deficits within the next few years. But the city and state set up guardrails decades ago to avoid a repeat of the irresponsible accounting and financial chaos of the 1970s.

The Manhattan Institute is not expecting another financial emergency to set in tomorrow. Still, to Mr. Salam and his colleagues, the ’70s fiscal crisis is not so much a historical event as a scriptural one — a Great Flood whose legacy should serve as a permanent warning to the city’s leaders that things can go terribly wrong when government spends more money on social services than it can actually afford.

A few weeks after Mr. Mamdani was elected last year, a crowd assembled at the institute’s headquarters around the corner from Grand Central Terminal for a panel titled “The Fiscal Crisis at 50: Lessons for a New Era of City Government.” The room was so packed that even Dean Fuleihan, a longtime Democratic Mr. Fix-It who had just been named Mr. Mamdani’s most senior aide, had to hunt for a seat.

In an impromptu exchange with the panelists, Mr. Fuleihan said the reforms that had been put in place to prevent future fiscal calamities were “making my life easier.”

“It is the responsibility of government to listen to the opinions of the people they serve, even when it leads to spirited discussions about the 1975 fiscal crisis,” Mr. Fuleihan told The New York Times in a statement.

Getting a consigliere of the mayor to show up at its office for any reason was a good sign for the Manhattan Institute and its efforts to start a conversation that city leaders might actually engage in.

The think tank, created in 1978, has always had a broader focus than New York. Many of the organization’s 85 scholars comment on national issues, and some have taken up arms in the conservative culture wars over public safety and transgender rights. But a subset of New York-focused wonks are now working overtime to try to come up with more Manhattan Institute-y solutions to some of the problems the mayor wants to solve.

“I try to be constructive,” said Eric Kober, the institute’s local housing expert.

“It’s not enough to simply criticize him,” he added, “it’s also necessary to offer something that he could do.”

Mr. Kober, who spent 35 years working under mayors of all stripes at the city’s planning department before joining the think tank, has tried to come up with tweaks of Mr. Mamdani’s policy proposals that could save money and lean more on private business.

The mayor could, for example, roll back regulations that require local government to decide how many parking spots should be required for commercial businesses, and leave it to developers, which might encourage investment in the city. Or, instead of spending $30 million on a new municipal grocery store in East Harlem, with prices subsidized by taxpayers, Mr. Kober wrote recently, the mayor could take that money and upgrade existing small supermarkets or try to bring in more discount stores like Aldi and Lidl.

Stephen Eide, a fellow focused on social services, is hoping that he can appeal to Mr. Mamdani’s interest in “sewer socialism,” the idea that progressive government should be laser focused on improving city services. He argues that decreasing spending can actually help orient local government to the city’s most urgent problems.

“Keeping government small to us is not an end to itself,” Mr. Eide said. “It’s a larger goal of making sure that government can focus on the stuff that only government can do,” like providing better treatment for mentally ill people on the subway or responding more quickly to 911 calls.

Nicole Gelinas is a transit expert whom even some critics of the Manhattan Institute take seriously. (Brad Lander, an ally of the mayor, said he had “learned a lot” from her even if they often disagree.) She has spent the last few months honing her central thesis of the Mamdani era: The mayor has promised a vision he can’t actually deliver on. She considers it her responsibility to help reset expectations.

She has noted that Mr. Mamdani showed some fiscal restraint by backtracking on two promises he made as a candidate; he has pushed state lawmakers to delay an expensive cap on public-school class sizes and scaled back a proposed expansion of a multi-billion-dollar housing voucher program.

But finding the money for free buses and more free child care, she contends, could force the mayor to make more difficult decisions about what gets funded and what doesn’t.

“The idea that you are going to have some magic bag of tricks and the city will become affordable,” Ms. Gelinas said, “it’s just not going to happen.”

Patrick Gaspard, a top adviser to Mr. Mamdani who led the Democratic National Committee, said he had found the Manhattan Institute’s work to be rigorous and thoughtful. Its scholars, he said, are engaging in “the kind of conversation reasonable people can have about the appropriate role of government, the relationship to the private sector, what it means to general growth.”

But Mr. Gaspard took a dim view of the institute’s relevance these days.

“They have neither the political heft or the cultural currency to be consequential,” he said. “They just don’t.”

It wasn’t always like that. In the 1990s, the Manhattan Institute had so much political heft that Rudolph W. Giuliani, the city’s Republican mayor, later joked about having basically plagiarized its ideas.

In those days, the group identified crime, poor city services and struggling public schools as New York’s biggest problems and helped steer city government toward solutions.

Many believe the city became safer and more functional as a result.

But the broken windows theory of policing evangelized by the Manhattan Institute, which held that the police should focus more on small crimes to prevent larger ones, exacerbated racial tensions in the city when police officers targeted Black and Latino New Yorkers at higher rates than other groups.

And the rightward pivot of the late 1990s arguably marked the beginning of the moment when New York became so desirable, and so expensive, that the city began to slip out of reach for its working-class and middle-class residents — and then for its reasonably well-off ones.

Today, Mr. Salam’s warnings about the mayor and his agenda still have an audience with New York’s moneyed elite.

Hundreds filed into a majestic old bank building in Midtown in May for the institute’s annual black-tie fund-raising gala. Outside, protesters greeted attendees with chants of “tax the rich,” a slogan of the city’s recent political revolution. Inside the room, Mr. Salam told the assembled donors — who were paying as much as $250,000 for a table — that the protesters represented a certain view: that “prosperity is something to be handed out by the state, and that the only thing standing in between them and the lives they want is someone else’s wealth.”

The Manhattan Institute, he told them, “exists to confront this seductive lie and to stand for something better.”

Recruiting allies in other precincts of Mr. Mamdani’s New York, though, could be harder.

They are trying. Some of the Manhattan Institute’s local fellows turn out a weekly newsletter on Substack about city government, the Bigger Apple. City Journal, the Manhattan Institute’s in-house magazine, recently delivered a scoop on how one of Mr. Mamdani’s commissioners had scheduled a meeting with an Iranian diplomat without the mayor’s knowledge.

One of the institute’s fellows, Daniel Golliher, teaches his own course about New York civics, and requires his students to attend community board meetings and memorize sections of city law. The goal is to create more educated voters — and perhaps eventually city employees and politicians.

The Manhattan Institute’s credibility with fellow New Yorkers may depend on the ability of its content creators to signal that their bias is, above all, pro-New York. Mr. Salam calls himself “an aggro partisan of urban life,” and draws a line between the institute and those on the right who see the city as inherently doomed.

“We are trying to make an argument for a multiethnic, metropolitan future for the country,” said Mr. Salam, whose parents immigrated here from Bangladesh before he was born. “That is a place where others on the right see as hopeless or deserving of their misery, we affirmatively reject that.” He says New York is the only place he’s ever wanted to live, the only place he could ever live, especially because he never got his driver’s license.

Despite its New York City roots, the Manhattan Institute is unquestionably part of the national conservative landscape, in ways that may alienate some New Yorkers.

Although the institute is not central to the MAGA movement, its work is funded by some of the same conservative megadonors who support President Trump. It produces proposals that Republicans marshal in polarizing national political fights, like recent draft legislation that would reclassify disruptive acts of protest like blocking roads as “civil terrorism” felonies. Christopher Rufo, a conservative activist and writer on the payroll, has led the movement against diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives.

Even some of its New York-focused scholars have dinged the mayor in ways that can come across as less than collaborative. Ms. Gelinas wrote a New York Post column headlined: “Mamdani acts like a petulant teen in front of the king and queen.” Another Manhattan Institute fellow wrote an article accusing Mr. Mamdani of being a “show-off,” more interested in photo opportunities “than the dirty work of governing.” And after Mr. Mamdani asked New Yorkers to keep their air-conditioners at 78 degrees during a heat wave, following the same advice as mayors before him, a Manhattan Institute fellow posted a video in which he turned his air-conditioning down to 67 degrees, while blasting the song “God Bless the U. S. A.”

Liz Krueger, an influential state senator from Manhattan, said she had stopped reading most of the think tank’s output years ago because she felt it was biased. “Too many of the far-right messengers in today’s era are nut jobs,” said Ms. Krueger, a Democrat. “I don’t know whether that includes the Manhattan Institute because that would require I actually read it.”

Mr. Salam said he does not need New Yorkers to like everything he and his colleagues say.

He imitated a serious-sounding scold who might say: “These guys are terrible, noxious, a dangerous force, but by the way, I agree with them on some things.”

If that’s the case, he added in his regular voice, “that’s wonderful.”

As for Mr. Mamdani, Mr. Salam doesn’t believe they have ever been in the same room, and isn’t sure they would have all that much to talk about. “He seems to have a rather well-developed theory about the world,” he said.

This is also something one could say about Mr. Salam. He holds an admittedly idealized memory of his own childhood, in Borough Park, during the Giuliani years. His parents worked long hours and saved enough money to eventually buy a small home in nearby Kensington. They rented out the top floors, and the family slept in a partially finished basement, until they saved enough money to take over the whole house.

Mr. Salam now makes about $800,000 a year from his post at the institute and lives with his own family in a home in a nearby neighborhood. The story of his family’s rise from one generation to the next is part of why he sees New York as the ultimate beacon of ambition, prosperity and capitalism.

His current neighbors in a leafy, low-slung part of the city close to Prospect Park are perfectly lovely, he said. Many of them have more than his parents did when he was a child: social and cultural capital, and at least some family money. And yet they seem to feel the city owes them even more, he said, in the form of free child care or buses or cheaper groceries.

Even if he can’t convince them otherwise, there may be something else that will: Mr. Mamdani failing to deliver all he has promised. He sees it as inevitable.

“Someone is going to have to pick up the pieces,” Mr. Salam said. “And I think that’s going to be our responsibility.”

A lot of people have tried a lot of different strategies to try to take Mayor Zohran Mamdani down a notch. Most of them have failed. My colleague Nicholas Fandos and I spent some time getting to know a conservative think tank that is trying to criticize New York's popular mayor the old fashioned way: by challenging him on ideas, not on his background or personality. The Manhattan Institute's roster of New York City obsessives stay up at night worrying about the mayor's proposed rent freeze, the cost of expanding child care and the pitfalls of municipal grocery stores. Here's what they've been up to.

Eliza Shapiro reports on New York City for The Times.

Nicholas Fandos is a Times reporter covering New York politics and government.

Matt Damon’s Biceps in That ‘Odyssey’ Fight Scene? They’re Hers.

The New York Times July 29, 2026

‘The Odyssey’

Advertisement

Supported by

Devyn Dalton, a 4-foot-6 woman, is the leading man’s stunt double in Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster.

By Alisha Haridasani Gupta

Last week, the actor Devyn Dalton received, quite possibly, the world’s biggest compliment.

She was in New Zealand filming her next project, when she was awakened at 4 a. m. by the buzz of her phone. “I was like, ‘What is going on?’ It just blew up — my phone was going crazy,” Dalton, 34, said.

What was going on was that the actor Matt Damon, who plays Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of Homer’s epic tale, had said in an interview that she had “the greatest arms I have ever seen.” Her friends were sending her clips of the interview as it was ripping through the internet.

Damon had been discussing one of the film’s pivotal scenes when he gently corrected his interlocutor, who had mistakenly assumed the biceps in the shot were his own: They belonged to Dalton, who some might be surprised to learn is his stunt double. She’s a woman standing in for a male actor, for starters; she’s also 4-foot-6 to Damon’s roughly 5-foot-10 frame.

It’s a bit of movie magic, Damon explained. To film the battle against the man-eating Laestrygonians, Nolan used a technique called “forced perspective” to make Odysseus’ army appear minuscule.

A shot of Dalton from behind in the scene, holding a sword and ready to pounce at the giants, is used in one of the posters for the movie.

Dalton, born and raised in Canada, trained as a dancer initially and started performing stunts in 2011 after she was cast in the “Planet of the Apes” trilogy. Her more recent credits include “Weapons” and “The Last of Us.”

She has found herself in such high-voltage action sequences that she can never tell her mother what she’s working on because “it freaks her out,” Dalton said. “I just tell her ‘I’m going to work.’”

“The Odyssey” is the first time Dalton has done stunts for a male A-lister — a rare feat in an industry where, according to the SAG-AFTRA union, women make up little more than 20 percent of performers.

In a conversation with The New York Times, edited and condensed for clarity, she discussed her latest role and her other stunt work.

Is it common practice for a woman to double for a male lead? Have you done that before?

Definitely not common. I think men have been doubling for women for longer in the industry. But with stunts, the main thing is, who is the best fit for what they’re looking for, physically? And, most importantly, who has the specific skill set needed? Increasingly, with wardrobe, hair and makeup, we get to do movie magic and transform people, and it doesn’t matter so much about gender. This is the first time doubling for a Hollywood leading man. I never thought I would have that on my résumé.

Have you received this kind of specific shout-out from a leading actor before?

It is uncommon because, even though you’re in front of the camera, if you’re doubling and you’ve done your job right, the audience shouldn’t know it’s you. Part of our job is being hidden. I have to say a huge thank-you to Matt for being so generous.

Were you and Damon on set together working on that fight choreography?

Yeah. Most of the time, on any film I’ve been on, you end up working with the actor and being there on the same day because you’re both a part of a sequence and you’re both portraying the same character.

When doubling for someone, I’ll always specifically watch like, what foot did they walk with first? People also just have little tendencies, like they might lean to one side or move a certain way. So I study all of that and try to mimic it exactly. That’s what sells it so well on camera.

Did you need any special training for this role?

This has been years of work building out my skills. I try to be very versatile by doing a lot of different training methods to just stay ready, so that whenever the phone rings, I’m like, “OK, I’m good to go.”

That’s the thing with stunts — the training never ends. In the past, I’ve done a few really cool underwater fight scenes, and so I took courses that focused on water safety, breath holding and cold water because a lot of the times you’re not working in a warm situation and so you have to learn how to manage the temperature. And you’re in costume and makeup and you have to be underwater with your eyes open.

Are there stunts you’ve had to do that scared you?

I think the fear for me always comes from a place of setting very high standards for myself. I always want to do a really good job.

When Matt Damon said, in an interview last week, that his stunt double in a pivotal scene in "The Odyssey" was a woman with the best biceps he's ever seen, I, like seemingly everyone else on earth, needed to find out more about her.

Alisha Haridasani Gupta is a Times reporter covering style and pop culture.

Trying to Make a Buck Off a Data Center, One 6-Pack at a Time

The New York Times July 29, 2026

What do you do when a $25 billion complex is under construction nearby? One couple in Abilene had an idea.

What do you do when a $25 billion complex is under construction nearby? One couple in Abilene had an idea.

The Elmdale Outpost convenience store in Abilene, Texas. Credit... Desiree Rios for The New York Times

Supported by

By Juliet Macur and Photographs by Desiree Rios

Reporting from Abilene, Texas

It was quitting time at the giant construction site, sending the afternoon rush down a crumbling two-lane country road toward a new convenience store called the Elmdale Outpost.

Dust-covered pickup trucks from near and far — Louisiana, North Carolina, Mexico — pulled into its parking lot, and weary workers walked through the door, their boots leaving a trail of dirt inside.

The tiny Swiss Army knife of a shop carries anything the workers might need. Toothpaste and toilet paper, sweet potatoes and spicy-hot snacks, and beer. At every turn, ice-cold beer. An entire separate room of floor-to-ceiling beer. More than 60 brands, including a dozen varieties of michelada alone.

The store’s primary appeal, though, is its proximity to the construction site, six miles away. Or, more precisely, its proximity to the sprawling, new 148-acre R. V. park next door, built to serve thousands of temporary laborers.

An armada of those workers — pipe fitters, HVAC technicians, ironworkers and more — has come to this rural area at the northeast edge of Abilene, Texas, to build the $25 billion Frontier data center complex, part of the half-trillion dollar Stargate project that President Trump promoted last year as “the largest A. I. infrastructure project in history.” The flagship Stargate data center campus is also under construction, on the other side of town.

“Y’all opened up a good spot right here,” a foundation contractor from Colorado told the store owner, Sam Holt Jr., while buying a six-pack of Dos Equis.

After a 10-hour day in the Texas sun, he said he couldn’t resist the red sign painted on the store’s corrugated tin roof: “BEER.”

“Yep, we’re just trying to serve our new neighbors,” Holt replied.

Late last year, “neighbors” meant a handful of families living on open farmland. Now it means a deluge of strangers who live in one of the biggest R. V. parks in the country, with 2,300 narrow gravel parking spots lined up like endless rows of piano keys.

“Everything around here’s changed overnight,” Holt said to another customer, this one an electrician from a South Texas border town who had stopped in for two bags of Flamin’ Hot Doritos, a bottle of the Mexican spice Tajín to sprinkle into his beer and a 12-pack of Michelob Ultra.

“We’re here for the money while it lasts!” said the man, who said he has his first child on the way and was drawn to the data center site for its big paychecks.

Holt, 48, is making the best of the situation. Several months ago, his store was a two-bedroom house. His father’s house.

It was, as his father had described it, his “place among the wheat fields.”

After retiring from his luxury sedan service in Dallas, Sam Holt Sr. moved in 2015 to the little yellow house on a sliver of an acre on Elmdale Road North. He lived alone.

A Vietnam veteran who survived several bouts of cancer, he marveled at the views, taking photos of Creamsicle-hued sunrises from his front door and cotton-candy-colored sunsets from his back one. He would share them online.

“11/18/24 @1800hrs. Lookin’ out on my back door area. No city lights.”

“12/12/24 @ 0717hrs. Sittin’ in my front door. Good morning. I have been up since 0630hrs CST, and I have not heard a sound, barring the clicking of my iPhone as I type. No vehicles or birds. ZILCH! So peaceful.”

Holt Sr. attended the Hamby Church of Christ less than two miles away. Wrote poetry about growing up on a farm in Missouri. Made cedar chests and children’s tables, and also a five-tiered birdhouse — for 60 bird families, he boasted — that he tucked into a tree in his front yard.

Morning and night, he cooked his specialty: meatloaf, pinto beans and cornbread.

When a real estate agent offered $150,000 for his house last summer, maybe $25,000 more than it was worth, Holt Sr. declined. “Where am I supposed to go?” he said at the time. “I like it here, and I’m going to ride this out.”

A few months later, on Thanksgiving, Sam Holt Sr. went to the hospital. He died there on Christmas Eve at 81.

Sam Holt Jr.’s girlfriend, Stacey Sanford, first raised the idea of using the house to make money. Others were profiting from the A. I. construction project, so why shouldn’t they?

Having turned farmland into the R. V. park, the developer charges $675 a month per spot — and will gross more than $18.6 million a year in rent alone.

So Holt and Sanford drew up a plan to open a dry goods store that would sell beer. Holt was a longtime managing partner at Texas Roadhouse restaurants and had experience in customer service. He would quit his job to run the store, while Sanford, a health care executive, would join him on nights and weekends.

“I’m ready to make a change,” he told her.

“Let’s roll the dice and hope it works out,” she said.

Sam Holt Sr., religiously conservative, was against drinking alcohol. But he would have supported anything his son did to improve his life, and the lives of his grandchildren — his son was sure of it.

“He would know that we have to adapt,” Holt Jr. told Sanford. “A lot of people don’t want to adapt to this, but we have no choice.”

He and Sanford invested $75,000 and figured the store would last as long as the R. V. park — at least several years, considering that the data center developer, Vantage Data Centers, said construction of all 11 buildings on its 1,200-acre Shackelford County site would finish by late 2028.

The couple’s goal: pay for college for Holt’s two teenage daughters and then retire to an island off the coast of Honduras. Starting this new chapter, however, was complicated by grief.

From the living room wall, staple by staple, Holt Jr. removed the drawings his daughters had given his father, including ones of their teeny traced hands. The girls called their grandfather Silly Sam and had their own bedroom in the house.

That room became a walk-in beer cave, with silver insulation on the walls and refrigeration pumped in. The kitchen bar top became a checkout counter. A wall in the living room was fitted with a sliding door, to create a drive-through.

“Every time I see a sunset in the backyard, I think of him,” Holt said of his father. “And that’s every single night.”

Business is slow on weekday mornings.

Hours before Holt opens the store at 10 a. m., many workers have already left the R. V. park on their way to their jobs, creating a conga line of traffic that has warped and chipped the road’s asphalt. Some don reflective vests and hard hats, and board double-decker buses bound for the construction site.

One Wednesday last month, Holt prepared for a busy afternoon by unloading beer from a delivery truck. He orders smaller cases now than when he started, having learned that many customers prefer 6- and 12-packs because the refrigerators in their R. V. s don’t have much room.

Laurel Sullivan, a mother of two, was inside working the cash register. A month before, she had walked over from the R. V. park to ask if they needed any help, looking for something to do. She told Holt that she manages her toddlers and three dogs in their R. V. until her husband — a heavy machinery operator — returns from his 14-hour workday, and the days can be long. She hires a babysitter while she is at the store.

She and Holt go out of their way to befriend the regular customers, remembering their orders and their roles at the construction site, in an effort to create something of a community and help people feel less lonely.

There’s a Spanish-speaking boy, maybe 11 years old. He once tried to pay with a Nicaraguan dollar. This time, he brought a jar of Alfredo sauce to the counter so his sister could make lunch for him and his siblings, dropping a pile of coins in front of Sullivan — but they didn’t quite add up to the price.

“I got you,” she told him, reaching for her wallet to make up the difference. Holt gives children a free flavored ice.

There’s also the guy who drives his white F-250 pickup into the drive-through and wants a 30-pack of Miller Lite placed on the back seat. Yet another shows up every other day for two bottles of Mickey’s Fine Malt Liquor, a special order reserved just for him.

Around lunchtime, Brenda Talamante, the spouse of a welder, ordered a bag of ice at the drive-through. She had gotten up at 3:55 a. m. to cook her husband barbacoa and was now on her third cup of coffee.

“This is an adventure for us, but for some people, this is a chance to send money to their families back home,” she said from the seat of her red pickup. “Some people don’t realize that this is life-changing money.”

Holt and Sanford learned quickly that data center construction is lucrative. No one ever asked the price of anything, so they never bothered with price tags. Cashiers at the Elmdale Outpost — including one of Holt’s daughters — can leave a shift with $100-plus in tips.

More than a dozen workers at the R. V. park said that it was not uncommon for the data center laborers to receive a per diem of $150 to $250, and earn $200,000-plus a year — after taxes — in hourly wages.

A typical schedule is 10 to 14 hours a day for 13 days on, then one day off, with no paid vacation. For some, it is a good trade-off. They can now retire early. Or pay off their mortgage.

Many of these workers are Latino, and Holt, who is 6-foot-5 and friendly, chats with them in Spanish. He and Sanford stock Mexican brands, like Bimbo, but also take requests — a concrete worker asked for neck gaiters to keep out dust. Sometimes, they make educated guesses about what might be popular.

One day, Sanford shouted to Holt, “Hey, Sam, someone just bought five condoms and a 24-case of Coronas!” making both of them laugh.

She added, “Next up, they might need a pregnancy test — and turns out that we sell that, too!”

On that Wednesday night last month, Sanford had joined Holt after her full-time job and, almost two hours after a blushing sunset, they closed the store together.

They tallied the sales, $3,000 that day — about four times more than they made on Memorial Day weekend, their grand opening. It was 10:30 p. m., past bedtime for most of their neighbors, as they swept clumps of dirt off the floor and restocked shelves, adjusting every bottle in the coolers even a millimeter so its label was facing exactly forward. Holt would return less than 12 hours later; he has been working seven days a week.

They’re making these sacrifices because the window to profit off the data center won’t stay open forever. They try not to listen to the critics who say they have sold out to Big Tech.

Carye Adkins, a detective at the Abilene Police Department and a longtime friend of Holt’s, understands the dilemma.

Fourteen years ago, Adkins moved into his dream house — near the yellow one Holt Sr. would move into. He and his family had relocated from the city, and he remembers his young son running out back, in a newly plowed field, shouting, “Look, Dad, we got dirt!” Eventually, they had 17 cows and donkeys on their 20 acres.

Then the data center came, and then plans for the R. V. park.

Adkins told Holt that he couldn’t stand the idea of living right next to an R. V. park. Heartbroken, he sold his property to the developer.

Yet on opening day for the Elmdale Outpost, Adkins was the first customer through the door.

“All of this was devastating,” he told Holt. “But you deserve every penny you make off this.”

Juliet Macur is a national reporter at The Times, based in Washington, D. C., who often writes about America through the lens of sports.
