This Country Is Ravaged by War, but Its Rich Feel ‘Positive Vibes Only’

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Myanmar dispatch

The lifestyles of the wealthy in Myanmar — nightclubs, caviar and trips abroad — have been largely untouched by years of deadly conflict.

Myanmar dispatch

The lifestyles of the wealthy in Myanmar — nightclubs, caviar and trips abroad — have been largely untouched by years of deadly conflict.

A D. J. performing at the Pioneer Plus nightclub in Yangon, Myanmar, last Christmas. Credit...

Supported by

By Hannah Beech

Visuals by Daniel Berehulak

Hannah Beech and Daniel Berehulak spent three weeks in Myanmar, traveling through big cities and small villages.

After midnight, amid a war, the D. J. hyped the crowd.

“Are you ready to party?” he yelled into the mic, adding an expletive for emphasis.

The partygoers of Pioneer Plus, the most exclusive nightclub in the war-torn nation of Myanmar, were ready. The D. J. had come all the way from Croatia, after all. Young women gyrated onstage. Johnnie Walker flowed, but only Blue Label because that is the way these high-rollers roll. A private table for the evening — with hookah, imported fruit and pyramids of frosted shot glasses — costs hundreds of dollars to book.

In the bathrooms, and on the dance floor in stolen moments between flashes of the strobe, some denizens of Pioneer Plus swallowed pastel tablets that tinged their breath with vanilla or grape candy. The kick from these methamphetamine and caffeine concoctions, branded with the names of local drug syndicates, lasts for hours.

Myanmar, which five years ago descended into full-scale civil war after a military junta overthrew the elected government, led by Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, is in desperate need of a diversion, a respite, a prolonged high.

No one in Myanmar is unaffected by the conflict, which has turned more than half the country into a battlefield but has largely spared the cities. Half the population is now impoverished. Drones, fighter jets and land mines bring horror to civilians. A military draft applies to both men and women. The Myanmar government is again an international pariah, just like it was during earlier decades of military rule.

But even in war, life goes on. The partying class must party, and their consumption is conspicuous.

International sanctions imposed by Western governments on military leaders and their business cronies — weapons dealers, drug lords, natural resource magnates, middlemen for Chinese enterprises — may have halted shopping jaunts to New York, Paris and London. Still, there’s always Dubai, Shanghai and Bangkok.

Yone Lay — the stage name means Little Bunny — is a regular at Pioneer Plus, which is in a tony district of Yangon, Myanmar’s largest city. He raps (“Stupid,” “Someone Who Was Unlucky in Love”), he acts (“Original Gangster,” “Underground”) and he lends his star power to military galas. He once made a music video praising U Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief who orchestrated the coup five years ago and became Myanmar’s president in April.

When Mr. Yone Lay saunters into the nightclub, entourage in tow, security guards envelop him like a sheath of fine Myanmar silk. The cordon isn’t for show. Some celebrities who publicly cast their lot with the junta, rather than protesting the military’s killing of unarmed protesters, have found themselves targets of urban guerrillas. In 2023, one of Mr. Yone Lay’s acquaintances, Daw Lily Naing Kyaw, a singer who socialized with the generals, was killed by a bullet to the head in Yangon. Months before, Mr. Yone Lay was accosted by a man with a knife but escaped injury. A year later, a bomb exploded in his vehicle. No one was in the car at the time.

“Those people, they want to show that if you’re famous and connected to the military, we can kill you,” Mr. Yone Lay said one recent evening. “From the outside, people don’t realize that people like me are also oppressed.”

Mr. Yone Lay, 40, said that it is easy to forget how much Myanmar has changed during his lifetime. Less than two decades ago, there was almost no internet. In secret, Mr. Yone Lay listened to Eminem, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg on bootlegged cassette tapes. But the advent of economic and political reforms in the 2010s, including elections in 2015 that ushered in a semi-civilian government, seemed to modernize the nation at warp speed. Mr. Yone Lay rapped about his concerns of that era: “Girls and parties and bling bling.”

Now, he said, his worries are existential. He travels with bodyguards. The stress, he said, makes decompressing at the blingiest nightclubs mandatory.

“We have to find ways to be happy,” Mr. Yone Lay said. “Why can’t we just love all our leaders and live peacefully?”

Yangon, buzzing during the reform years with new construction and advertisements for investment opportunities and business English classes, has largely reverted to a state of decay. Western businesses have mostly left; billboards that once showed off American soft drinks and German sedans now display local instant coffee mixes and bathroom piping.

Still, with enough squinting or blinkering, it is possible to pretend that life in Yangon is not so different from before the coup, at least for a privileged set. At The Yangon Restaurant, partly owned by the son of Mr. Min Aung Hlaing, the menu is showy European and studded with foie gras and caviar. With enough advance notice, a maître d’ said, a sommelier can be flown in from Singapore.

On their social media accounts, Ma Christina Lim, 36, and her husband, Ko Thu Rayn Kyaw Moe, 38, parade their fabulous lifestyles in Yangon and beyond, at Club Med in the Maldives, at the Great Wall in China. There are color-coordinated outfits in leather and velvet, plus more than 200 brand collaborations with the likes of Samsung, Carlsberg and a local yacht club. On YouTube, Facebook and Instagram — the latter two are officially banned in Myanmar, requiring VPNs to access — the couple has garnered millions of views for baby gender reveals (a popped balloon cascading pink confetti for their firstborn, a girl) and photos with celebrities who are tight with Mr. Min Aung Hlaing’s family.

“Our content, we like to stick to positivity, like positive vibes only,” Ms. Lim said. “You want viewers to feel good after watching our videos.”

In the days after the coup, Ms. Lim, like many members of Myanmar’s English-speaking jet set, posted photos on social media of the couple joining the protesters who peacefully marched to oppose the military intervention. Millions of people had taken to the streets nationwide to support the ousted civilian leader, Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi.

Within weeks, the military began killing protesters by gunshot — as well as children who happened to be nearby — and jailing dissenters. An armed resistance coalesced in the rainforests of Myanmar’s borderlands. Celebrities and influencers decried the military’s deadly crackdown. Ms. Lim posted on Facebook, the couple’s hands forming the three-finger gesture of resistance and memorializing “the martyrs who will never be able to return home.”

Then, the couple went silent. In early 2022, in their first post since Myanmar’s civil war flared, Ms. Lim and Mr. Thu Rayn Kyaw Moe celebrated their wedding anniversary, outfitted in matching crimson. In the years since, the pair, whose families made their fortunes in real estate, paper, imported vehicles and cold storage, has eschewed politics, instead gushing over luxury cars, breast pumps and American vitamin gummies. They extol the best dishes at the best French restaurant in town. They lavish attention on a French bulldog named Blue, as well as their two children.

“I feel like what happened happened,” said Ms. Lim, referring to the coup and its violent aftermath. She acknowledged that “it’s dark” — but because of chronic electricity shortages.

“At the same time,” she added, “people are just going to work regularly, going to school regularly.”

Even their mundane posts attract big audiences, but perhaps that’s the point. A Facebook video in which Mr. Thu Rayn Kyaw Moe inexpertly fried eggs and boiled instant noodles received 1.1 million views.

The coup and civil war have thrown into relief the choices of Myanmar’s rich. In Mandalay, the nation’s second-largest city, the Chinese traders who once came for jade and other jewels are mostly gone. Occasionally, handmade bombs target military officers or people considered accomplices to the regime.

Still, Ma May Nwe Htun, an actor, singer and social influencer better known as Sweet, said she had no interest in escaping Myanmar, where her family owns a gold business. Many friends have left for safer lives overseas, she said, but this is home, with its bustling teahouses and golden pagodas.

“We gotta have fun, baby,” Ms. May Nwe Htun said. “We have to do our best if we want to stay in the country we love.”

One recent evening, she threw a birthday party for her teenage son, who goes to an international school that has now lost most of its international students. There was a basketball-themed cake and a band of transgender entertainers. Overhead, in the hot, dark sky, fighter jets roared past on sorties to rebel-held territory, where civilians are terrorized by airstrikes. By the river in Mandalay, the thud of the bombing campaigns echoes in the night.

Back in Yangon, at Pioneer Plus, the singer-girlfriend of Mr. Yone Lay, the rapper, downed shot after shot. A member of an ethnic minority group that has a large militia at war with the Myanmar military, she is afraid, she said, of being targeted as a turncoat for dating a musician close to the army regime. She spoke to The New York Times on the condition that her name not be used.

“The people outside, they only know that the military kills, they only know one side,” she said. “I just want to be an artist, not a businessman or politician.”

She stood up unsteadily, the alcohol muddling her movements. Her friends linked their arms with hers, supporting her.

“Let’s dance,” she said, reaching out a manicured hand, her mascara smudged from earlier tears. “Let’s forget everything.”

Hannah Beech is a Times reporter based in Bangkok who has been covering Asia for more than 25 years. She focuses on in-depth and investigative stories.

Daniel Berehulak is a staff photographer for The Times based in Mexico City.

It Looks Like Nothing Can Dent MAGA’s Support for ICE

Wired July 29, 2026

On Tuesday, the day after hundreds of thousands of Haitian migrants effectively lost their temporary protected status that allowed them to live and work in the US, Republican pundit Steve Bannon wasted little time in demanding their instant removal.

“I was under the assumption that when they pulled TPS and their eligibility for that program ended … they were going to be boarding planes or buses today … today, this morning at dawn to go back to Haiti,” said Bannon, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, on his War Room podcast on Tuesday. “Why are they not out of the country?”

Mike Davis, a conservative political strategist agreed with Bannon: “The solution is to get these people the hell out of our country as fast as possible, and that includes these Haitians.”

White nationalist Nick Fuentes, who has been a vocal critic of Trump’s deportation policies because he doesn’t find them extreme enough, called Haitians “the worst of the worst” and “very low IQ people” on his Rumble show Tuesday night.

In a Telegram channel run by the Proud Boys of Columbus, one member posted a clip of the song “I’m Walking on Sunshine” alongside the news about the revoking of temporary protected status. “They gotta go back,” the member wrote.

It’s been a while since shock-and-awe tactics from Immigration and Customs Enforcement first gained national notoriety. For months, figures like former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino terrorized cities like Minneapolis and Chicago. But since replacing former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin—derisively referred to by Bannon as the “Kung fu plumber”—ICE’s operations have shrunk into the shadows, though the agency’s deportation and arrest numbers have remained astronomical.

In recent weeks, things are boiling over again.

Earlier this month, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas. Araujo had lived in the country for 35 years, had three children, and owned his own business. Just days later, another ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Both men were shot while in their vehicles. ICE, as WIRED has revealed, is also tracking its critics online, using data brokers to “identify unaccompanied minors,” and working to prevent state health inspectors from reviewing its network of detention centers. On Tuesday, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration was now targeting immigrants at airports whose visas have expired, or are in a transition status, arresting spouses of American citizens.

Even so, Steve Bannon and the other Republican pundits aren’t alone: Support for ICE among Trump’s most loyal supporters remains incredibly high, with 74 percent of people who identify as MAGA Republicans professing confidence in ICE, according to a YouGov poll published last week. The same poll shows that 80 percent of MAGA Republicans oppose abolishing ICE.

The YouGov findings were backed up by another poll published last week by the Public Religion Research Institute , which found that three-quarters of Republicans had a positive view of ICE, would be in favor of more funding for the agency, and disagreed that ICE was making communities less safe. The poll also found that 73 percent of Republicans are in support of internment camps to hold “immigrants who are in the country illegally” until they can be deported.

The YouGov poll also found that just 51 percent of Republicans had, in the week of the shootings, read, seen, or heard anything about immigrants being shot and killed by ICE agents. What they may have seen however is Trump’s Truth Social post around the same time. In the post, Trump appeared to overrule an internal ICE memo telling agents to suspend vehicle stops, after a furious response from his MAGA base. He also told his supporters that ICE was “loved and respected in America.”

Much of his base thinks that deportations are actually not happening fast enough. ICE is on track to deport 458,000 individuals this year according to its own data, a colossal figure that still falls well short of the 1 million deportations Trump promised shortly after his inauguration. (This, in the words of border czar Tom Homan, is what the administration calls “deportation-maxxing.”)

Americans have been caught in the dragnet as well, as ICE’s actions have resulted in widespread civil rights violations, according to a report published this month by the American Civil Liberties Union, which found that across eight states, ICE agents targeted 155 US citizens, 32 of whom were children, during the first year of Trump’s second term. Previous research from UC Berkeley found that half of all the people ICE has arrested had no criminal records, despite the administration claiming to be deporting the “worst of the worst.” Federal agents have shot and killed four people, including two US citizens.

On the other hand, the majority of Americans believe ICE has used too much force, according to YouGov, and as a result have little or no confidence in the agency. Almost half of Americans believe it's time for ICE to be abolished.

What these polls show is that while America as a whole is rejecting Trump’s immigration policies, his base is almost completely supportive. And rather than distancing themselves from ICE’s actions, Republicans seem to be leaning in again, even spending more money and running more ads about immigration than Democrats, NPR reported last week.

With just months left before the midterms offer voters a chance to have their say on these policies, Republicans are gambling that their base doesn’t actually want ICE going anywhere. In November, the country will see if they’re right.

Which of Dyson’s 2026 Stick Vacuums Is Worth the Upgrade?

Wired July 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Dyson's vacuum lineup has a whole new look these days, but that doesn't necessarily make it easier to decide if you're looking to buy one.

The Dyson V16 Piston Animal ($980), V10 Konical ($500), and V8 Cyclone ($400) arrived to change up Dyson's cordless vacuum options. The older V15 Detect ($650) and Gen5Detect ($800) are also still available and great vacuums, which raises the question: Should you upgrade? Which Dyson model is worth the cash with so many options (and widely ranging price points) to choose from?

I tested all five of these vacuums against each other in a series of tests to see which ones stood out among the pack. The two overall winners? The Gen5Detect was the number one winner, with the V16 Piston Animal right behind it, and the V10 Konical coming up third even though it's a much cheaper option. Read on to find out which model did best in each test, what the stats look like for each Dyson vacuum, and how I scored the final results.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Amazon

Amazon

Dyson

Dyson's naming convention is fun, and the numbers usually represent which models are more powerful or offer better accessories, but not always. Most of its vacuums have the V name, which, to my best guess, simply stands for “vacuum.” The numbers aren't always in order of release and usually reflect a vacuum's power level and capabilities. The V10 and V8 have the same power level but different heads, for example, while the V16 is more powerful than the V15. But not all vacuums are named the same; the Gen5Detect has a different name entirely, and falls in between the V15 and V16 when it comes to suction power and price tag.

Here's a quick chart to understand the power levels and compatible accessories that differentiate each vacuum from the other. You might also spot things like “Plus” or “Total” when you're shopping for a Dyson vacuum, and that usually reflects the attachments included with the vacuum.

This gives you a pretty easy look at what you're getting for each model. As the models increase in number (both in the name and in the price tag), the vacuum usually gains more accessories or cleaner heads, more air watts of suction power, and sometimes the option to add the Submarine wet cleaner head on for an additional price, or future compatibility with Dyson's Auto-empty Dok station that's coming out soon.

The Digital Motorbar and All Floor Cones cleaner heads are both compatible with soft and hard floors, which is why sometimes it's the only head included. More expensive Dyson models will also include the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, which is designed specifically for hard floors and has an illuminated light to help you spot dust and debris. The All Floor Cones cleaner head includes a light too, so you're able to get that feature on both the V16 and V10 without switching heads.

Here are the tests I ran for each vacuum, and which ones did best—and worst.

The V10 Konical and the sand obstacle.

After one pass of the V10, only a few thin lines remained of sand, the best results of these five vacuums on this rug.

BEST: V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

I tested all five Dyson models on a small black rug onto which I poured fine, white sand to see how well it was vacuumed up. The best was the V10 Konical, followed by the V15 Detect. Both left a small trail of sand behind in different spots, which makes sense since they have different head designs, but the V10's trail was smaller than the V15's, with a small line in the middle compared to the larger trail the V15 had on its right side.

The V8, meanwhile, stalled entirely when I tried to use it on the rug and couldn't vacuum up sand whatsoever. It weirdly seemed to have an issue with the thin rug, even though equally or more powerful vacuums were able to vacuum on it.

Both Gen5Detect and V16 Piston Animal were able to vacuum on the thin rug, but the stronger suction also kept trying to take the rug with it, giving both mixed results and leaving a lot of sand behind on each pass. I retested both of these on a thicker rug in case the suction level wasn't a match for the thin rug, and both did much better, but the Gen5Detect did the best, getting every bit of sand in one swoop. The V16 got most of its sand, but pushed some sand into a little pile in front of itself.

The Gen5Detect and the Cheerios obstacle.

After one pass of the Gen5Detect, it only missed Cheerios that were out of its cleaner head range and didn't send any pieces flying.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: None

When I last did a cereal test, I used a cornflake-style cereal. This time I switched to the cereal I know many parents like myself are much more likely to have all over the floors: Cheerios. I crushed up several in my hand and dropped those along with full Cheerios onto my thicker living room rug. Overall, every Dyson did a good job cleaning this up on the first pass.

The results on this one had pretty minimal differences for these models. The V8, V10, and V15 Detect all usually got the Cheerios and pieces on the first run, sending one to three pieces flying while it did so, but not so far away you wouldn't get to vacuum them up. The Gen5Detect sent nothing flying, though, so it pulls slightly ahead. The V16 sent only a single tiny piece flying forward. But it was right behind the Gen5Detect out of these Dyson models.

The V16 Piston Animal and the litter obstacle.

After one pass of the V16, the only litter left behind was out of the cleaner head range. It did create a thin pile of litter in front of itself as it went, which was vacuumed before moving the head back to the start point to check if any litter had been missed.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

Next, I tested these vacuums against a thing I vacuum the most off my vinyl plank floors: cat litter. For this test, since it was on a hard surface instead of a rug, I switched the vacuums' heads to the Fluffy Optic cleaner head when available. That's only on the V15, V16, and Gen5Detect, so those heads changed while the other two models still used the Digital Motorbar (V8) or the All Floor Cones (V10) heads they came with.

It's no surprise that the two standouts both had a Fluffy Optic head. The Gen5Detect left the cleanest floor behind, with not a spec of litter dust to be found from the vacuum's illuminated light after a single pass. The V16 Piston Animal mostly did well, leaving no litter behind, but it did push a small amount of litter in front of itself, similar to the sand test. This only happened in a pass of extremely thick litter, so more day-to-day litter cleanup shouldn't have this issue. Still, the Gen5Detect pulls slightly ahead once again.

The V15 is right behind these two, but left a little dust behind that I could see with the Fluffy Optic's headlight (though no large pieces, and it looked just as clean to the naked eye). Meanwhile, the V10 Konical did fine enough, but needed two passes to get all the debris. The V8 landed last after it pulled a similar move when vacuuming sand and simply pushed the litter into a pile in front of itself, so I then had to move the vacuum on top of and around to vacuum it up, and it took a few passes to do so.

The V16 Piston Animal in handheld mode with the All Floor Cones Sense cleaner head attached.

The V16 Piston Animal without the cleaner head and only the built-in crevice tool on the handheld motor.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal ($980) and Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Dyson's vacuums function nicely as a handheld vacuum, no matter the model. I tested all five models on my carpeted stairs, and I'd recommend any one of them if that's a big use in your household. The V16 and Gen5Detect pull ahead for me because you can really feel the higher suction at work when you're in handheld mode, and both vacuums showed serious results afterward of dustbins filled with new hair and dust. Especially as a cat owner and a parent of a small child, the carpeted stairs around my house have a lot of debris worked into them. Plus, both of these vacuums have built-in crevice tools you can use in handheld mode, but the V16's will always stay attached, while you need to remove the Gen5's to attach the head directly to the handheld motor.

The V15 also did a fine job, but it felt like it was gliding over my stairs rather than locking into the carpet like the other Dyson vacuums. Even the V8 and V10 with lower power levels felt more suctioned into my carpet than the V15 did for me during my handheld stair testing. Both those cheaper models fell into the runner-up range for me with this test.

The Gen5Detect on my rug.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800) and V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Originally, I tested an early release version of the V16 Piston Animal that had some clogging issues on carpet. But after getting a current release model, the V16 did much better overall. Both the V16 and the Gen5Detect did an impressive job on my carpets and rugs, and pulled an impressive amount of cat hair and dust out of my recently vacuumed carpets. These both have different heads, but the powerful suction really comes into play on carpet more than anywhere else, especially if you have pets.

Meanwhile, the V10 Konical has the All Floor Cones cleaner head that glided nicely on carpet. The V10's head was a little easier to push around than the Digital Motorbar head (which both the V8 and V15 have) on rugs. The V8 Cyclone took the most effort to push around on my rug, but moved much better on carpet.

The V15 Detect was similar, but unlike the rest of these vacuums, it has a trigger button instead of a power button. That means you have to keep that engaged the entire time when doing a longer vacuuming session. The rest of these vacuums have a power button you click instead, so I don't love the trigger for longer vacuuming sessions. If you're a big vacuumer or have a home with a large amount of carpet, you're going to want a power button, and likely one of the higher-suction vacuums.

(L to R) V10 Konical, Gen5Detect, and V16 Piston Animal.

The results, as you can tell above, are a little murky. The higher-suction vacuums usually took home the prize in most categories, but the V10 Konical was a surprisingly solid all-around performer. To find my winner, I put all of my tests and Dyson models into a chart and scored them on a 1 to 4 point scale, allowing 4 points if the vacuum did the best, 1 if the worst, and a 2 or 3 depending on how middle-of-the-road the results were. One vacuum had a nice lead with a near-perfect score of 19 points.

Dyson

Amazon

Wayfair

The biggest standout from these tests was the Gen5Detect. It came out of these tests with a near-perfect score after the five rounds of testing. It does a great job with its level of powerful suction, and it transitions well between most kinds of debris. As a pet owner, I especially like it for carpet, since the 280 air watts do a great job pulling out hair and pet dander from deep in the carpet. I've actually filled up this vacuum's debris tank before after vacuuming only a few days before with a weaker option.

It's one of the most expensive for a reason, and comes with more attachments than any other model. I do find myself regularly grabbing the Fluffy Optic head for vacuuming my hard floors, which cover many square feet of my home. If you're looking to really splurge on the best vacuum, this is still the one to get.

The only downside is compatibility with Dyson's bigger attachments, namely a mop head or docking station. It doesn't have a Submarine option like the V16 or V15, and Dyson's Auto-empty Dok won't work with this model. But if you aren't worried about add-ons, this is the vacuum to buy. It's had better sales since the launch of the new models, too.

Dyson

Amazon

Amazon (Submarine)

Dyson

Dyson (Submarine)

The V16 Piston Animal's powerful 315 air watts of suction did pretty well on almost every test. My only issue with this vacuum compared to the Gen5Detect is that it was more likely to push small debris (in my tests, both sand and litter) into a pile in front of itself if you were vacuuming a large spill. Gen5Detect did better all around, but the V16 Piston Animal stayed close behind that hiccup.

It's a powerful all-around vacuum with some nice design upgrades to make it a little easier to use. This newer model has a release below the vacuum motor to release the cleaner head without having to bend down, and built-in crevice tools to both the handheld motor and the long wand that makes up the middle of the device. There's also a compressor to help push dust out of the dustbin, and it'll be compatible with Dyson's upcoming self-emptying docking station. There's also a Submarine version ($1,100) so you can use this vacuum as a mop, too.

It has some nice quality-of-life upgrades, but it's really expensive. I'd recommend it if you know you also want to invest in the mop head and docking station; otherwise, just get the Gen5Detect.

Dyson

Dyson

Best Buy

One of the best overall performers is nearly half the price of my winners. The Dyson V10 Konical never once scored in last place, and was especially comfortable to use on carpets and rugs with the new cleaner head design. It did much better than the more expensive and powerful Gen5Detect and V15 Detect when vacuuming up sand, and I found it more comfortable to push around than the Digital Motorbar head on the V15 and V8 when it came to vacuuming a low-pile rug.

It didn't do as well on hard floors, but it didn't do poorly, either. This cheaper model comes with just the single head, but if you don't want to spend the better part of a grand, I'd rather only have this head than the Digital Motorbar head. The All Floor Cones cleaner head also has a built-in light, which you won't get on cheaper or older models. Plus, it'll be compatible with the self-emptying docking station Dyson has coming out soon. For the price point, it's a fantastic buy.

V10 Konical with the Auto-emptying Dok.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal Submarine ($1,100) and V10 Konical with Auto-empty Dok ($650)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400) and Gen5Detect ($800)

I'm putting this section after the testing because if you're just looking for a good vacuum, this might not be relevant for you. But there are some interesting upgrades with certain Dyson models you might want to consider, which might sway you toward a certain model over the testing aspects—like if you want a stick vacuum that can work with a self-emptying docking station, or one that can double as a mop. Not all of Dyson's vacuums can do these things, but some of them can—and one can do both.

Both the V16 Piston Animal and the V15 Detect have a Submarine variant (that retail for $1,100 and $750, respectively) that will give you the Submarine head along with the rest of the vacuum accessories. They have slightly different designs, but both are a wet roller head that stores both clean and dirty water while being powered by the motor in the rest of the vacuum. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved the Submarine version of the V15, and I've been really impressed by the V16's version as well.

If you hate emptying your cordless vacuum, there's an add-on for that, too. You can buy the V10 Konical now with Dyson's new Auto-emptying Dok that can hold up to 60 days of debris. It's a great add-on I've tried with other vacuums like Shark and Tineco and loved because it keeps my vacuum charged and upright, and it stores accessories as well. Dyson has mentioned launching one of these for the V16 in the future, but I'm not sure when that could come to fruition.

If I were to assign points based on these, the V16 Piston Animal ties with the Gen5Detect after getting its add-on while the Gen5Detect has none since it has neither of these additions, and once its own docking station arrives it would pull into first. The V10 Konical remains close behind. It's up to you whether these add-ons make it worth buying, or if you want to choose the models that actually performed best for what you need vacuumed most.

It’s Frighteningly Easy to Jailbreak Some Frontier AI Models

Wired July 29, 2026

I recently got to watch what happens when you jailbreak some of the world’s most powerful artificial intelligence models.

Don’t worry—this AI manipulation wasn’t used to hack anyone or build a nuclear bomb. I simply got to see firsthand how vulnerable some frontier models are to ditching their safety guardrails.

FAR. AI, an AI safety nonprofit based in California, built a tool that takes a range of problematic prompts, and generates more than a thousand different versions in an attempt to identify functioning jailbreaks. I saw some models generate a detailed plan for launching a cyberattack on an imaginary hydroelectric dam, among other things. Often, it involved trying dozens of prompts, with models rejecting many of them out of hand.

I chatted with FAR. AI in advance of a new report, which saw the group test the safety guardrails of models from four popular US companies: Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and Fable 5; OpenAI’s GPT 5.5 and 5.6; Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro; and Grok 4.3 and 4.5, from Elon Musk’s newly combined SpaceXAI. It auto-generated prompts designed to trick the models into doing potentially harmful things, like generating software exploits and providing details for developing chemical or biological weapons.

The report found that Grok was most vulnerable to jailbreaks, with 448 jailbreaks found, followed by Gemini, with 249 found, while Claude, Fable, and GPT were impervious to the attacks. However, that doesn’t mean those models are immune to more sophisticated jailbreaks, which may involve interacting with a model in more complex ways, according to FAR. AI and other experts.

The report also calculated the cost of getting models to misbehave by using another AI model to automatically generate different jailbreaks. The results are dirt cheap, all things considered—$58 to jailbreak Grok and $278 to jailbreak Gemini.

“AI models right now are less regulated than restaurants,” says Adam Gleave, the CEO of FAR. AI and an expert on AI safety and alignment.

Gleave says that the findings demonstrate the need for externally imposed standards and regulations. “Talk of relying on voluntary commitments, that AI companies are going to be able to self-regulate, is nonsense,” he says.

But Gleave also believes that the findings show that models can be systematically tested for safety. “There's an optimistic angle here,” he says. “Defense and safety really are possible.”

Rohin Shah, the director of AGI safety and alignment at Google DeepMind, says the results of the report “should not be interpreted as a comprehensive assessment of Gemini’s safety and security,” because not all jailbreaks are equally severe.

“We are constantly working to improve our safeguards,” Shah says. “We conduct extensive red teaming and evaluations across severe misuse risks and apply multiple layers of protection throughout development and deployment.”

“These findings reflect the sustained investment we've made in our safeguards,” Anthropic spokesperson Michael Aciman tells WIRED. “We continue to evolve our safety systems as these attacks become more sophisticated.”

OpenAI and SpaceXAI did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Recently passed state laws in California and New York require frontier AI developers to publish safety reports, and soon, an Illinois law will require those companies to have their safety practices evaluated by third-party auditors. But the federal government hasn’t yet passed any specific safety requirements, and chaos has ensued as the industry—and officials—try to figure it out.

In June, the Trump administration imposed export controls on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, citing national security concerns, and the company took them offline for several weeks. The White House has also asked both Anthropic and OpenAI to delay recent model releases over fears they could introduce new cybersecurity risks.

The tide might be shifting—a recent executive order calls for collaboration between the government and the private sector on related cybersecurity initiatives, and the president has hinted that light-touch regulations are in the works. But for now, preventing major catastrophes is largely up to model makers.

The potential for AI to misbehave is all too apparent after OpenAI models took it upon themselves to hack a popular code repository and other services. Meanwhile, a report from researchers at the University of Cambridge found evidence that members of Boko Haram in northeast Nigeria have used ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, and DeepSeek to plan violent attacks.

Some outsiders believe that more serious incidents are increasingly likely. “In the AI research community, there is a broad, somber expectation that we are probably months rather than years away from particularly grim incidents involving bio, cyber, or chemical misuse of a frontier AI system's capabilities,” says Stephen Casper, a computer scientist at Harvard University. “If a major misuse incident happens in the near- or medium-term future, it will almost certainly be from a system that was not deployed with state-of-the-art safeguards.”

Anka Reuel, a computer scientist at Stanford University specializing in AI policy, says the key takeaway from the FAR. AI’s report is that the safety measures employed by Anthropic and OpenAI should be the default for all models. “Some companies clearly know how to defend against at least the subset of attacks tested in this report,” Reuel says. “The question is why some companies are using them and others are not.”

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Tropical Diseases Like Dengue Fever and Chikungunya Are on the Rise in Europe

Wired July 29, 2026

In September 2024, a handful of patients showed up at the emergency room in the coastal city of Fano, Italy, with mysterious symptoms: a rash on their hands and feet, fever, nausea, and diarrhea. Doctors sent for various tests until one came back with a positive result for dengue, a viral infection spread by mosquitoes, usually in tropical regions of the world. They tested the other patients, and, sure enough, they had dengue too. The strange thing? None of the patients had recently traveled to a country where they might expect to pick up a dengue infection. The only thing they had in common was visiting a particular neighbourhood in Fano.

As climate change increases temperatures across Europe, invasive mosquitoes are spreading and introducing disease agents that Europeans would usually think about only when traveling to other continents. The Fano outbreak wasn’t the first time dengue had been detected as spreading locally in mainland Europe, but it was significantly larger than previous incidents, with 199 cases detected between mid-August and mid-October of 2024. Over the past few years, European countries have reported outbreaks of other mosquito-borne viruses such as chikungunya, a painful disease that causes joint swelling, and West Nile virus. In a heating world, so-called tropical diseases are no longer restricted to tropical regions—and researchers expect the trend to continue.

The main current culprit is the mosquito Aedes albopictus, commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito (or just the tiger mosquito, given it’s now found across all continents). Unlike many mosquito species, it bites in the daytime as well as at night. The tiger mosquito already has established populations across Europe, particularly in the south, and we can expect it to move north, says Riccardo Moretti, a senior researcher at the Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA), who has been working on tiger mosquitos for more than 20 years.

The tiger mosquito thrives between 20 and 30 degrees Celsius (68 to 86 Fahrenheit), but it can still live at around 10 Celsius (50 Fahrenheit). “This means that at the moment there are already conditions that could allow for the spread of the Asian tiger mosquito, even in England,” Moretti says. At the moment, these conditions are limited to the warmest part of the year in northern European countries. But farther south, such as in Greece, the mosquito season is elongating. Moretti says researchers have found adults buzzing around until December and reappearing already in March; they overwinter as eggs. “There is a concrete risk that in the next few years, we could have a population capable of surviving throughout the year,” Moretti says.

At the moment, cases of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe tend to occur toward the end of summer. This is when tiger mosquitoes are most prevalent, and it’s also when more people return from travel. Someone unwittingly brings back an infection that isn’t found in Europe—dengue, say—and gets bitten by a tiger mosquito. The mosquito goes on to bite other people, and the disease spreads locally. But as the weather cools, the mosquitoes get less active and cases subside. If the mosquito season lasts longer, however, more infections can occur. Ultimately, says Moretti, there’s a risk that tropical diseases like dengue could become endemic in parts of Europe, meaning the disease is always there. “It is completely different dealing with occasional cases of virus transmission, and instead dealing with a permanent status of possibility of transmission,” he says.

A difference of a couple of degrees can make a big difference. Earlier this year, a study found that the conditions required for tiger mosquitoes to transmit chikungunya were cooler than previously thought. The mosquitoes can spread the virus at just 14 degrees Celsius (57 degrees Fahrenheit) rather than 16 (61 degrees Fahrenheit), meaning outbreaks could occur in most European countries and for longer periods. “That difference of two degrees matters a lot when we are talking about global warming,” says Sandeep Tegar, an epidemiological modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, who led the study.

While warmer temperatures may generally create better conditions for mosquitoes, this isn’t the full story. Too hot—more than 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit)—and tiger mosquitoes struggle to survive. Southern France and Spain, impacted by recent heat waves and wildfires, may actually have fewer mosquitoes this year, says Frederic Bartumeus, an ecologist at the Spanish scientific research center CEAB: “It’s not been a great mosquito season in these areas, because it’s too hot and it’s too dry.”

Rain is important, as mosquitoes need standing water to breed: This is where they lay their eggs, and where the larvae and pupae develop. “If it rains too little, then there’s not sufficient breeding sites,” explains Felipe Colón González, technology lead and expert in climate and infectious diseases at the UK-based health foundation Wellcome. “But if it rains too much, then it can wash away the mosquito breeding sites.” Humidity also plays a role. Beyond mosquitoes, climate conditions can have different effects on the viruses they carry, and on the behavior of humans—an important consideration in the spread of disease. This all makes modeling patterns of mosquitoes and the diseases they spread more complex, so ongoing surveillance is critical.

It may be possible to reduce mosquito populations if they’re caught early enough. ENEA’s Moretti is part of a team that recently ran an experiment to control a tiger mosquito population in Italy by releasing more than a million male mosquitoes that were reproductively incompatible—meaning when they mate, the female lays sterile eggs. This significantly reduced the number of fertile mosquito eggs in the area. But breeding mosquitoes in a specialized biofactory was expensive. In this case, the mosquitoes were bred in Miami by Google’s Debug program and shipped to Italy.

In any case, it would be impossible to eliminate mosquitoes, Moretti says—they’re too efficient at colonizing new areas. “But what is important is to drastically reduce the risks of transmissions of tropical viruses.”

Colón González says the main test for European countries is whether public health systems can keep isolated outbreaks from becoming major crises. “A common misconception is that preparedness is mainly about predicting disease outbreaks,” he says. “In reality, preparedness is about building the system that allows the public health infrastructure to effectively react when the risks emerge.” In this regard, Europe has an advantage over some parts of the world: Reliable public health and information systems mean that, so far, cases of mosquito-transmitted diseases have remained lower than in other areas of the world with a similar climate.

As invasive mosquitoes continue to settle across the Continent, Europeans may have to get used to taking the kinds of precautions that people in tropical regions are accustomed to. In Spain, Bartumeus already has mosquito nets on his windows and regularly empties standing water, such as that left sitting in flower pots. He uses mosquito repellant and wears long trousers if he’s going to be outside in the evening. “Simple things like that, that’s the only thing you can do,” he says.

Soon, the tiger mosquito may have company. Another invasive species, Aedes aegypti, or the yellow fever mosquito, has already established populations in Cyprus and the Portuguese archipelago of Madeira. As its name would suggest, it can transmit yellow fever, but it also carries dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. Yellow fever mosquitoes can’t tolerate temperatures quite as cool as the tiger mosquito can, but it has been detected making occasional jaunts north, likely transported on cargo. Its most recent destination: a service station in Luxembourg.

X Says Australia’s Under-16 Social Media Ban Risks Interfering With Foreign Law

Wired July 29, 2026

X has a new argument against sweeping underage social media bans that would limit usage of its platform: They interfere with international law.

The social media platform, which sits within Elon Musk’s SpaceX, issued a submission to the Australian parliament published Tuesday that called for the government to drop efforts to strengthen its underage social media ban. It complained that the proposals to increase pressure on sites to demonstrate efforts to crack down on underage access are unnecessary, ill-suited, unfair, and could violate privacy rights.

X pushed back against the “highly invasive” information gathering powers the proposed amendment would allow, accusing the commissioner of having “seemingly no understanding” of how this would work for the platforms and no safeguards for confidential and commercially sensitive information. Demanding data, documents, and compliance evidence from non-Australians in other countries could cause issues “for the comity of nations,” the firm also warned.

Australia is leading a growing global movement to restrict children’s access to social media, after banning under-16-year-olds from the sites in December. In May, the country ordered X to pay a $463,000 fine for failing to comply with child safety measures. The country’s internet regulator, eSafety, first issued the fine in 2023, claiming X did not respond sufficiently to a request for information on how it was tackling the spread of online child sexual abuse content, submitted one month before Elon Musk took over Twitter, now X.

X has previously criticized the country’s “excessive” penalty regime and complained in the most recent submission that a proposal to increase penalties against individuals is “entirely unjustified and disproportionate.”

Musk has been a particularly vocal critic of Australia’s bill to make 16 the minimum age for social media. “Seems like a backdoor way to control access to the Internet by all Australians,” he wrote on X when the legislation was announced in late 2024. When Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez announced similar measures in February of this year, Musk called him a “tyrant” and “true fascist totalitarian.”

While many digital rights campaigners believe blanket age bans on social media are “problematic,” the information-gathering powers are not the issue, says Stefania Di Stefano, a researcher in international law and technologies.

“For me, the complete ban from social media on children and minors is problematic from an international human rights perspective,” says Di Stefano. “It is disproportionate with respect to the right of children to exercise their right to freedom of expression, their right to access information, their right to association, and so on and so forth.”

But Julia Hörnle, a professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, is skeptical about X’s submission. “A regulator in Australia ordering X to disclose a document in relation to their business activities in Australia, that’s perfectly fine,” she tells WIRED. “From all the data in the possession of the social media company, they can distinguish between Australian and non-Australian children, and therefore keep regulation to Australia.”

The Best Festival Gear

Wired July 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The best festival gear, of course, depends on which festival you’re attending, the weather, your sleeping arrangements, and a ton of other factors. But as a longtime festival veteran, I’ve field-tested enough gear (and made enough mistakes) to have solid recommendations for preventing blisters, dehydration, a dead phone, and other common pitfalls in most situations. You'll find my top picks below.

Be sure to check out our other related buying guides, including the Best Tents, the Best Sleeping Bags, and the Best Bluetooth Speakers.

Updated July 2026: I've reformatted this guide with refreshed picks and a new look. I've also checked prices and accuracy throughout.

These electrolytes are my favorite in general, and I especially like them for festivals because the ingredient concentrations are high enough that they actually help with efficient hydration when you're hot and sweaty. And the flavors are tasty, too, so I can pass them out to my crew and know they’ll actually drink them. Hydration is of utmost importance when it comes to preventing hangovers and “wook flu,” and this mixture can help. Plus, the packets don’t take up much space in your bag or pocket.

Rumpl

I have yet to try a blanket from Rumpl that I dislike. They pack up and unfurl easily, and most of them have enough space for seating multiple people. They also have little hooks to convert the blanket into a cape, which is nice if it gets chilly at camp but you aren’t ready to go to bed yet. They’re also easy to clean, whether they’re covered in dust or grass blades or spilled White Claw.

For just one or two people, this smaller blanket is perfect. It’s thin, so it’s best for summer or as an added layer.

Anker

I’m not sure what it is about festivals that seems to make my phone die twice as fast, but it’s practically a law of the universe at this point. (It’s likely that the lack of cell service means my phone is constantly searching for a signal; read our tips on how to save battery life here.) Or maybe it's just overheating in my backpack. In any case, a power-bank phone charger with a large capacity is really handy. This Anker power bank isn’t the slimmest or the lightest, but it charges up quickly and can rapidly top off multiple devices per charge. Added bonus: You won’t be overpaying for the luxury of a charging locker. I bring two of these to four-day festivals and they keep my phone, speaker, Apple Watch, and other essentials charged the whole time. You might also want a MagSafe power bank around as a backup, though I prefer the efficiency of a larger brick.

Totem Labs

Totem Labs

The Totem Compass was designed with festivals in mind. It uses satellites and its own proprietary mesh network to let you find your friends without any cell service or Wi-Fi. No more manually time-stamping your text messages or waving your phone around in the air trying to get a signal. Once these trackers are set up, you'll be able to navigate to your friend group with ease, just by looking down and walking toward their corresponding light color. Setup is a little tricky, and the battery life could be longer. You'll also need a way to charge them overnight for a multiday camping festival (the power bank I recommended above is an option). But they worked reliably for my pals and I to hunt each other down, and I felt safer going to stages by myself with another layer of security. And yes, they look cool while you're dancing, which certainly isn’t a detractor.

I like how the case flips open, so I'm not jostling to unscrew a metal case in a crowd.

Chillbo

This inflatable couch is clutch if you don’t mind toting around a carrying case. These days, I keep my on-person carry pretty minimal, so I prefer to only use one if I have a wagon where I can chuck it when not in use. Fully inflated, it can support one to three people (provided everyone’s alright with getting cozy). When there's limited seating, or you’re on day three with two more days to go, an inflatable couch can provide respite with little effort. I also like that it comes in a ton of fun colors. Just make sure you’re aware of your surroundings—if you’re at a music festival, it’s bad manners to set up a couch in the middle of the crowd. Consider chilling back by the sound booths instead.

Pro tip: A folding hand fan makes inflation super easy if you don’t want to run around to fill the couch with air (yes, that’s really how you inflate it). It’s also cheaper to buy one of these ahead of time than from a vendor at the festival.

Solbari

Solbari

This soft sun hat is easy to pack and bring along, since it folds up, but it still retains its shape to protect your head. It's a nice large size to keep your scalp, forehead, and neck protected without feeling too suffocating or providing too much coverage to be cute. It’s reversible, too; I like flipping between brown and beige depending on how sunny it is outside and which one matches my outfit better. —Nena Farrell

Vacation

Amazon

If you prefer lotion sunscreen, I like everything I’ve tried from Vacation, and this big jug is the perfect size to keep at camp. It contains enough product for me and my friends, and it absorbs quickly without feeling greasy or sticky.

Epic Water Filters

Amazon

Epic

Bring a water bottle if you can. Nalgene's light weight and wide mouth make this a favorite.

JBL

Best Buy

Amazon

Walmart

JBL

Most festivals have limits on speaker size, but this top pick still packs a punch and is nice and portable.

Soundcore by Anker

Amazon

If your fest doesn't have a size limit, this loud speaker is incredible. But make sure to double-check the rules before packing.

Frogg Toggs

Amazon

Getting caught in the rain is less stressful with this packable poncho. I like it way more than the clear disposable ones.

Kandi-making kits: Trading beaded bracelets is a hallmark of the electronic music scene, but thanks to the Taylor Swift Eras tour, fans of more music genres are joining in. Any beads will work, but I highly recommend Stretch Magic elastic—the cheap stuff falls apart way too easily.

Flow props: Some dancers like to use flow toys, as you’ll quickly see on the fringes of any festival crowd. I’m partial to the Fiberflies Pixel Whip, but the Flowtoys PodPoi are another popular choice. You can even get levitating wands and light-up staffs. These are super fun to dance with (and they’ll entertain your fellow attendees). Consider finding a Flow Jam in your area to try a few out before investing in your own.

Little gifts: Tiny ducks. Sprouts for your hair. Squishy animals. Festivals often have a culture of gift-giving. It’s not expected, but it can be nice to have something to pass out to the folks you meet. Consider bringing some trinkets with you—you might even make a new friend or seven. Even better if they're thrifted or repurposed.

Fun clothes: When it comes to festival clothing, you can be as bold or as practical as you’d like. Don’t sacrifice comfort in the name of fashion, but if you’re looking for fun clothes to wear, I recommend checking out IHeartRaves and Rave Wonderland. These are EDM-adjacent, but they’ll work for everything from Bonnaroo to Burning Man to EDC. Your favorite artists’ merch is probably a good starting point, too. And when in doubt, you can always accessorize—consider a bucket hat or a Pashmina-style shawl to make your outfit a little more adventurous.

How Does WIRED Test Festival Gear?

I test this gear at festivals by using it the same exact way you would. Speaker recommendations are tested with EDM Soundcloud mixes; earplugs are tested in front of Funktion Ones and Danley rigs; outdoor blankets are tested at silent discos and in dusty fields. I also solicit the opinions of my friends both old and new when testing gear. Most of the items in this guide have been tested at at least three fests.

Why I Know What I'm Talking About

I’ve been attending live music events since I was a teenager and have been to festivals all around the country, including heavy hitters such as Lost Lands and Electric Forest as well as smaller festivals that are still gatekept and require “roughing it.” I've experienced camping, car camping, glamping, and hotel and Airbnb stays. I haven't traveled internationally for a fest yet, but otherwise, I’ve probably experienced every situation you can think of, including severe weather and days-long security delays.

On Harm Reduction

Regardless of your personal habits, drug use can be prevalent at festivals. It's important to know the location of medical tents, pay attention to your surroundings, and look out for your fellow festival attendees the way you'd want them to look out for you.

I highly recommend getting trained in administering naloxone (Narcan). It prevents opioid overdose, and it’s cheap and easy to obtain along with training on how to use it. I took training through EndOverdose online. It took half an hour and cost $5. I liken it to knowing CPR or choking rescue; you hope you never have to use it, but it’s really good to have the knowledge just in case.

I also recommend looking into drug testing kits. You can obtain these from The Bunk Police and DanceSafe. Fentanyl testing strips are affordable, and it takes little time to test any substances that may be around. Some festivals have vendor tents that will test substances with amnesty. It doesn't hurt to be prepared.

Finally, I recommend signing up for alerts from BunkBot when applicable. It's an emergency alert system that texts folks if dangerous substances are found. It adds another layer of harm reduction and helps you be extra aware when needed.

The 15 Best Pool Accessories to Upgrade Your Summer

Wired July 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Pools are hard. This is not news to anyone who owns one, but the uninitiated may not know about the inordinate amount of daily labor and chores that lie behind a pool’s clear, sparkling, perfectly chlorinated (or salted) water.

Luckily, pool tech has come a long way in the past decade—gone are the hours spent scooping leaves and dead bugs out of the water with a long-handled net, laboring over pH strips, and trying to relax on floaties too small for your adult-sized behind. We've now got robots that clean your pool, apps that monitor water quality from your phone, and even a slushie machine for proper pool-party margs.

With gas and plane ticket prices soaring to astronomical levels, there's never been a better time for a staycation at your own pool. (If you don't have a pool of your own, you can always rent one nearby on Swimply.) My colleague Christopher Null has a 12- by 36-foot, L-shaped, in-ground pool lined with PebbleTec, and I have a 20- by 12-foot above-ground pool lined with vinyl. Between the two of us, we have pretty much tried it all, so whether you've got a custom-built in-ground complex or an Intex pop-up from Walmart, these time- and life-tested swimming pool accessories are sure to level up your backyard pool game.

For more yard-tech tips, check out our guides to the Best Pool Cleaning Robots, Best Smart Sprinklers and Irrigation Systems, Best Robot Lawn Mowers, and Best Smart Bird Feeders.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added a sun hat, a wave machine, a pool thermometer, a whimsical speaker, and a water bottle. I also ensured up-to-date links and prices. Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

iGarden

Amazon

iGarden

What, you’re still swimming in a still-water pool? Get with the ’20s and add an artificial wave machine that uses jets of water to create a strong current that you can swim against.

iGarden’s Swim Jet X (also available in a few cheaper, lower-power versions) is a massive pump that clips onto the edge of your pool deck, cycling up to 1,100 gallons of water per minute through its 31-pound chassis, creating its powerful stream. At higher settings, this current is downright extreme, able to blast an unprepared swimmer halfway across the pool. The result is a very effective way to exercise without swimming long laps in a traditional lap pool. And if the kids just want to splash around a bit for fun, you can lower the Swim Jet’s intensity level to create a lighter, surface-level disturbance.

The Swim Jet isn’t perfect, though. The workouts are challenging and also adjustable, thanks to the machine’s six power modes. Even so, swimming in place may not provide quite as vigorous an exercise session as traditional laps. Battery life is another consideration: You’ll get 10 hours of running time on the slowest, lowest setting, but its efficiency plummets as you ratchet up the output. On the higher power modes, the system is good for about two hours of wave-blasting operation.

It’s also very expensive, with the top-tier version running $4,320 at some sellers. That’s astronomical in price, but what pool product isn’t? And compared to the cost of a membership at a gym that has a pool, it might make more sense than it seems.

Lifebuoy

Amazon

Walmart

If you (or your neighbors) have small children, investing in a pool alarm may very well be an invaluable insurance policy. Lifebuoy’s Bcone is the blue-chip alarm option on the market right now. It’s a bright red, double-ended cone that floats in your pool (or hot tub) and sounds a siren if something ends up in the water that isn’t supposed to be there.

The system works by detecting disturbances to the water’s surface, analyzing wave patterns to distinguish between the splash of a person (or pet) falling in and ripples caused by the wind. If the Bcone detects an event, it fires off its internal Klaxon and relays the alarm to a Wi-Fi bridge that remains inside the home (plus the Bcone app). The bridge and app both let you easily disable the alarm when people are swimming—and can even turn the system back on automatically when the water is clear, so “I forgot” doesn’t become a deadly excuse. —Christopher Null

Though I personally have an older Arlo model, I agree that the brand makes the most consistently user-friendly security cameras on the market right now. Recorded footage of your pool is another important investment in safety and potential liability, especially if you have children or curious animals living nearby. A camera can also function as a tool to help proactively spot potential issues while you're away from home, such as the water level, cleaning-equipment functionality, and cover positioning.

It's not cheap, but if you have a large pool that doesn't have an in-wall skimming system, a robotic skimmer is a must-have, and this is the pool-cleaning robot reviewer Christopher Null likes best. It's solar-powered, so you never have to take it out to charge, and it's got sensors that help it avoid damaging itself by running into your pool walls. Read the full rundown in our guide to the Best Pool Cleaning Robots.

Iopool

Cleaning out debris is only one part of regular pool maintenance. Equally important, if not more so, is keeping chemicals in balance. If things get out of whack for even a few days, you can be left with a green, algae-ridden mess that is a major challenge to remedy. Test strips and kits have long been standard, but they're a hassle to use and only give you a snapshot of your pool’s chemistry at a specific moment in time. Smart technology offers a much more elegant solution; it lets you keep tabs on chemistry in real time and alerts you if something’s amiss. Of the handful of smart-pool chemistry monitors I’ve tested, I like Iopool’s Eco Start the best.

This floating gadget monitors temperature, pH, and ORP (a stand-in for free chlorine), together giving you a solid picture of your pool’s disinfection capabilities. It automatically updates every 15 minutes. While many chemistry monitors require replaceable supplies (which is a costly approach) and regular battery replacements to work, Iopool’s solution is solid-state, needing no maintenance at all except for storing it out of the pool in winter months. I used mine for two full swimming seasons until it died (at which point it must be replaced)—and I like it so much I just dropped its successor into the water for the summer. —Christopher Null

Notice you tend to burn faster when you’re in the pool than hiking or performing activities on land? It’s not your imagination—water acts as a mirror, reflecting a portion of the sun’s UV rays. This means every time you’re in the water or even just hanging out nearby, your UV exposure is compounded from both direct sunlight and the water around you. A wide-brimmed hat can help protect a larger skin surface area, and this one from Solbari sports UPF 50+ nylon-and-cotton fabric as well as a brim that’s larger than typical hats of this style—5 inches in the front and 6 in the back. I tested this hat in the pool on days pushing 100 degrees Fahrenheit, and not only did I not get burned, but I also found the hat itself didn’t feel very hot, especially if I flipped the color side (it comes in navy, pink, ice blue, or green) to the cream side.

First Drive: Ferrari Luce

Wired July 29, 2026

Some still believe that you can’t manage a car company unless you’re a fully paid-up “car guy.” Tell that to Benedetto Vigna, Ferrari’s CEO. He’s a physicist by education, hired to run the company in 2021 after a career in semiconductors, although he did significant business with automotive during that time.

Vigna also helped develop a three-dimensional motion sensor first used in airbags, later adapted for the Nintendo Wii and the iPhone’s screen rotation function. An inventor, then. “I prefer innovator,” he once told me. “A lot of the time inventors are just thinking, but innovators conceive new things and make them happen.”

This is all useful background to the Luce, Ferrari’s first fully electric car, engineered in Maranello, Italy, but designed in California by LoveFrom, the agency set up by renowned iPhone designer Jony Ive. It’s not Apple’s abandoned car, reskinned and rebooted for the world’s most famous automotive name, but more the product of a union between like-minded innovators—Italian spirit and attitude, Silicon Valley lateral thinking.

But unless you’ve been hiding under a rock on Mars with Elon Musk these past few months, you’ll also know that the result didn’t land the way its creators would have anticipated. Ferrari’s immense global fan base is seemingly not on board with the idea of an electric car on a point of principle. And hiring Ive and his team to reimagine the aesthetic has proven as welcome as Kryptonite is to Superman.

Part of the frequently obnoxious discourse around the Luce centered around the idea that a Ferrari’s design should deliver an instant dopamine rush. These aren’t cars that require a PhD in design to understand; they’re meant to hit hard and fast, seeding desire the moment you see them. The Luce spectacularly breaks from tradition, and without the famous Prancing Horse badge, there’s little here that yokes it to perhaps the most revered automotive back catalog of all. But that was all part of the brief: Do something different.

The driving experience amplifies this feeling. The Luce is a Ferrari, just not the sort we’re used to. “In the past 100 years, technology has changed for sure,” Raffaele de Simone, Ferrari’s chief test driver, tells me. “But what hasn’t changed is our bodies. We have two hands, two eyes and ears, and two feet. The interface is the same—steering, brakes and throttle—but the Luce has a different sort of driving emotion and a different way of announcing driving thrills.”

WIRED drove a preproduction model of the Luce before the May reveal in Rome, which is why there's a camo wrap hiding the design.

I was at a test track in northern Italy in May to find out how successfully that’s been achieved. I was in a preproduction car, still disguised at the time of driving because it pre-dates the car’s reveal in Rome. First impressions? The Luce’s cab-forward proportions mean you sit closer to the front axle than usual, and higher because there’s a large battery pack beneath the cabin. It’s clearly not low-slung or sporty.

You can’t help but take in that interior, clearly Apple-inspired but positing a whole new approach to territory that has seen an entire generation of new cars lose sight of first principles. The three-spoke wheel’s design is inspired by a classic Ferrari’s, and it feels fantastic. The air vents pivot with a deeply engineered precision. Even the seat runners are elegant. The space in the rear is almost limo-like.

One of Ive’s superpowers is being able to detect the level of care invested in a product's design, and whether you like the Luce’s aesthetic or not, that’s indisputable. But he rejects the concept of a touchscreen inside a car, choosing instead to elevate haptic feel and the clarity of the dials to a level previously unseen in the automotive context. Ive is all about input and output. The Luce is a special place to be.

The Ferrari Luce's interior.

There’s a slickness to the first driving impressions, too. Ferraris have become less highly strung over the years, with greater emphasis now placed on daily usability. As befits its four-door, five-seat layout, the Luce is arguably the most accessible Ferrari in the company’s near-80-year history. Its major controls—the throttle and brake pedal—are beautifully calibrated, so it moves away effortlessly with an impressively and perhaps unexpectedly light touch. On some classic Ferraris, you have to let the gearbox oil warm thoroughly before going anywhere. This is not an issue on the Luce, despite its complex electronic drive units.

The structure is all new. The chassis consists of hollow castings, extrusions and aluminum sheets, to reduce weight and optimize load paths. The 800-volt battery architecture is integrated into the chassis, positioned as low in the Luce’s floorpan as the engineers could achieve. So it has a center of gravity that’s 95 mm lower than the Purosangue, Ferrari’s quasi-SUV, and a yaw moment of inertia 15 percent less than that car. That means it’s more agile and changes direction more keenly.

That’s physics in play. Ferrari’s commitment to technology is greater than ever, and the Luce deploys everything it knows to manage those external forces. It enjoys unprecedented control of each wheel in all three axes (lateral, longitudinal, and vertical), with particular emphasis on lateral body dynamics. A new “vehicle control unit” oversees power delivery and energy recovery, and updates target metrics 200 times per second. As with all high-end electric vehicles, the Luce’s master controller has a lot to do.

The Ferrari Luce’s steering wheel and center console.

The electric Ferrari has a 122-kWh battery and four e-motors, two on each axle, and optimum weight distribution. The front motors deliver 282 brake horsepower (bhp), the rears 831 bhp, so the total output is north of 1,000 bhp. And there’s mammoth torque: 5,900 pound-feet (around 8,000 Newton-meters) at the rear wheels, a crazy amount of force.

The front motors can spin at up to 30,000 revolutions per minute and can go from nothing to maximum in less than a second. The chassis and body consist of 75 percent recycled aluminum. There’s also a separate rear subframe for the first time on a Ferrari; it’s connected to the rest of the chassis by elastomeric bushes—polymers with a high viscosity—which helps reduce noise and vibration.

A new “e-manettino” dial on the lower left of the steering wheel joins the existing one on the right, a staple of all Ferraris since its arrival in 2004’s F430 model. The new addition has three settings that govern power and traction, as well as the shape of the torque curve. In Range mode, power is limited to 429 bhp, and the car is predominantly rear-drive. Select Tour, and the driver has 608 bhp to enjoy, with all-wheel drive capability. In the Performance setting, that rises to 958 bhp, and the top speed is raised to a maximum of 190 mph.

Engineering this sort of bandwidth into an EV is nothing new. However, the application here is more emotionally charged: Ferrari has an obligation to organize the possibilities as entertainingly as possible. How else will it be able to silence that fan base seemingly intent on shunning the concept of an electric Ferrari?

“What excites me is that we have more tools available than ever before to give the driver exactly what they’re asking from the car,” de Simone tells me. “Let’s say you’re entering a corner and suddenly the radius tightens. Instantly the driver is asking the car for a little more rotation. In that moment, rear-wheel steering, active suspension, and torque vectoring from the four motors are all working together to help achieve that response. What’s interesting is that you don’t necessarily feel the individual systems at work. What you feel is confidence.”

Because it can vector torque on both axles, the Luce’s dynamic behavior plays out in hi-def widescreen. The front end is positive without being overly sensitive; it remains neutral throughout the middle phase of the corner and has incredible traction on the exit. Ferrari long ago mastered the chassis hardware, but it's a software leader now, too; its Side Slip Control system reaches v10 in the Luce, and its traction control has evolved to suit the car’s quad-motor configuration. Select Performance mode and switch the other manettino to “CT off” (traction control off), and the Luce gets distinctly more playful. It’s doubtful that many owners will ever drift their $600,000 electric Ferrari, but it can certainly do it.

Like all engineers, Ferrari’s people love graphs and charts and will happily share what they deem is proof that the 4,982-pound Luce feels significantly less than that. Subjectively, it has the alertness and willingness to change direction of a much lighter car, but given that it’s five meters long and two meters wide, you still need space to explore these limits.

The rear seats of the Ferrari Luce.

Further interactivity (and graphs) arrive in the form of the Luce’s Torque Shift Engagement. This is Ferrari’s answer to one of the issues with EVs: the rather one-dimensional way that they deliver their energy. Pull the right paddle on the steering column and you get five power and torque levels; the left one delivers five grades of regenerative engine braking, with incremental illumination within the instrument display so you can keep track of the deployment.

The Luce plays with the torque curve so that you feel like you’re fully in command during cornering entry and exit rather than simply riding a huge wave of torque. In essence, it’s designed to conjure the sensation you feel driving a car with a conventional transmission and engine braking. The amount of energy corresponds with the available grip and the nature of the corner itself. It’s a step up from the synthesized gearbox in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N and the e-shift option available in the latest Porsche Taycan, as good as they are.

The Luce’s dynamic bandwidth extends to its ride quality, even on 23- and 24-inch wheels, and on the gnarliest surfaces. It’s fitted with the third generation of Ferrari’s 48-volt active suspension and controls its mass very adroitly without ever becoming floaty.

Finally, there’s the way it sounds. Largely silent, barring some mild wind and tire noise, the Luce finds its voice in Performance mode. There’s something of the harmonic rasp of a six-cylinder to it, and it’s not quite as rumbly as a V-8, never mind a V-12. But it’s real and musical—more Kraftwerk-adjacent than Pavarotti, perhaps—and has been achieved by using an accelerometer and by equalizing naturally occurring frequencies on the rear inverter.

“You can think about it like a musical instrument. It has its own timbre,” says Antonio Palermo, who led this part of the Luce’s development team. “We need to take away the annoying noise, because there’s no point amplifying gear whine, for example. But there are lots of other beautiful frequencies we can work with and let out. We talk about orchestras when it comes to ICE. Well, there’s a different type of orchestra inside this machine, too.”

The Luce clearly repositions and reimagines the very idea of what a Ferrari could be. For most people, that’s a romantic notion likely steeped in dreams of Italy at its most seductive, or a wailing combustion engine closing in on an 8,500-rpm redline. Hence the fallout. The Luce is on a different path, and it demands an alternative response. But in terms of how it drives, there’s no question it’s authentically Ferrari. We can’t wait to drive it again.

Smart Gifts for Travelers Who Live Out of a Suitcase

Wired July 29, 2026

July

Solbari

Amazon

Nordstrom

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Gifts for travelers should focus on ease and peace of mind. Even the most seasoned globetrotter can find traveling stressful. Between packing, navigating overcrowded terminals, and living out of a suitcase, it can be overwhelming. Most jet-setters have their travel routine down to a science, but the perfect gift can enhance any experience, whether it's a three-day business retreat or a two-week adventure across Europe.

We’ve put together a list of essentials and luxurious gifts for travelers, from noise-canceling headphones to a weekend bag that carries it all. Be sure to check out our other gift guides as well, including the Best Gifts for Women, Gifts for Coworkers, and Best Stocking Stuffers.
